sci_closure_g4exp_001.stem: What is a simple hypothesis in an investigation?
options: A testable guess about what will happen
The final result that can never change
Deleting all the data
A drawing with no measuring
sci_closure_g4exp_001.explanation: A hypothesis is a guess you can check with an experiment.
theoryLines: A hypothesis guides the plan.
Results may support or reject it.

sci_closure_g4exp_002.stem: Which statement correctly describes the recording step?
options: Writing down observations and measurements during the investigation
Erasing evidence so nobody can check
Choosing a result before collecting data
Skipping notes because memory is enough
sci_closure_g4exp_002.explanation: Recording keeps a clear trail of what happened in the investigation.
theoryLines: Good notes support analysis later.
Science depends on evidence you can review.

sci_closure_g4es_003.stem: What describes day and night in one place?
options: Earth’s rotation makes the Sun appear to rise and set
The Sun turns off each night like a lamp switch
Night happens only when it rains
Day and night never change
sci_closure_g4es_003.explanation: As Earth turns, places move into sunlight and then into shadow.
theoryLines: One full rotation is about one day.
Day and night are a repeating cycle.

sci_closure_g4es_004.stem: What is an example of a weather observation?
options: Recording the temperature in a journal
Guessing without looking
Ignoring the clouds
Counting only vacation days
sci_closure_g4es_004.explanation: Weather observations are measurements or notes about conditions outside, such as temperature.
theoryLines: Observation is a basic science skill.
Written records make weather patterns easier to compare.

sci_closure_g4env_005.stem: What is a simple link between a plant and water?
options: A plant needs water to grow
A plant never touches water
Water only gets in the way
There is usually no link
sci_closure_g4env_005.explanation: Plants take in water to grow and stay healthy.
theoryLines: Roots help plants get water from soil.
Without water, most plants wilt.

sci_closure_g4env_006.stem: What is an example of a difference between living and nonliving things?
options: A cat breathes and moves
A rock jumps by itself
Water never moves
There is no difference
sci_closure_g4env_006.explanation: Living things can grow, move, and respond; nonliving things like rocks do not live.
theoryLines: Breathing and movement are signs of life in many animals.
Sorting living and nonliving things is a basic science skill.

sci_closure_g5an_007.stem: What is a reasonable result when a habitat changes?
options: A population may drop if it can no longer find what it needs
It always grows without limit
Habitat change usually has no effect
All animals become identical
sci_closure_g5an_007.explanation: When a habitat changes, some species may lose food, shelter, or space.
theoryLines: Habitats supply what living things need to survive.
Population size can change when conditions change.

sci_closure_g5an_008.stem: How are adaptation and survival connected?
options: A helpful adaptation can improve survival chances
There is no connection
Survival depends only on luck
All animals are equally adapted in every place
sci_closure_g5an_008.explanation: Traits that fit an environment can help an animal survive and reproduce.
theoryLines: Adaptations match living things to their surroundings.
Better fit often means better survival.

sci_closure_g5ex_009.stem: In a simple experiment, what is a well-chosen variable to change?
options: One factor you change on purpose
Everything at once
Usually no variable at all
Only the color of someone’s pants
sci_closure_g5ex_009.explanation: A fair test usually changes one planned factor while keeping other conditions steady.
theoryLines: The independent variable is what you change.
Controlling other conditions makes results clearer.

sci_closure_g5ex_010.stem: Why do scientists sometimes repeat an experiment?
options: To check that the result is consistent
To ban experiments
To cancel measurements
Usually to shorten time
sci_closure_g5ex_010.explanation: Repeating a test helps confirm that a result was not a one-time accident.
theoryLines: Consistent results build confidence.
Repeats can reveal mistakes.

sci_closure_g5es_011.stem: What is a basic description of a season?
options: A period with a typical weather pattern
Usually only one day
Usually only room temperature
Always identical every year with no variation
sci_closure_g5es_011.explanation: Seasons are parts of the year with characteristic weather patterns.
theoryLines: Climate describes long-term seasonal patterns.
Weather on one day can still vary within a season.

sci_closure_g5es_012.stem: What is an example of a sedimentary rock?
options: A rock formed from piled-up sediments that harden
Only liquid ice
Usually natural plastic
Usually a solid cloud
sci_closure_g5es_012.explanation: Sedimentary rocks form when layers of sediment build up and harden over time.
theoryLines: Sandstone and limestone are common sedimentary rocks.
Sediments can come from worn rock, shells, or other materials.

sci_closure_g5env_013.stem: What is a basic example of recycling?
options: Collecting bottles for recycling
Burning trash with no sorting
Throwing everything in the same bin
Never sorting materials
sci_closure_g5env_013.explanation: Recycling means collecting used materials so they can be made into new products.
theoryLines: Sorting materials helps recycling work.
Recycling can save resources and reduce landfill waste.

sci_closure_g5env_014.stem: How are plants connected to the air?
options: Plants take in and give off gases as they make food and grow
There is usually no connection
Plants never exchange gases
Only animals need air
sci_closure_g5env_014.explanation: Plants exchange gases with air during photosynthesis and respiration.
theoryLines: Plants take in carbon dioxide when they make food in light.
Living things share Earth’s air.

sci_closure_g6bd_015.stem: What is a correct link between pulse and activity?
options: Physical activity can raise the pulse rate
Pulse never changes
Activity always drops the pulse to zero
Pulse has no link to the heart
sci_closure_g6bd_015.explanation: During exercise the heart often beats faster to send more blood to muscles.
theoryLines: Pulse is a way to feel heartbeats.
The body raises heart rate when muscles need more oxygen.

sci_closure_g6bd_016.stem: What is a simple job of blood vessels?
options: Carry blood to organs
Make oxygen from air
Digest food directly
Hear sounds
sci_closure_g6bd_016.explanation: Blood vessels are tubes that carry blood around the body.
theoryLines: Arteries, veins, and capillaries are kinds of blood vessels.
Blood delivers oxygen and nutrients to organs.

sci_closure_g6es_017.stem: How do inner planets often differ from outer planets in the solar system?
options: Inner planets are relatively smaller and often rocky
They are usually all the same
Outer planets are always smaller than inner ones
There is usually no difference at all
sci_closure_g6es_017.explanation: The inner planets are generally smaller and rockier; many outer planets are larger gas giants.
theoryLines: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are the inner planets.
Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are the outer planets.

sci_closure_g6es_018.stem: What is an example of the day–night cycle?
options: Earth’s rotation brings a place into sunlight and then into shadow
Only seasons, with no day and night
Night without any sky objects
Day with no light at all
sci_closure_g6es_018.explanation: Day and night happen because Earth rotates, so sunlight reaches different places over time.
theoryLines: One full rotation takes about 24 hours.
The side facing the Sun has day; the other side has night.

sci_closure_g6env_019.stem: What is a reasonable health effect of air pollution?
options: Breathing trouble for sensitive people
Always the exact same result for everyone
No scientific effect
Effects only on plants
sci_closure_g6env_019.explanation: Dirty air can make breathing harder, especially for people with sensitive lungs.
theoryLines: Air quality affects human health.
Reducing pollution helps communities.

sci_closure_g6env_020.stem: What is a classroom-level example of global warming?
options: A long-term rise in average temperature
Usually just one hot day
Ordinary daily weather change alone
Usually only extreme cold
sci_closure_g6env_020.explanation: Global warming refers to a lasting rise in Earth’s average temperature, not one warm afternoon.
theoryLines: Climate is a long-term pattern; weather is short-term.
Average temperature trends need many years of data.

sci_closure_g3bd_021.stem: What is a logical sequence for how the body responds to heat?
options: Sense the heat → then respond (for example by sweating or moving to shade)
Cool down with no sensing at all
Usually no response
Only a pulse change with no link to heat
sci_closure_g3bd_021.explanation: The body senses heat and then responds to help cool down or stay safe.
theoryLines: Sense organs and nerves detect temperature changes.
Sweating and seeking shade are common heat responses.

sci_closure_g3an_022.stem: What is a careful hypothesis about animal behavior in winter?
options: Some animals may seek shelter or store energy, depending on the species
All animals usually disappear
Behavior usually never changes
Every animal hibernates in the exact same way
sci_closure_g3an_022.explanation: Different species use different winter strategies, such as migrating, resting more, or storing food.
theoryLines: A hypothesis is a testable idea.
Winter conditions can change animal behavior.

sci_closure_g3mat_023.stem: What is a simple difference between metal and plastic in kitchen pots?
options: Metal usually conducts heat better
Plastic always conducts better
There is usually no difference
Both are identical insulators
sci_closure_g3mat_023.explanation: Metal cookware often heats food quickly because metal conducts heat well.
theoryLines: Conductors transfer heat more easily than many plastics.
Material choice depends on the job.

sci_closure_g3mat_024.stem: What is a simple difference between a physical change and a chemical change?
options: A chemical change makes a new substance
There is usually no difference
A physical change always makes a new substance
A chemical change never changes properties
sci_closure_g3mat_024.explanation: Physical changes alter form or state; chemical changes make new materials.
theoryLines: Melting ice is a physical change.
Burning paper is a chemical change.

sci_closure_g3ex_025.stem: What is true about measuring with units?
options: Compare numbers only in the same units, or convert first
You can mix centimeters and liters with no conversion
Units usually do not matter
Only drawing matters
sci_closure_g3ex_025.explanation: Measurements need matching units before you compare or add them.
theoryLines: Units tell what a number means.
Converting keeps comparisons fair.

sci_closure_g3es_026.stem: What is a simple description of a cloud?
options: Tiny water droplets or ice crystals floating in the air
Always an acid gas
Only one solid material
Usually no material at all
sci_closure_g3es_026.explanation: Clouds are made of many tiny water droplets or ice crystals in the air.
theoryLines: Water vapor can cool and form cloud droplets.
Clouds are part of the water cycle.

sci_closure_g3es_027.stem: What is a reasonable link between wind and local sea level at a shore?
options: Strong wind can push water toward or away from the coast
There is usually no link
Wind always flattens waves to zero
Usually only darkness affects the water
sci_closure_g3es_027.explanation: Wind can pile water up along a shore or push it away, changing local water height.
theoryLines: Wind transfers energy to the water surface.
Storms can raise water levels along coasts.

sci_closure_g3env_028.stem: What is an example of a plant as a basic food producer?
options: A fruit tree that makes fruit people can eat
A rock that usually makes fruit
A cloud that usually makes fruit
Plastic that makes fruit
sci_closure_g3env_028.explanation: Plants produce food that people and animals can use.
theoryLines: Producers make food using sunlight.
Fruit trees are plant producers people rely on.

sci_closure_g3env_029.stem: How can trash relate to garden soil?
options: The wrong trash can pollute or harm garden soil
Trash always improves soil with no checking
There is usually no link
Usually only air is affected
sci_closure_g3env_029.explanation: Litter and unsafe waste can dirty soil and hurt plants or animals.
theoryLines: Healthy soil supports plant growth.
Sorting and disposing of waste carefully protects gardens.

sci_closure_g4bd_030.stem: What is a basic explanation of pulmonary circulation?
options: Blood goes to the lungs to pick up oxygen and then returns to the heart
Blood usually never goes through the lungs
Lungs make brand-new blood
The heart usually has no link to the lungs
sci_closure_g4bd_030.explanation: In pulmonary circulation, blood travels between the heart and lungs for gas exchange.
theoryLines: Lungs add oxygen to blood and remove carbon dioxide.
The heart pumps blood to the lungs and then to the body.

sci_closure_g4mat_031.stem: What is an example of a physical change that happens to water?
options: Freezing or evaporating under the right conditions
Water always turning into a new kind of rock
Water never changing at all
Always a chemical reaction
sci_closure_g4mat_031.explanation: Freezing, melting, and evaporating change water’s state but keep it as water.
theoryLines: State changes are often physical changes.
Ice, liquid water, and vapor are the same substance.

sci_closure_g5bd_032.stem: Which statement correctly describes protecting skin from the Sun?
options: Clothing and shade can reduce risk
Protection is usually unnecessary
Sunlight never affects skin
Usually only water protects skin
sci_closure_g5bd_032.explanation: Covering up and staying in shade help protect skin from strong sunlight.
theoryLines: Too much sun can harm skin.
Shade, clothes, and sunscreen are common protections.

sci_closure_g5mat_033.stem: What is the difference between a conductor and an insulator in class?
options: A conductor lets electric current pass more easily
An insulator always conducts more strongly
There is no difference
They are always identical
sci_closure_g5mat_033.explanation: Conductors allow current to flow more easily than insulators.
theoryLines: Metal wires are common conductors.
Plastic coatings often act as insulators.

sci_closure_g6mat_034.stem: What is an example of using a material’s property in engineering?
options: Choosing a strong material that fits the job and safety needs
Material never affects the result
Always using the same material for every job
Safety has no link to material choice
sci_closure_g6mat_034.explanation: Engineers pick materials based on strength, flexibility, heat resistance, and other properties.
theoryLines: Properties guide how materials are used.
The right material makes designs safer and stronger.

sci_pb1_g3_body_easy_01.stem: What is the main job of the lungs in the human body?
options: Exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide with the air
Make red blood from ready-made material
Filter poisons only through the skin, with no link to lungs
Store food for a long time without breathing
sci_pb1_g3_body_easy_01.explanation: The respiratory system exchanges gases between the body and outside air.
theoryLines: Oxygen enters the blood in the lungs.
Carbon dioxide leaves the blood to be exhaled.

sci_pb1_g3_body_easy_02.stem: Which organs help digest food after you swallow?
options: The stomach and intestines
Usually the lungs
The optic nerve
Only the arm muscle
sci_pb1_g3_body_easy_02.explanation: The digestive system includes organs such as the stomach and intestines that break down and absorb food.
theoryLines: Food travels from the mouth through the digestive tract.
Nutrients are absorbed mainly in the intestines.

sci_pb1_g3_body_hard_01.stem: Which statement correctly describes the blood vessels that carry blood from the heart to body tissues?
options: Arteries carry blood pumped out of the heart to the body
Veins always carry oxygen-rich blood
Capillaries connect only two nerves
Capillaries create the heartbeat
sci_pb1_g3_body_hard_01.explanation: Arteries generally carry blood away from the heart; veins return blood to the heart.
theoryLines: The heart pumps blood into arteries.
Capillaries are tiny vessels where exchange with tissues happens.

sci_pb1_g3_body_hard_02.stem: Which statement correctly describes how breathing works with circulation?
options: Breathing loads blood with oxygen, and blood carries that oxygen to tissues
Blood usually makes oxygen inside lung cells
Muscles take oxygen straight from air
The heart only drains waste and has no link to oxygen
sci_pb1_g3_body_hard_02.explanation: Gas exchange in the lungs changes the oxygen in blood, which then travels to tissues.
theoryLines: Lungs and blood vessels work as a team.
Cells need oxygen delivered by blood.

sci_pb1_g3_animals_easy_01.stem: What is a usual trait of young mammals?
options: They nurse soon after birth or early in life
They bark in order to fly
They breathe only with gills like fish
They usually grow only inside a shell
sci_pb1_g3_animals_easy_01.explanation: Young mammals usually get milk from a parent.
theoryLines: Nursing is a mammal trait.
Mammal babies often need parental care.

sci_pb1_g3_animals_hard_01.stem: What is a good example of an animal adaptation to a hot, dry habitat?
options: Being active mainly at night to avoid extreme heat
Living only in fresh water with no exceptions
Every bird needing exactly the same food
Fish needing long legs for the desert
sci_pb1_g3_animals_hard_01.explanation: Behavior and body features that fit the habitat help animals survive.
theoryLines: Desert animals often avoid the hottest hours.
Adaptations reduce water loss and heat stress.

sci_pb1_g3_plants_easy_01.stem: What do plants need for photosynthesis on a bright day?
options: Light, water, and carbon dioxide from the air
Usually only hot sand with no water
Usually only loud music
Soil with no minerals at all
sci_pb1_g3_plants_easy_01.explanation: In photosynthesis, plants use light, water, and carbon dioxide to make sugar.
theoryLines: Leaves capture light energy.
Photosynthesis also releases oxygen.

sci_pb1_g3_materials_easy_01.stem: How can you simply tell an electrical conductor from an insulator in class?
options: Test whether a circuit with a bulb closes through the material
Always cover the material with oil without testing a circuit
Stamp on the material with no experiment
Treat every metal as an insulator
sci_pb1_g3_materials_easy_01.explanation: Conductors let current flow in a simple circuit; insulators block the flow.
theoryLines: A working bulb shows a complete conducting path.
Safety matters when testing electrical materials.

sci_pb1_g3_materials_hard_01.stem: What affects how fast a small ice cube melts in the same classroom?
options: Room temperature and airflow around the ice
Usually only the wall color
The name of the student watching the experiment
Table height with no link to surroundings
sci_pb1_g3_materials_hard_01.explanation: Temperature and the surrounding air affect how quickly ice changes to liquid water.
theoryLines: Warmer air usually melts ice faster.
Moving air can speed heat transfer.

sci_pb1_g3_experiments_easy_01.stem: What is an important step before repeating a measurement in the same experiment?
options: Clearly define what stays the same and what changes
Change every variable together
Erase earlier results without recording them
Make sure there is no planned variable
sci_pb1_g3_experiments_easy_01.explanation: In a controlled experiment, change one variable and keep other conditions as steady as possible.
theoryLines: Clear variables make repeats meaningful.
Good planning comes before measuring.

sci_pb1_g3_earth_space_easy_01.stem: Which statement correctly describes Earth’s motion around the Sun?
options: Earth travels around the Sun on a nearly circular elliptical path
Earth stays still while the Moon orbits the Sun with no link to Earth
The Sun orbits Earth once a day with no seasons
Seasons are caused only by daily spin on Earth’s axis
sci_pb1_g3_earth_space_easy_01.explanation: Earth’s yearly path around the Sun is linked to seasons and changing sunlight angles.
theoryLines: One trip around the Sun takes about one year.
Earth also spins daily to make day and night.

sci_pb1_g3_earth_space_hard_01.stem: How are seasons linked to the angle of sunlight in a region?
options: When sunlight hits more directly, that region tends to get warmer seasons
Seasons happen only because of daily spin on the axis
Sun angle usually has no link to seasonal temperature
The Moon sets the seasons directly every day
sci_pb1_g3_earth_space_hard_01.explanation: Seasons relate to day length and how directly sunlight hits a place through the year.
theoryLines: More direct sunlight delivers more energy per area.
Earth’s tilt helps create seasonal patterns.

sci_pb1_g3_environment_easy_01.stem: What is a simple way to reduce packaging waste at school?
options: Bring a reusable lunch box and use fewer single-use packages
Usually burn packages in the classroom
Never recycle packages
Throw packages into any bin with no sorting
sci_pb1_g3_environment_easy_01.explanation: Using fewer throwaway packages and bringing reusable containers reduces waste.
theoryLines: Reduce comes before recycle.
Reusable items cut trash at school.

sci_pb1_g3_environment_hard_01.stem: What is a likely result of adding plants to a yard damaged by landslides?
options: Roots can help stabilize soil over time when the planting is planned carefully
One planting completely removes all risk forever
Heavy rain always weakens soil immediately with no other factors
You can plant without checking the slope at all
sci_pb1_g3_environment_hard_01.explanation: Plants can help hold soil, but slope safety still needs planning and care.
theoryLines: Roots bind soil particles together.
Steep slopes need careful land management.

sci_pb1_g4_body_easy_01.stem: Which statement correctly describes the digestive system at a basic level?
options: It breaks food into smaller parts and absorbs materials into the body
It usually makes oxygen directly from food
It only swaps jobs with the lungs to make red blood
It works only during fast leg movement
sci_pb1_g4_body_easy_01.explanation: Digestion breaks food down and helps the body absorb nutrients.
theoryLines: Food travels through a digestive pathway.
Absorption moves useful materials into the blood.

sci_pb1_g4_body_hard_01.stem: Which explanation best links pulse to body activity?
options: During hard physical effort, heart rate often rises to supply muscles
Pulse is always the same no matter the activity
The heart stops during effort
Pulse depends only on room temperature, not muscles
sci_pb1_g4_body_hard_01.explanation: During exercise the body needs more oxygen, so the heart usually beats faster.
theoryLines: Working muscles need more blood flow.
Pulse rate is a useful activity clue.

sci_pb1_g4_animals_easy_01.stem: What typically describes the life cycle of an insect with complete metamorphosis?
options: Stages such as egg, larva, pupa, and adult that look different
Every stage looks exactly the same
Usually no development stages at all
The adult returns to being an egg with the same shape
sci_pb1_g4_animals_easy_01.explanation: Complete metamorphosis has clear stages with major changes in form.
theoryLines: Butterflies and beetles are examples.
Each stage can use different resources.

sci_pb1_g4_animals_hard_01.stem: What happens in a food web when a basic producer plant is sharply reduced?
options: Energy pathways and consumer dependence can change
Nothing changes because plants do not matter in a web
All animals automatically grow more
Waste disappears with no ecological effect
sci_pb1_g4_animals_hard_01.explanation: Producer plants make organic material that feeds many levels of a food web.
theoryLines: Producers form the base of most food webs.
Losing producers can stress consumers.

sci_pb1_g4_materials_easy_01.stem: What is a typical physical way to separate a mixture of sand and water in a container?
options: Let the sand settle, then filter or carefully pour off the water
Always light the mixture with no safety checks
Usually make new substances without sampling
Turn sand into new water without an experiment
sci_pb1_g4_materials_easy_01.explanation: Components can be separated by density and particle size using settling and filtering.
theoryLines: Sand is denser than water and settles.
Filtration separates solids from liquids.

sci_pb1_g4_materials_hard_01.stem: When should a classroom change be classified as physical rather than chemical?
options: When the same substance keeps its chemical identity but changes shape or state
When a new substance with totally different properties forms
When irreversible new gas bubbles and a new smell appear
When a dye on paper changes color permanently with no return
sci_pb1_g4_materials_hard_01.explanation: A chemical change makes a new substance; a physical change keeps the same substance.
theoryLines: Melting and freezing are physical changes.
Burning and rusting are chemical changes.

sci_pb1_g4_experiments_easy_01.stem: What is the role of a hypothesis in an organized investigation?
options: A prediction you can test with an experiment
A final result that never changes
Usually a step for deleting data
A list of equipment with no link to the question
sci_pb1_g4_experiments_easy_01.explanation: A hypothesis is a prediction that measurements and experiments can check.
theoryLines: Hypotheses guide what to test.
Evidence may support or reject a hypothesis.

sci_pb1_g4_experiments_hard_01.stem: What is a correct reason to repeat measurements in the same experiment?
options: Repeats help reveal spread and measurement mistakes
Repeats are always unnecessary if a result looks nice
One trial is always enough no matter the precision needed
Repeats change the original goal for no reason
sci_pb1_g4_experiments_hard_01.explanation: Repeating improves reliability and helps show how much results vary.
theoryLines: Random error can appear in single trials.
Consistent repeats strengthen confidence.

sci_pb1_g4_earth_space_easy_01.stem: What affects day length in summer compared with winter in our region?
options: Earth’s tilt and its path around the Sun
Only sky color, with no link to season
Only cloud amount, with no link to time of year
Usually only building height
sci_pb1_g4_earth_space_easy_01.explanation: The yearly cycle and sun-ray angle affect how long daylight lasts.
theoryLines: Summer days are often longer than winter days.
Earth’s tilt helps create seasons.

sci_pb1_g4_environment_easy_01.stem: What is a safe way to handle used batteries at home?
options: Take them to a proper collection point instead of the regular trash
Usually burn them in a private garden
Break them and pour them into the sink with no guidance
Usually bury them in soil near school
sci_pb1_g4_environment_easy_01.explanation: Batteries need special recycling or disposal because they can contain harmful materials.
theoryLines: Hazardous waste should not go in regular trash.
Collection points keep chemicals out of soil and water.

sci_pb1_g5_body_easy_01.stem: Which statement correctly describes the kidneys’ role with blood and body fluids?
options: They filter wastes and help keep fluid balance
They make oxygen for blood
They are usually responsible only for vision
They replace the lungs in gas exchange
sci_pb1_g5_body_easy_01.explanation: Kidneys filter blood and help regulate fluids and wastes.
theoryLines: Urine carries filtered wastes out of the body.
Kidneys work with the circulatory system.

sci_pb1_g5_body_medium_01.stem: What usually happens to heart rate when you move from rest to moderate effort for several minutes?
options: It rises gradually to send more oxygen to muscles
It drops immediately with no rise
It stays fixed forever with no link to blood flow
It is set only by room temperature
sci_pb1_g5_body_medium_01.explanation: During sustained effort the heart works harder to meet oxygen demand.
theoryLines: Active muscles need more oxygenated blood.
Heart rate is a useful fitness indicator.

sci_pb1_g5_animals_medium_01.stem: What ecological risk can come from reducing top predator species?
options: Some prey populations may grow and create imbalance
It always improves the system with no side effects
It affects only fur color, with no food-web link
It usually prevents all population growth
sci_pb1_g5_animals_medium_01.explanation: Changing predators can change prey numbers and food-web balance.
theoryLines: Top predators help control prey populations.
Food webs connect many species.

sci_pb1_g5_materials_medium_01.stem: What can a simple experiment show about the electrical properties of materials?
options: Building a circuit with a battery and bulb to test whether a material conducts
Usually lighting a material with no supervision
Usually tasting an unknown material
Measuring only color with no circuit
sci_pb1_g5_materials_medium_01.explanation: A simple electric circuit can test conductivity safely with adult guidance.
theoryLines: A lit bulb shows a conducting path.
Insulators keep the bulb from lighting.

sci_pb1_g6_body_medium_01.stem: What is a reasonable link between balanced eating and steady energy during a school day?
options: Timed meals with complex carbohydrates and protein support steadier energy
Skipping breakfast always improves focus with no exceptions
Only quick sugar is a source of steady energy
Lots of coffee usually replaces sleep with no effects
sci_pb1_g6_body_medium_01.explanation: Regular, balanced meals help keep energy more stable through the day.
theoryLines: The body needs fuel from food.
Sleep and hydration also support energy and focus.

sci_pb1_g2_earth_space_easy_01.stem: What correctly describes how the sky looks during a clear day?
options: The Sun appears to move across the sky, and shadows change
The Moon always stays fixed with no motion
Stars disappear at noon because of desk height
Time of day has no link to shadow direction
sci_pb1_g2_earth_space_easy_01.explanation: As the day goes on, the Sun’s position in the sky changes and shadows shift.
theoryLines: Earth’s rotation makes the Sun appear to move.
Shadow length and direction change with time.

sci_pb1_g2_earth_space_easy_02.stem: What describes the Moon in the night sky in a simple observation?
options: It looks like a bright disk that can be seen without special tools
It is always full every evening with no cycle
It shines with its own light like the Sun
It is usually visible only at noon
sci_pb1_g2_earth_space_easy_02.explanation: The Moon reflects sunlight and appears in changing shapes through its cycle.
theoryLines: Moon phases change over about a month.
The Moon does not make its own light.

sci_pb1_g2_earth_space_easy_03.stem: What can a simple weather log include?
options: Approximate temperature, cloud clues, and wind direction
Only the observer’s shirt color
Only the number of classroom windows
Only the teacher’s name, with no link to the sky
sci_pb1_g2_earth_space_easy_03.explanation: Weather records use observations that others can repeat and compare.
theoryLines: Temperature, clouds, and wind are common weather measures.
Logs help spot patterns over days.

sci_pb1_g2_earth_space_easy_04.stem: What is a safe way to observe the Sun during the day?
options: Use a proper solar filter or a supervised projection or shade method
Stare directly for a long time with no protection
Use a regular telescope with no filter
Usually point a laser at the Sun
sci_pb1_g2_earth_space_easy_04.explanation: Looking at the Sun can hurt eyes. Use approved filters and adult supervision.
theoryLines: Sunlight is intense enough to damage vision.
Safe solar viewing needs special tools.

sci_pb1_g6_environment_easy_01.stem: What is a practical class-level step to reduce emissions from school travel?
options: Organize carpools or bike on safe routes when possible
Increase private car trips for every student
Usually avoid any transportation planning
Usually burn trash near the classroom
sci_pb1_g6_environment_easy_01.explanation: Shared rides and low-emission travel reduce pollution from school trips.
theoryLines: Fewer solo car trips mean fewer exhaust emissions.
Walking and biking also support healthy habits.

sci_p0_g1_body_medium_01.stem: What helps us breathe air into the body?
options: The lungs
The teeth
The hair
The fingernails
sci_p0_g1_body_medium_01.explanation: The lungs take air in and let gases out.
theoryLines: We need air to live.
Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs.

sci_p0_g1_body_medium_02.stem: Why is it important to wash hands before eating?
options: To reduce germs that could enter the body
So hands are always dry
Usually only to strengthen muscles
Usually so we do not need sleep
sci_p0_g1_body_medium_02.explanation: Handwashing reduces germs that can travel into the digestive system.
theoryLines: Germs can live on hands.
Clean hands help keep you healthier.

sci_p0_g1_body_medium_03.stem: Which organ helps us hear sounds?
options: Ears
Nose
Knees
Joints
sci_p0_g1_body_medium_03.explanation: Sound enters the ears and signals travel to the brain.
theoryLines: Ears are the organs of hearing.
Protecting ears helps protect hearing.

sci_p0_g1_body_medium_04.stem: What is the job of the eyes?
options: To see the surroundings
To digest food
To pump blood
To make sound
sci_p0_g1_body_medium_04.explanation: The eyes are the organs of sight.
theoryLines: Light enters the eyes so we can see.
The brain helps make sense of what we see.

sci_p0_g1_body_medium_05.stem: Why is it helpful to get enough sleep at night?
options: To let the body rest and recover
So we do not need to eat
So hair grows faster
Usually so we do not breathe
theoryLines: Rest helps the body and brain.
Kids need enough sleep to feel ready for the day.

sci_p0_g1_body_medium_06.stem: What does the heart do in the body?
options: It pumps blood to all parts of the body.
It digests food in the stomach.
It helps you hear sounds.
It grows new bones.
sci_p0_g1_body_medium_06.explanation: The heart is a strong muscle that pumps blood. Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to every part of your body.
theoryLines: The heart beats without stopping.
Blood moves through tubes called blood vessels.

sci_p0_g1_body_medium_07.stem: Which body part helps you smell?
options: Your nose
Your elbows
Your knees
Your hair
sci_p0_g1_body_medium_07.explanation: Your nose senses smells in the air. Nerves in your nose send smell messages to your brain.
theoryLines: Smell is one of the five senses.
The nose also helps you breathe.

sci_p0_g1_body_medium_08.stem: Why does your body need water every day?
options: Water helps your body stay healthy and work well.
Water makes your bones turn into metal.
Water stops your heart from beating.
Water replaces the need for sleep.
sci_p0_g1_body_medium_08.explanation: Your body is made of a lot of water. Drinking water helps you stay cool, move nutrients, and feel well.
theoryLines: People need water every day.
Thirst is a signal that your body needs a drink.

sci_p0_g1_body_medium_09.stem: How can you help keep your teeth healthy?
options: Brush your teeth and avoid lots of sugary snacks.
Never brush your teeth at all.
Only wash your hair each morning.
Sleep with candy under your pillow.
sci_p0_g1_body_medium_09.explanation: Brushing removes food and germs that can hurt teeth. Limiting sugary snacks also helps prevent cavities.
theoryLines: Teeth help you chew food.
Healthy teeth need daily care.

sci_p0_g1_body_hard_01.stem: What happens when you exercise hard?
options: You breathe faster to get more oxygen.
Your body stops needing air.
Your bones turn soft.
You stop using your muscles.
sci_p0_g1_body_hard_01.explanation: Working muscles need more oxygen. You breathe faster and your heart beats faster to deliver it.
theoryLines: Exercise makes the heart and lungs work harder.
Oxygen helps muscles keep moving.

sci_p0_g1_body_hard_02.stem: Why should you not stick small objects in your nose?
options: They can get stuck and make it hard to breathe.
They make your hair grow faster.
They turn your tongue blue.
They help you smell better.
sci_p0_g1_body_hard_02.explanation: Your nose is for breathing and smelling. Small objects can block air or get stuck and need a doctor's help.
theoryLines: Keep small objects away from your nose and ears.
Tell an adult if something feels stuck.

sci_p0_g1_body_hard_03.stem: Where does your body get energy to play and learn?
options: From the food you eat
From watching TV only
From sitting still all day
From holding your breath
sci_p0_g1_body_hard_03.explanation: Food gives your body energy and building materials. Different foods help you grow, move, and think.
theoryLines: Eating gives your body fuel.
A balanced meal helps you stay strong.

options: It supports your body and protects important organs.
It digests your lunch.
It pumps blood like a heart.
It smells the air around you.
sci_p0_g1_body_hard_04.explanation: Bones form your skeleton. They give your body shape, help you stand, and protect parts like your brain and heart.
theoryLines: Bones are hard and strong.
Muscles pull on bones so you can move.

sci_p0_g1_body_hard_05.stem: Why should you wear a helmet when you ride a bike?
options: A helmet helps protect your brain if you fall.
A helmet makes your bike go faster by itself.
A helmet replaces the need for brakes.
A helmet feeds your muscles.
sci_p0_g1_body_hard_05.explanation: Your brain is inside your skull. A helmet adds extra protection if you bump your head.
theoryLines: The brain controls thinking and movement.
Safety gear helps prevent injuries.

sci_p0_g1_body_hard_06.stem: What do your lungs do when you take a deep breath?
options: They fill with air so your body can get oxygen.
They chew food into tiny pieces.
They turn water into bone.
They stop blood from moving.
sci_p0_g1_body_hard_06.explanation: Lungs take in oxygen from the air. Oxygen moves into your blood and travels through your body.
theoryLines: Breathing in brings oxygen.
Breathing out removes carbon dioxide.

sci_p0_g1_body_hard_07.stem: Why does your pulse feel faster after you run?
options: Your heart is beating faster to send blood to your muscles.
Your bones are melting from heat.
Your skin stops sensing touch.
Your stomach turns into a lung.
sci_p0_g1_body_hard_07.explanation: Running uses a lot of energy. Your heart speeds up so blood can carry more oxygen to working muscles.
theoryLines: Pulse is the beat of blood from the heart.
You can feel a pulse on your wrist or neck.

sci_p0_g1_body_hard_08.stem: What should you do if you feel strong pain in your chest?
options: Tell a trusted adult right away.
Ignore it and keep playing hard.
Put candy on your forehead.
Hold your breath until it stops.
sci_p0_g1_body_hard_08.explanation: Strong pain can be a warning that something is wrong. An adult can help you get care if you need it.
theoryLines: Pain can be a signal from your body.
Adults help keep kids safe.

sci_p0_g1_body_hard_09.stem: What is the main job of your muscles?
options: They help your body move.
They store all your memories.
They turn light into food.
They grow your fingernails only.
sci_p0_g1_body_hard_09.explanation: Muscles pull on bones so you can walk, jump, smile, and lift things. Your heart is a special muscle too.
theoryLines: Muscles work with bones.
Exercise helps muscles stay strong.

sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_01.stem: How are animals different from plants?
options: Animals eat food; plants make their own food using light.
Animals never need water.
Plants always chase other plants.
Animals grow roots in the soil.
sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_01.explanation: Most plants use sunlight to make food. Animals must eat plants or other animals to get energy.
theoryLines: Living things need energy.
Plants and animals get energy in different ways.

sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_02.stem: Which animal lives in water and breathes with gills?
options: A fish
A cat
A chicken
A butterfly
sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_02.explanation: Fish live in water. Gills help them take oxygen from the water.
theoryLines: Different animals live in different habitats.
Gills work underwater.

options: Grass and other plants
Only metal cans
Only rocks
Only plastic bags
sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_03.explanation: Cows are plant-eaters. They chew grass and other plants to get energy.
theoryLines: Animals eat different kinds of food.
Plant-eaters are called herbivores.

options: Wings and light bodies
Heavy stone shoes
Roots underground
Gills on their beaks
sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_04.explanation: Birds flap their wings to push against the air. Light bones and feathers also help with flight.
theoryLines: Not every bird flies well, but many do.
Wings are adapted for moving through air.

sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_05.stem: How do bees help flowering plants?
options: They carry pollen from flower to flower.
They turn flowers into rocks.
They water plants with saltwater only.
They eat all the plant roots.
sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_05.explanation: When bees visit flowers for nectar, pollen sticks to them. Moving pollen helps plants make seeds.
theoryLines: Pollination helps plants reproduce.
Bees are important helpers in nature.

options: A dog
A frog
A goldfish
An ant
sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_06.explanation: Mammals are animals that have hair or fur and feed their babies milk. Dogs are mammals.
theoryLines: People are mammals too.
Mammals are warm-blooded.

options: Their bodies need water to stay alive and healthy.
Water turns animals into plants.
Animals only drink water on birthdays.
Water replaces the need for air.
sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_07.explanation: Like people, animals need water for their bodies to work. Without enough water, animals get sick or die.
theoryLines: All animals need water.
Habitats must provide water somehow.

sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_08.stem: Where do house cats usually live and move?
options: On land
Only deep under the ocean
Only inside tree bark
Only in clouds
sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_08.explanation: Cats are land animals. They walk and run on solid ground, though they may climb or swim a little.
theoryLines: Animals live where they can find food and shelter.
Land, water, and air are different habitats.

sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_09.stem: Why do many lizards sit in the sun?
options: They use the sun's heat to warm their bodies.
They are melting into puddles.
They are turning into birds.
They do not need any heat ever.
sci_p0_g1_animals_medium_09.explanation: Lizards are reptiles. Their body temperature depends a lot on the environment, so sunshine helps them warm up.
theoryLines: Reptiles often bask in warm places.
Warmth helps reptiles move and hunt.

sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_01.stem: Why do some animals hibernate in winter?
options: To save energy when food is hard to find.
To practice flying to the moon.
To grow leaves like trees.
To turn into fish underwater.
sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_01.explanation: In cold months, food can be scarce. Hibernating animals slow down and rest through the hard season.
theoryLines: Hibernation helps animals survive winter.
Bears and some other animals may hibernate.

sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_02.stem: What do baby birds in a nest need from parent birds?
options: Food and care
Homework worksheets
Car keys
Ice cream every hour
sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_02.explanation: Young birds cannot care for themselves at first. Parent birds bring food and keep them safe until they grow stronger.
theoryLines: Many animal parents care for their young.
Nests give baby birds a safe place.

options: Gills help fish take oxygen from water.
Gills help fish bark like dogs.
Gills help fish make honey.
Gills help fish grow feathers.
sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_03.explanation: Fish need oxygen just like we do. Gills pull oxygen out of the water so fish can breathe underwater.
theoryLines: Land animals usually breathe with lungs.
Water animals may use gills.

options: An animal that hunts and eats other animals
A plant that never needs sunlight
A rock that grows legs
A cloud that rains candy
sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_04.explanation: Predators catch prey for food. Lions, hawks, and sharks are examples of predators.
theoryLines: Food chains include predators and prey.
Predators help keep animal numbers in balance.

sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_05.stem: Why are many bats active at night?
options: Night can make finding food safer or easier for them.
They melt in sunlight like ice cream.
They can only fly when it snows.
They are afraid of trees.
sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_05.explanation: Bats are often nocturnal. Night activity can help them hunt insects and avoid some dangers.
theoryLines: Nocturnal animals are active at night.
Different animals are active at different times.

sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_06.stem: How do birds stay warm in cold weather?
options: Fluffed feathers trap warm air near their bodies.
They turn off their hearts.
They grow fish scales overnight.
They stop eating forever.
sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_06.explanation: Feathers act like a coat. Fluffing them traps air that helps hold in body heat.
theoryLines: Animals have ways to handle cold weather.
Some birds migrate to warmer places.

sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_07.stem: How do a cat's claws help it?
options: Claws help a cat climb, catch prey, and grip surfaces.
Claws help a cat breathe underwater.
Claws make a cat photosynthesize.
Claws turn a cat into a bird.
sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_07.explanation: Sharp claws are tools. Cats use them for climbing, hunting, and holding on.
theoryLines: Body parts help animals survive.
Claws are an adaptation for cats.

options: Coloring or patterns that help an animal blend into its surroundings
A loud song that scares the sun away
A way plants turn into animals
A type of nest made of metal
sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_08.explanation: Camouflage makes an animal harder to see. It can help prey hide and help predators sneak up.
theoryLines: Many animals use camouflage.
Blending in can mean survival.

sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_09.stem: Why should you not disturb a bird's nest?
options: Disturbing a nest can scare parents away or harm the eggs and chicks.
Nests explode if people look at them.
Birds stop needing food if nests are touched.
Eggs turn into rocks when watched.
sci_p0_g1_animals_hard_09.explanation: Birds need quiet, safe nests to raise young. People should watch from a distance and leave nests alone.
theoryLines: Respect wildlife and their homes.
Young animals need protection.

sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_01.stem: What do most plants need to grow?
options: Light, water, air, and nutrients from soil
Only video games
Only plastic bags
Only darkness and salt
sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_01.explanation: Healthy plants need sunlight, water, air, and nutrients. Without these, many plants grow poorly or die.
theoryLines: Plants are living things with needs.
Gardeners give plants what they need.

sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_02.stem: What do plant roots usually do?
options: Take in water and nutrients and hold the plant in place
Flap like wings so the plant can fly
Make loud music for bees
Turn sunlight into ice
sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_02.explanation: Roots grow in the soil. They soak up water and nutrients and keep the plant from tipping over.
theoryLines: Different plant parts have different jobs.
Strong roots support tall plants.

sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_03.stem: What is an important job of leaves?
options: They help the plant make food using sunlight.
They dig tunnels under roads.
They pump blood through the plant.
They chew insects for dinner.
sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_03.explanation: Leaves catch sunlight. Plants use light, water, and air to make sugar food in a process called photosynthesis.
theoryLines: Green leaves often do photosynthesis.
Food made in leaves feeds the whole plant.

sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_04.stem: Why are many flowers brightly colored?
options: Bright colors help attract bees and other pollinators.
Colors make the soil disappear.
Colors stop plants from needing water.
Colors turn flowers into animals.
sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_04.explanation: Bees and other animals notice bright flowers. When they visit, they can move pollen and help plants make seeds.
theoryLines: Flowers help plants reproduce.
Color and scent can attract helpers.

sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_05.stem: What does a seed need to begin germinating (sprouting)?
options: The right amount of water and warmth
A television and headphones
Only frozen ice forever
A pair of shoes
sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_05.explanation: Germination is when a seed starts to grow. Water and a good temperature help the tiny plant inside wake up.
theoryLines: Seeds hold a baby plant and food stores.
Not every seed sprouts right away.

options: They make their own food using sunlight.
They buy snacks at a store.
They only eat other animals.
They never need energy.
sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_06.explanation: Producers make food energy from sunlight. Animals that eat plants depend on that food.
theoryLines: Plants are the start of many food chains.
Without producers, other life would struggle.

sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_07.stem: What should you do around dry plants and fire?
options: Be careful—dry plants can burn easily.
Light fires next to dry grass for fun.
Pour gasoline on dry leaves outdoors.
Ignore fire rules in forests.
sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_07.explanation: Dry grass, leaves, and wood can catch fire quickly. Stay safe and follow adult rules about fire.
theoryLines: Fire can spread through dry plants.
Prevention keeps people and nature safer.

sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_08.stem: What is one important role of fruit on a plant?
options: Fruit helps protect and spread seeds.
Fruit turns the plant into a rock.
Fruit stops the plant from needing light.
Fruit digests food for animals' bones.
sci_p0_g1_plants_medium_08.explanation: Fruits hold seeds. Animals may eat fruit and carry seeds to new places, helping plants spread.
theoryLines: Seeds grow into new plants.
Fruit is part of a plant's life cycle.

sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_01.stem: What may happen if a green plant gets no light for a long time?
options: It may grow weak, turn pale, and stop making enough food.
It will turn into a fish.
It will need no water forever.
It will grow metal leaves.
sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_01.explanation: Plants need light to make food. Without light, they cannot keep growing well.
theoryLines: Photosynthesis needs light.
Window plants lean toward light sources.

sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_02.stem: What can happen if you give a plant too much water?
options: Roots can get too wet and the plant may get sick or die.
The plant will never need soil again.
The plant will turn into a cloud.
The leaves will become magnets.
sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_02.explanation: Roots need some air in the soil. Constant flooding can hurt roots and the whole plant.
theoryLines: Plants need the right amount of water—not too little or too much.
Good drainage helps many houseplants.

options: Trees can give birds places to nest, rest, and find food.
Trees turn birds into mammals overnight.
Trees stop birds from ever needing water.
Trees erase bird habitats.
sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_03.explanation: Trees provide shelter and food such as seeds, fruit, or insects living on them. Many birds depend on trees.
theoryLines: Living things depend on each other.
Habitats include food and shelter.

sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_04.stem: In a simple food chain, what do plants provide?
options: Food energy for animals that eat them
Only plastic for packaging
Electricity for televisions
Clouds made of sugar
sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_04.explanation: A food chain shows who eats whom. Plants make food energy that plant-eaters use first.
theoryLines: Energy moves from plants to animals.
Food chains start with producers.

sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_05.stem: How can wind help some seeds?
options: Wind can carry lightweight seeds to new places.
Wind turns seeds into water instantly.
Wind stops all seeds from ever growing.
Wind glues seeds to the moon.
sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_05.explanation: Some seeds are light or have wings and fluff. Wind spreads them so new plants can grow farther away.
theoryLines: Seeds travel in many ways.
Wind, water, and animals can move seeds.

sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_06.stem: Why do some trees lose their leaves in fall?
options: Losing leaves helps those trees save water and energy in cold seasons.
Leaves fall because trees become animals.
Leaves fall to make the sun colder.
Leaves fall only when it never rains.
sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_06.explanation: In cold seasons, water can be harder to use. Dropping leaves helps some trees rest through winter.
theoryLines: Deciduous trees lose leaves seasonally.
Evergreen trees keep leaves longer.

sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_07.stem: What is a careful way to pick flowers or plants outdoors?
options: Only pick with permission, and leave enough plants growing for nature.
Pull up every plant you see.
Pick rare plants from protected parks.
Dig up whole trees without asking.
sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_07.explanation: Plants are part of habitats. Taking too many can hurt wildlife and future growth.
theoryLines: Respect living things outdoors.
Ask an adult before picking plants.

sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_08.stem: What does a seed coat do?
options: It protects the tiny plant inside the seed.
It teaches the seed to swim.
It turns the seed into a bird egg.
It makes the seed photosynthesize like a leaf.
sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_08.explanation: A seed coat is a tough outer cover. It guards the embryo until conditions are right to sprout.
theoryLines: Seeds have protective coverings.
Inside a seed is a baby plant and stored food.

sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_09.stem: Why might gardeners slowly move seedlings outdoors before planting?
options: To help young plants get used to sun, wind, and outdoor temperatures
To turn seedlings into rocks
To stop seedlings from ever needing water
To make seedlings afraid of soil
sci_p0_g1_plants_hard_09.explanation: Sudden outdoor weather can shock tender plants. Gradual hardening helps them adjust safely.
theoryLines: Young plants can be delicate.
Careful changes help plants survive.

sci_p0_g2_body_medium_01.stem: What is one main role of the skeleton?
options: It supports the body and protects organs like the brain and heart.
It digests sugar in the mouth only.
It senses smells better than the nose.
It makes all of your memories.
sci_p0_g2_body_medium_01.explanation: Bones give shape and support. The skull protects the brain, and the rib cage helps protect the heart and lungs.
theoryLines: The skeleton is a living framework.
Joints let bones move where they meet.

sci_p0_g2_body_medium_02.stem: Why is eating a variety of healthy foods important?
options: Different foods give different nutrients your body needs.
One candy bar gives every nutrient forever.
Food is only for changing hair color.
People do not need nutrients at all.
sci_p0_g2_body_medium_02.explanation: Nutrients include proteins, vitamins, minerals, and more. A balanced diet helps growth, energy, and health.
theoryLines: No single food has everything you need.
Fruits, vegetables, grains, and proteins each help in different ways.

options: It controls thinking, senses, and many body actions.
It pumps blood like a second heart.
It only stores unused food.
It grows roots into the soil.
sci_p0_g2_body_medium_03.explanation: Your brain is the control center. It helps you learn, feel, move, and respond to the world.
theoryLines: Nerves carry messages to and from the brain.
The brain needs oxygen and nutrients from blood.

options: Breaking food into smaller parts the body can use
Pumping blood through the lungs only
Growing new teeth from sunlight
Turning bones into water
sci_p0_g2_body_medium_04.explanation: Digestion starts in the mouth and continues in the stomach and intestines. Nutrients then move into the blood.
theoryLines: Teeth help begin digestion by chewing.
The digestive system turns food into usable fuel.

sci_p0_g2_body_medium_05.stem: Why is warming up before hard exercise helpful?
options: It gently prepares muscles and joints for activity.
It freezes your muscles solid.
It removes the need to breathe.
It turns sweat into glue.
sci_p0_g2_body_medium_05.explanation: A warm-up increases blood flow and loosens muscles. That can help you move better and lower injury risk.
theoryLines: Start activity slowly, then go harder.
Stretching and light movement are common warm-ups.

options: Your body needs more water.
Your bones are too long.
Your ears need louder music.
Your hair is growing too fast.
sci_p0_g2_body_medium_06.explanation: Thirst is a signal from your body. Drinking water helps replace fluids you lose through sweat and other activities.
theoryLines: Water keeps body systems working.
Drink water during play and sports.

sci_p0_g2_body_medium_07.stem: How does skin help you sense the world?
options: Skin has sensors that detect touch, pressure, heat, and pain.
Skin digests food for the stomach.
Skin pumps oxygen into bones.
Skin makes all red blood cells.
sci_p0_g2_body_medium_07.explanation: Touch sensors in skin send messages to the brain. That is how you feel soft, rough, hot, cold, or painful things.
theoryLines: Skin is the body's outer covering.
Skin also helps protect against germs and injury.

options: Brushing, flossing, and limiting sugary drinks
Never cleaning your teeth
Chewing only sticky candy all day
Using soda instead of toothpaste
sci_p0_g2_body_medium_08.explanation: Sugar feeds germs that make acid, and acid can damage teeth. Cleaning teeth and smart snack choices protect enamel.
theoryLines: Dentists help check tooth health.
Healthy teeth help you eat and speak.

sci_p0_g2_body_medium_09.stem: What happens to your heart during active play?
options: It beats faster to send more blood to working muscles.
It turns off until you sit down.
It stops blood from carrying oxygen.
It moves into your foot.
sci_p0_g2_body_medium_09.explanation: Active muscles need extra oxygen and nutrients. A faster heartbeat helps deliver them quickly.
theoryLines: Heart rate rises with exercise.
Resting brings the heart rate back down.

sci_p0_g2_body_hard_01.stem: Why do you breathe harder when you run?
options: Your body needs more oxygen and must remove more carbon dioxide.
Your lungs shrink and disappear.
Running replaces breathing forever.
Your nose stops working in motion.
sci_p0_g2_body_hard_01.explanation: Running increases energy use. Faster, deeper breaths help trade gases so muscles can keep working.
theoryLines: Lungs and heart work as a team during exercise.
Carbon dioxide is a waste gas you breathe out.

sci_p0_g2_body_hard_02.stem: Why do working muscles need oxygen?
options: Oxygen helps muscles release energy from food nutrients.
Oxygen turns muscles into bones.
Oxygen makes muscles stop moving.
Oxygen is only used by hair follicles.
sci_p0_g2_body_hard_02.explanation: Cells use oxygen to get usable energy from nutrients. Without enough oxygen, muscles tire more quickly.
theoryLines: Blood carries oxygen to muscles.
Breathing and circulation support activity.

sci_p0_g2_body_hard_03.stem: What is one important job of blood?
options: It carries oxygen, nutrients, and waste around the body.
It digests rocks in the stomach.
It grows feathers on your arms.
It replaces the need for a brain.
sci_p0_g2_body_hard_03.explanation: Blood is a transport system. It delivers what cells need and carries away wastes.
theoryLines: The heart keeps blood moving.
Blood travels in blood vessels.

sci_p0_g2_body_hard_04.stem: What protects the brain inside the head?
options: The skull (and also fluid and soft tissues around the brain)
Only a layer of tree bark
Only the fingernails
Only the tongue
sci_p0_g2_body_hard_04.explanation: The hard skull surrounds the brain. Soft tissues and fluid add cushioning against bumps.
theoryLines: Helmets add extra protection during sports.
The brain is delicate and important.

sci_p0_g2_body_hard_05.stem: Why can breakfast help many kids at school?
options: It gives energy and nutrients after a night without eating.
It makes homework finish itself.
It replaces the need to drink water all day.
It turns books into toys.
sci_p0_g2_body_hard_05.explanation: After sleep, your body needs fuel again. A good breakfast can support focus, energy, and learning.
theoryLines: Food provides energy for brain and body.
Regular meals support healthy habits.

sci_p0_g2_body_hard_06.stem: What do arm muscles do when you lift a backpack?
options: They contract (tighten) to pull on bones and lift the load.
They turn into water vapor.
They stop blood from moving.
They make the backpack lighter by magic.
sci_p0_g2_body_hard_06.explanation: Muscles pull; they do not push on their own. Contracting arm muscles move bones at the joints so you can lift.
theoryLines: Muscles and bones work together.
Practice and exercise can strengthen muscles.

sci_p0_g2_body_hard_07.stem: Why should you drink water during sports on a hot day?
options: You lose water when you sweat, and your body needs to replace it.
Water makes your shoes run for you.
Water stops your heart permanently.
Water removes the need for practice.
sci_p0_g2_body_hard_07.explanation: Sweating cools you but uses body water. Drinking fluids helps you stay safe and keep performing.
theoryLines: Dehydration can cause tiredness and headaches.
Water is usually the best everyday sports drink for kids.

sci_p0_g2_body_hard_08.stem: What does your pulse tell you?
options: How fast your heart is beating
How tall you will be next year
What color your eyes will become
How many teeth you will grow tomorrow
sci_p0_g2_body_hard_08.explanation: Each heartbeat pushes blood, making a pulse you can feel. Counting pulse beats shows heart rate.
theoryLines: Pulse is linked to heart activity.
Heart rate changes with rest and exercise.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_easy_01.stem: What should you do before starting a classroom science experiment?
options: Read the steps, gather materials, and follow safety rules.
Guess wildly and skip all instructions.
Taste unknown chemicals first.
Throw away the measuring tools.
sci_p0_g2_experiments_easy_01.explanation: Good preparation keeps you safer and makes results clearer. Knowing the plan helps the experiment go smoothly.
theoryLines: Scientists plan before they test.
Safety comes first in any investigation.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_easy_02.stem: What tool would you use to measure the length of a seedling?
options: A ruler
A thermometer only
A musical instrument
A flashlight battery
sci_p0_g2_experiments_easy_02.explanation: A ruler measures length. Scientists choose tools that match what they want to measure.
theoryLines: Measurement needs the right tool.
Length is often recorded in centimeters or inches.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_easy_03.stem: Why do scientists often record results in a table?
options: A table organizes data so patterns are easier to see.
A table makes plants grow without water.
A table replaces the need for any measurements.
A table erases mistakes automatically.
sci_p0_g2_experiments_easy_03.explanation: Tables keep numbers and observations neat. Clear records help you compare trials and share findings.
theoryLines: Organized data supports better conclusions.
Columns and rows make comparisons simple.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_01.stem: In a fair test, what is a variable?
options: Something that can change in the experiment
A rule that forbids measuring anything
A decoration on the classroom wall
A type of lunchbox
sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_01.explanation: Variables are factors that can change, like water amount or light time. In a fair test, you usually change only one main variable.
theoryLines: Identify what you change and what you keep the same.
Fair tests help show cause and effect.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_02.stem: Why do scientists often repeat an experiment?
options: Repeating helps check whether results are reliable.
Repeating erases the need for any data.
Repeating makes safety rules unnecessary.
Repeating turns opinions into magic spells.
sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_02.explanation: One trial might be a lucky accident. Similar results across repeats make findings more trustworthy.
theoryLines: Reliable results can be repeated.
More trials can reveal mistakes or chance differences.

options: A testable idea about what might happen and why
A final answer that can never be checked
A list of unrelated doodles
A broken measuring cup
sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_03.explanation: A hypothesis is an educated guess you can test. Experiments give evidence that supports or does not support it.
theoryLines: Hypotheses guide investigations.
Evidence matters more than guessing alone.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_04.stem: Why do experiments often include a control?
options: A control is a comparison that helps show what the change caused.
A control is a prize for finishing early.
A control deletes all measurements.
A control means changing every factor at once.
sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_04.explanation: A control setup stays unchanged on purpose. Comparing it with the test setup shows the effect of the variable you changed.
theoryLines: Controls make tests fairer.
Compare results to see real differences.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_05.stem: What should a good conclusion be based on?
options: The evidence and data from the investigation
Only what you hoped would happen
A random story with no measurements
Someone's favorite color
sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_05.explanation: Conclusions explain what the results show. Scientists connect claims to evidence, even if the result was surprising.
theoryLines: Evidence supports scientific claims.
It is okay if a hypothesis was not supported.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_06.stem: Should you taste materials in a science experiment?
options: No—never taste experiment materials unless a teacher says a food test is safe.
Yes—taste every liquid to identify it.
Yes—taste powders to check if they are sweet.
Yes—taste first, then read labels later.
sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_06.explanation: Many lab materials are unsafe to eat or drink. Follow teacher rules and use senses that are safe for the activity.
theoryLines: Science safety protects your body.
Ask before touching or smelling unknown substances.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_07.stem: Which practice makes experimental results more reliable?
options: Measuring carefully and repeating trials
Changing many things at once on purpose
Throwing away data you dislike
Skipping units on every number
sci_p0_g2_experiments_medium_07.explanation: Careful methods and repeats reduce mistakes and chance errors. Reliable work can be checked by others too.
theoryLines: Good methods build trust in results.
Clear records help others understand your work.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_01.stem: How is an experiment different from only observing?
options: In an experiment, you test an idea by changing something on purpose.
Experiments never use any observations.
Observing always requires tasting chemicals.
Experiments forbid writing anything down.
sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_01.explanation: Observation means carefully noticing. An experiment adds a planned test, often changing one variable to see the effect.
theoryLines: Both observing and experimenting are scientific skills.
Tests help answer cause-and-effect questions.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_02.stem: What should you do if you notice a measurement mistake?
options: Record what happened and measure again carefully.
Hide the mistake and invent a number.
Quit science forever.
Blame the plant for moving the ruler.
sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_02.explanation: Mistakes happen. Honest recording and careful repeats help you fix errors and keep results trustworthy.
theoryLines: Scientists expect and check for errors.
Honesty is part of good science.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_03.stem: Why is changing two variables at the same time a problem in a fair test?
options: You cannot tell which change caused the result.
It makes the experiment perfectly fair.
It removes the need for any control.
It guarantees the same result every time.
sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_03.explanation: If light and water both change, either one—or both—might explain the outcome. Change one main variable at a time.
theoryLines: Fair tests isolate one factor.
Keep other conditions the same.

options: Units tell what the number means, like centimeters or grams.
Units are only for decoration.
Units make numbers unnecessary.
Units erase differences between trials.
sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_04.explanation: A number without units is unclear. Saying "5 centimeters" is different from "5 grams."
theoryLines: Always label measurements with units.
Matching units helps you compare data.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_05.stem: Which is a strong science conclusion?
options: One that matches the data and explains what it shows
One that ignores all measurements
One based only on a lucky guess with no test
One that changes the numbers to look nicer
sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_05.explanation: A strong conclusion stays tied to evidence. It may also note limits, like needing more trials.
theoryLines: Claims need support from results.
Clear language helps others understand findings.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_06.stem: Why do scientists keep experiment conditions the same when possible?
options: So differences in results are more likely caused by the variable being tested
So no one needs to measure anything
So safety rules can be ignored
So hypotheses become facts automatically
sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_06.explanation: Controlled conditions make comparisons fair. Then you can better link the changed variable to the outcome.
theoryLines: Same conditions support fair tests.
Write down the conditions you used.

sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_07.stem: What can a graph help you do with experiment data?
options: See patterns and compare results more easily
Grow plants without water or light
Delete incorrect safety rules
Replace the need for any observations
sci_p0_g2_experiments_hard_07.explanation: Graphs turn numbers into a visual picture. Trends, highs, and lows are often easier to notice in a graph.
theoryLines: Choose a graph that fits your data.
Labels and units make graphs clear.

sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_01.stem: What feature helps fish live in water?
options: Gills that take oxygen from water
Fur that makes honey
Lungs that only work on mountaintops
Feathers for flying underground
sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_01.explanation: Fish are adapted for aquatic life. Gills let them get oxygen without coming onto land.
theoryLines: Adaptations help animals survive in habitats.
Fins help fish swim and steer.

sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_02.stem: What kind of food do rabbits mainly eat?
options: Plants such as grass, leaves, and vegetables
Only other rabbits
Only metal scraps
Only ocean fish
sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_02.explanation: Rabbits are herbivores. Their teeth and digestive systems are suited to plant foods.
theoryLines: Diet matches an animal's body features.
Plant-eaters help shape plant growth in habitats.

sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_03.stem: What major change happens in a butterfly's life cycle?
options: It goes through stages, including caterpillar and chrysalis, before becoming an adult butterfly.
It stays a caterpillar forever with no changes.
It hatches as a mammal with fur.
It skips being young and starts as a tree.
sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_03.explanation: Butterflies metamorphose. The caterpillar feeds and grows, then transforms inside a chrysalis into a winged adult.
theoryLines: Life cycles show how animals grow and change.
Different stages may use different foods or habitats.

sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_04.stem: How does a bird's beak help it survive?
options: Beak shape helps the bird get the foods it eats.
Beaks pump blood through feathers.
Beaks photosynthesize like leaves.
Beaks turn birds into reptiles overnight.
sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_04.explanation: A hummingbird's thin beak suits nectar, while a hawk's hooked beak helps tear meat. Form matches function.
theoryLines: Body parts are adapted to needs.
Comparing beaks shows different diets.

sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_05.stem: How can fur help a mammal?
options: Fur can trap heat and protect the skin.
Fur lets mammals breathe underwater with gills.
Fur makes mammals produce flower nectar.
Fur replaces the need for food.
sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_05.explanation: Fur is an adaptation for temperature and protection. Some mammals have thicker coats in cold seasons.
theoryLines: Mammals often have hair or fur.
Insulation helps hold body heat.

sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_06.stem: What is true about many lizards?
options: They are reptiles that often warm up in sunlight.
They are mammals that make milk for plants.
They are fish with feathers.
They are insects with six bones only.
sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_06.explanation: Lizards belong to the reptile group. Basking in the sun helps them reach temperatures needed for activity.
theoryLines: Reptiles usually have dry skin with scales.
Habitat and behavior help regulate body heat.

sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_07.stem: Why are bees important to many flowering plants?
options: Bees help pollinate flowers as they collect nectar.
Bees turn flowers into plastic.
Bees stop seeds from ever forming.
Bees replace sunlight for plants.
sci_p0_g2_animals_medium_07.explanation: Pollen sticks to bees and moves between flowers. Pollination helps plants make fruits and seeds.
theoryLines: Pollinators support food webs and farms.
Protecting bees helps ecosystems.

sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_01.stem: How are camels adapted to dry desert life?
options: They can go a long time between drinks and handle hot, dry conditions.
They need rainforest humidity every hour.
They breathe only through underwater gills.
They hibernate inside snowbanks all summer.
sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_01.explanation: Camels store resources and conserve water well. Wide feet and other traits also help in sandy deserts.
theoryLines: Desert animals have special adaptations.
Saving water is key in dry habitats.

sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_02.stem: How do many bats find prey in the dark?
options: They use echolocation—sound echoes to sense nearby objects.
They read tiny printed maps with flashlights.
They grow plant roots to feel insects.
They wait for the sun to turn on.
sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_02.explanation: Bats send out sounds and listen for echoes. Echo patterns help them locate insects and obstacles at night.
theoryLines: Senses can be adapted to an animal's lifestyle.
Nocturnal hunters need ways to navigate in low light.

sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_03.stem: What can happen when animals lose their habitat?
options: They may struggle to find food, shelter, and safe places to raise young.
They instantly turn into a different species.
They no longer need water or space.
They automatically become pets.
sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_03.explanation: Habitat loss from cutting forests, building, or pollution removes what animals need. Populations can shrink or disappear locally.
theoryLines: Healthy habitats support biodiversity.
Protecting habitats helps wildlife survive.

sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_04.stem: What role can predators play in an ecosystem?
options: They help control the numbers of prey animals.
They produce all the plant food with sunlight.
They remove the need for any food chains.
They stop animals from needing habitats.
sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_04.explanation: By hunting prey, predators can prevent some populations from growing too large. This helps keep ecosystems balanced.
theoryLines: Predators and prey affect each other.
Energy flows through food webs.

sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_05.stem: What do fins help a fish do?
options: Swim, steer, and keep balance in water
Walk on land like a horse
Make pollen for flowers
Pump blood without a heart
sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_05.explanation: Different fins have jobs like moving forward, turning, and staying upright. Together they help fish move well underwater.
theoryLines: Body structures match the environment.
Water animals need ways to move through water.

sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_06.stem: What is special about a frog's life cycle?
options: Frogs often begin as tadpoles in water and later live more on land as adults.
Frogs hatch already as furry mammals.
Frogs never change form as they grow.
Frogs start life as seeds in soil.
sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_06.explanation: Many frogs metamorphose from aquatic tadpoles with gills into adults with lungs and legs. Their needs change with each stage.
theoryLines: Amphibians often need moist habitats.
Life-cycle stages can look very different.

sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_07.stem: Why do wild animals need enough space?
options: Space helps them find food, mates, and safe shelter.
Space is only for drawing maps in school.
Wild animals prefer living inside closed jars.
Space stops animals from breathing air.
sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_07.explanation: Crowding can mean less food and more stress or disease. Enough habitat space supports healthy wild populations.
theoryLines: Animals have home ranges and territories.
Conserving land protects wildlife needs.

sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_08.stem: What is one way birds cope with winter?
options: Some migrate to warmer places; others use feathers and food stores to stay.
All birds freeze solid until spring with no adaptations.
Birds turn into reptiles each December.
Birds stop needing energy in cold weather.
sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_08.explanation: Migration, fluffing feathers, and finding enough food are common winter strategies. Different species use different solutions.
theoryLines: Seasons change available resources.
Adaptations and behaviors help survival.

sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_09.stem: How do whiskers help a cat?
options: Whiskers sense nearby objects and help with movement in tight spaces.
Whiskers digest food outside the body.
Whiskers photosynthesize sunlight into fur.
Whiskers replace the cat's need to see anything.
sci_p0_g2_animals_hard_09.explanation: Whiskers are sensitive touch tools. They help cats judge openings and sense movement close to the face.
theoryLines: Special sensors support animal survival.
Touch can be as important as sight for some tasks.

sci_p0_g2_plants_medium_01.stem: What do plants make during photosynthesis?
options: Food (sugar) using light, water, and carbon dioxide
Rocks using only darkness
Plastic using saltwater only
Electricity using sand
sci_p0_g2_plants_medium_01.explanation: In photosynthesis, plants capture light energy and build sugar. Oxygen is released as a useful byproduct.
theoryLines: Leaves are major sites of photosynthesis.
Animals depend on plant-made food energy.

sci_p0_g2_plants_medium_02.stem: What is one job of a plant's stem?
options: It supports the plant and carries water and nutrients between roots and leaves.
It hunts insects with teeth.
It digests food like a stomach for animals.
It replaces sunlight completely.
sci_p0_g2_plants_medium_02.explanation: Stems hold leaves up toward light. Tubes inside move water upward and food to other plant parts.
theoryLines: Plant parts work as a system.
Strong stems help tall plants stand.

sci_p0_g2_plants_medium_03.stem: Besides holding a plant in place, what else do roots do?
options: Absorb water and minerals from the soil
Make pollen for bees only
Flap to fly the plant across fields
Pump blood through leaves
sci_p0_g2_plants_medium_03.explanation: Roots are the plant's underground uptake system. Water and minerals enter here and travel upward.
