theoryLines: Healthy soil helps roots work well.
Root hairs increase water absorption.

sci_p0_g2_plants_medium_04.stem: What does it mean when a seed germinates?
options: The seed sprouts and a young plant begins to grow.
The seed turns into an adult animal.
The seed freezes forever and never changes.
The seed becomes a cloud.
sci_p0_g2_plants_medium_04.explanation: Germination starts the plant life cycle from a seed. A root and shoot emerge when conditions are right.
theoryLines: Water and temperature affect germination.
Stored food in the seed fuels early growth.

sci_p0_g2_plants_medium_05.stem: Why do many plant leaves look green?
options: They contain chlorophyll, a green pigment that captures light.
They are painted green by insects every night.
They reflect only heat and no light.
They are made of pure copper metal.
sci_p0_g2_plants_medium_05.explanation: Chlorophyll helps capture light energy for photosynthesis. It reflects green wavelengths, so leaves look green.
theoryLines: Pigments affect plant color.
Chlorophyll is key to making food from light.

sci_p0_g2_plants_hard_01.stem: Why might a plant shed leaves?
options: Shedding can help the plant save water or respond to seasons and stress.
Shedding means the plant is turning into a mammal.
Shedding always means the plant no longer needs sunlight.
Shedding replaces roots with wings.
sci_p0_g2_plants_hard_01.explanation: Deciduous trees drop leaves in fall. Plants may also drop damaged leaves. These changes can protect the plant.
theoryLines: Leaf drop is sometimes a survival strategy.
Not all plants shed leaves the same way.

options: A powdery material from flowers that helps plants reproduce
A type of root that stores blood
A liquid that replaces soil
A rock formed inside tree bark
sci_p0_g2_plants_hard_02.explanation: Pollen carries material needed for fertilization in flowering plants. Wind, water, or animals can move pollen.
theoryLines: Pollination leads to seeds and fruits.
Some people are allergic to certain pollens.

sci_p0_g2_plants_hard_03.stem: What is a safe habit when watering plants near electricity?
options: Keep water away from outlets, cords, and devices.
Pour water directly onto plugged-in electronics.
Water plants while holding a toaster in the sink.
Ignore spills on electric equipment.
sci_p0_g2_plants_hard_03.explanation: Water and electricity are a dangerous mix. Water plants carefully so cords and outlets stay dry.
theoryLines: Safety matters in everyday science care.
Wipe spills and ask an adult for help with electricity.

sci_p0_g2_plants_hard_04.stem: Where do plants usually sit in a food chain?
options: At the beginning, as producers that make food energy
Only at the end as top predators
Nowhere—plants are never in food chains
Only as animals that hunt fish
sci_p0_g2_plants_hard_04.explanation: Producers start food chains by making energy-rich food. Herbivores eat plants, then other animals may eat those herbivores.
theoryLines: Energy flows from producers to consumers.
Removing plants affects the whole chain.

sci_p0_g2_plants_hard_05.stem: What is a tropism in plants?
options: A growth response toward or away from something like light or gravity
A loud sound plants use to call animals
A way plants hunt with teeth
A type of animal camouflage
sci_p0_g2_plants_hard_05.explanation: Stems often grow toward light (phototropism). Roots often grow downward with gravity. These responses help plants thrive.
theoryLines: Plants can sense their environment.
Growth direction can improve survival.

sci_p0_g2_plants_hard_06.stem: What happens to most plants without enough water?
options: They wilt and may die if the drought continues.
They instantly become desert cameras.
They stop needing sunlight forever.
They turn into mushrooms overnight.
sci_p0_g2_plants_hard_06.explanation: Water keeps plant cells firm and supports photosynthesis. Without it, leaves droop and life processes slow or stop.
theoryLines: Wilting is an early water-stress sign.
Different plants tolerate drought differently.

sci_p0_g3_body_hard_01.stem: What happens to blood when it travels through the lungs?
options: It picks up oxygen and drops off carbon dioxide.
It turns into stomach acid.
It stores leftover bones.
It becomes plant sap.
sci_p0_g3_body_hard_01.explanation: In the lungs, gas exchange occurs. Blood gains oxygen for the body and releases carbon dioxide to be exhaled.
theoryLines: The heart sends blood to the lungs and body.
Oxygen-rich blood fuels active cells.

sci_p0_g3_body_hard_02.stem: What do the kidneys help do?
options: Filter waste from the blood and help make urine
Pump air into the ears
Digest food using chlorophyll
Grow new skull bones each hour
sci_p0_g3_body_hard_02.explanation: Kidneys clean the blood by removing wastes and extra water. The wastes leave the body as urine.
theoryLines: Healthy kidneys support internal balance.
Drinking enough water helps body systems, including the kidneys.

sci_p0_g3_body_hard_03.stem: Why must the heart keep beating?
options: It must keep moving blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to body cells.
It only beats to make musical sounds.
It beats to cool the room temperature.
It beats so hair can photosynthesize.
sci_p0_g3_body_hard_03.explanation: Cells need a constant supply of oxygen and nutrients. If blood stops moving, tissues cannot work for long.
theoryLines: The heart is a lifelong pump.
Circulation links lungs, digestive nutrients, and body cells.

sci_p0_g3_body_hard_04.stem: During hard exercise, why might muscles feel tired?
options: They are using energy quickly and may not get oxygen fast enough for a while.
They have turned into cartilage permanently.
They no longer connect to bones.
They are allergic to breathing.
sci_p0_g3_body_hard_04.explanation: Active muscles demand lots of energy and oxygen. When demand is high, fatigue builds until you rest and recover.
theoryLines: Blood delivery and breathing support muscles.
Rest helps muscles recover after activity.

sci_p0_g3_body_hard_05.stem: What do nerves do in the body?
options: They carry messages between the brain, spinal cord, and body parts.
They digest vitamins in the stomach only.
They store fat for plant growth.
They replace blood vessels completely.
sci_p0_g3_body_hard_05.explanation: Nerves are like communication lines. They let you sense the world and control movement and many automatic body functions.
theoryLines: The nervous system coordinates the body.
Signals travel quickly along nerves.

options: Temperature
Length only
Loudness of music only
The number of leaves on a tree
sci_p0_g3_experiments_easy_01.explanation: Thermometers show how hot or cold something is. Scientists use them when temperature matters in a test.
theoryLines: Choose tools that match the question.
Record temperature with correct units, like °F or °C.

sci_p0_g3_experiments_easy_02.stem: Why should a science log include the date?
options: Dates help you track when observations were made and compare changes over time.
Dates make plants grow faster by themselves.
Dates replace the need for measurements.
Dates erase experimental errors.
sci_p0_g3_experiments_easy_02.explanation: Time stamps keep records organized. You can see growth, weather links, or which trial came first.
theoryLines: Clear notebooks support good science.
Details make data useful later.

sci_p0_g3_experiments_easy_03.stem: If you test how water affects seed growth, what should you change?
options: The amount of water, while keeping other conditions the same
Water, light, soil type, and temperature all at once
Only the color of your notebook
Nothing at all, and still claim a fair test
sci_p0_g3_experiments_easy_03.explanation: To learn about water's effect, water should be the main changed variable. Keep light, soil, and temperature steady for fairness.
theoryLines: One main variable makes results clearer.
Controls and constants support fair comparisons.

sci_p0_g3_experiments_easy_04.stem: What is a safe practice near hot equipment in a science activity?
options: Use care, follow adult directions, and never touch hot surfaces.
Grab hot glassware with bare hands to test heat.
Lean over boiling liquids without attention.
Ignore warning signs about heat.
sci_p0_g3_experiments_easy_04.explanation: Heat can burn skin quickly. Teachers set rules—like using tongs and waiting for cooling—to prevent injuries.
theoryLines: Heat safety is part of lab responsibility.
Ask before handling warm materials.

sci_p0_g3_experiments_easy_05.stem: Which sentence is written like a hypothesis?
options: If a plant gets more light, then it will grow taller.
Science is fun sometimes.
I like blue notebooks.
Today is Tuesday.
sci_p0_g3_experiments_easy_05.explanation: A hypothesis often uses an if-then idea you can test. It predicts a relationship you can check with evidence.
theoryLines: Hypotheses should be testable.
Results may support or not support a hypothesis.

sci_p0_g3_experiments_easy_06.stem: Why do scientists compare results from different trials or groups?
options: Comparing helps them see differences and decide what the evidence shows.
Comparing deletes the need for any hypothesis.
Comparing means changing every variable randomly.
Comparing forbids using tables or graphs.
sci_p0_g3_experiments_easy_06.explanation: Comparison is how patterns appear. Side-by-side results show whether a change made a real difference.
theoryLines: Evidence becomes clearer with comparison.
Fair groups make comparisons meaningful.

sci_p0_g3_experiments_hard_01.stem: What is a controlled variable (constant) in an experiment?
options: A condition you keep the same on purpose
The only thing you change every minute
A guess you never write down
A broken tool you still use
sci_p0_g3_experiments_hard_01.explanation: Constants stay steady so they do not confuse the results. For example, same soil type while testing water amount.
theoryLines: Identify change, measure, and keep-the-same factors.
Controls and constants improve fairness.

sci_p0_g3_experiments_hard_02.stem: What does it mean to replicate an experiment?
options: Do it again to see if you get similar results
Invent new numbers without testing
Change the question after seeing the answer
Hide the method from everyone
sci_p0_g3_experiments_hard_02.explanation: Replication checks reliability. If others—or you—can repeat the method and find similar results, confidence grows.
theoryLines: Science values results that can be repeated.
Clear methods make replication possible.

options: Using tools correctly and measuring more than once
Estimating wildly without looking
Rounding to whatever looks nicest
Switching units mid-table without noting it
sci_p0_g3_experiments_hard_03.explanation: Careful technique and repeats lower mistakes. Knowing a tool's limits also helps you interpret data wisely.
theoryLines: All measurements have some uncertainty.
Good habits improve data quality.

sci_p0_g3_experiments_hard_04.stem: You measure plant growth as 4 without units. What is the problem?
options: Without units, nobody knows if you mean 4 centimeters, 4 inches, or something else.
Numbers never need labels in science.
Units only matter for temperature.
Four is not allowed in data tables.
sci_p0_g3_experiments_hard_04.explanation: Units give numbers meaning. Clear labels prevent confusion when sharing or graphing results.
theoryLines: Always include units with measurements.
Convert carefully if you change unit systems.

sci_p0_g3_experiments_hard_05.stem: A student's conclusion disagrees with all of the data. What should they do?
options: Revise the conclusion so it fits the evidence.
Erase the data and keep the conclusion.
Ignore the mismatch completely.
Add made-up points until it matches.
sci_p0_g3_experiments_hard_05.explanation: In science, evidence leads. If data do not support a claim, the claim should change—or more testing may be needed.
theoryLines: Honesty about results matters.
Surprising data can still be valuable.

sci_p0_g3_experiments_hard_06.stem: What is a control group used for?
options: It provides a baseline to compare with the group that received the change.
It is the group allowed to break safety rules.
It is a group that skips all measurements.
It is a group that changes every variable.
sci_p0_g3_experiments_hard_06.explanation: The control group does not get the experimental treatment. Differences from the test group help show the treatment's effect.
theoryLines: Comparison needs a baseline.
Control groups strengthen fair tests.

options: They have hair or fur and feed milk to their babies.
They all breathe with gills underwater only.
They all lay hard-shelled eggs in nests like birds do exclusively.
They make food from sunlight using leaves.
sci_p0_g3_animals_easy_01.explanation: Mammals are a group of animals with shared traits, including fur/hair and milk for young. Dogs, cats, and humans are mammals.
theoryLines: Classification groups living things by shared features.
Not all mammals look alike, but they share key traits.

sci_p0_g3_animals_easy_02.stem: Cows are best described as which kind of eater?
options: Herbivores that eat plants
Carnivores that eat only meat
Animals that eat only rocks
Animals that do not need food
sci_p0_g3_animals_easy_02.explanation: Cows graze on grass and other plants. Their digestive systems are adapted for a plant-based diet.
theoryLines: Herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores have different diets.
Teeth and digestion often match diet type.

sci_p0_g3_animals_easy_03.stem: Why must animals living on land still get water?
options: Their body processes need water to keep working.
Water is only for fish and never for land animals.
Land animals drink water only to change color.
Water replaces oxygen for land animals.
sci_p0_g3_animals_easy_03.explanation: Water is essential for life on land and in water. Animals drink or get moisture from food and habitats.
theoryLines: All animals need water somehow.
Dry habitats make water especially precious.

sci_p0_g3_animals_easy_04.stem: What do bees collect from flowers?
options: Nectar (and they also pick up pollen)
Only bird feathers
Only fish scales
Only tree bark for nests in oceans
sci_p0_g3_animals_easy_04.explanation: Bees visit flowers for nectar to make food. While doing so, they often move pollen between flowers.
theoryLines: Flower visits can help both bees and plants.
Pollination supports seed and fruit production.

sci_p0_g3_animals_easy_05.stem: What covering do birds have that helps with flight and warmth?
options: Feathers
Wet fish scales only
Thick tree bark
Plastic shells
sci_p0_g3_animals_easy_05.explanation: Feathers are a key bird trait. They help with flying, steering, and keeping warm.
theoryLines: Birds are the only living animals with feathers.
Different feathers have different jobs.

sci_p0_g3_animals_easy_06.stem: Which animals use gills to get oxygen from water?
options: Most fish
Dogs
Eagles
House cats
sci_p0_g3_animals_easy_06.explanation: Gills are specialized for underwater gas exchange. Land pets like dogs and cats use lungs instead.
theoryLines: Breathing structures match habitats.
Oxygen is needed whether it comes from air or water.

sci_p0_g3_animals_hard_01.stem: What is one adaptation that helps animals survive cold climates?
options: Thick fur, fat layers, or behaviors that conserve heat
Losing all body covering in winter
Standing in wind with wet skin on purpose all night
Stopping food intake for months without any stores
sci_p0_g3_animals_hard_01.explanation: Insulation and smart behaviors reduce heat loss. Some animals also hibernate or migrate.
theoryLines: Adaptations solve environmental challenges.
Cold places select for heat-saving traits.

sci_p0_g3_animals_hard_02.stem: What does a food web show?
options: Many linked feeding relationships in an ecosystem
Only the weather forecast
A list of classroom rules
The planets in order from the sun
sci_p0_g3_animals_hard_02.explanation: Food webs are more complete than single chains. They show how energy connects many plants and animals.
theoryLines: Most ecosystems have complex feeding links.
Changes to one species can affect others.

sci_p0_g3_animals_hard_03.stem: How can camouflage help both predators and prey?
options: Prey can hide from hunters, and hunters can sneak closer to prey.
Camouflage removes the need for any food.
Camouflage turns animals into plants permanently.
Camouflage only works on animals that live in space.
sci_p0_g3_animals_hard_03.explanation: Blending into surroundings is useful on both sides of a hunt. Color, pattern, and shape can all contribute.
theoryLines: Camouflage is a common adaptation.
Survival strategies differ by species and habitat.

sci_p0_g3_animals_hard_04.stem: How do most mammal babies begin life compared with many insects?
options: Most mammals are born live and are fed milk by a parent.
Most mammals hatch as caterpillars first.
Most mammals start as seeds in soil.
Most mammals never need parental care.
sci_p0_g3_animals_hard_04.explanation: Mammal life cycles usually include live birth and milk feeding. Insect life cycles often include very different looking stages.
theoryLines: Life cycles vary across animal groups.
Parental care is common in mammals.

sci_p0_g3_animals_hard_05.stem: Why do many birds build nests?
options: Nests give eggs and chicks a safer place to develop.
Nests are used to store sunlight for winter.
Nests replace a bird's need to eat.
Nests turn eggs into mammals.
sci_p0_g3_animals_hard_05.explanation: A nest holds eggs and shelters chicks. Location and materials vary by bird species.
theoryLines: Animal homes support reproduction and survival.
Disturbing nests can harm young birds.

sci_p0_g3_animals_hard_06.stem: If predators disappear from an ecosystem, what might happen?
options: Some prey populations may grow too large and harm plants or balance.
Nothing in the ecosystem would ever change.
Plants would stop needing sunlight.
Prey would instantly become producers.
sci_p0_g3_animals_hard_06.explanation: Predators help regulate prey numbers. Without them, overgrazing or other imbalances can follow.
theoryLines: Ecosystem roles are connected.
Balance depends on many species, not one alone.

sci_p0_g3_plants_easy_01.stem: Which set lists basic needs of most plants?
options: Light, water, air, and nutrients
Homework, Wi-Fi, and headphones
Only darkness and motor oil
Only plastic and salt crystals
sci_p0_g3_plants_easy_01.explanation: Plants use light energy and take in water, air, and nutrients to live and grow. Missing needs limit growth.
theoryLines: Living things have requirements for survival.
Garden care matches plant needs.

sci_p0_g3_plants_easy_02.stem: Why are leaves especially important for a plant?
options: Capture light and help make food for the plant
Chase insects across the ground
Pump blood to animal hearts
Store electricity for cities
sci_p0_g3_plants_easy_02.explanation: Most photosynthesis happens in leaves. That food energy supports roots, stems, flowers, and fruits.
theoryLines: Leaf shape and arrangement can affect light capture.
Green plants rely on leaf function.

sci_p0_g3_plants_easy_03.stem: How do roots growing into soil mainly help a plant?
options: Anchoring it and taking up water and minerals
Flying it to new gardens
Making nectar for its own stomach
Hearing sounds underground
sci_p0_g3_plants_easy_03.explanation: Anchoring prevents tipping. Absorption supplies materials the plant needs for growth and photosynthesis.
theoryLines: Root systems can be shallow or deep.
Soil quality affects root health.

sci_p0_g3_plants_easy_04.stem: What is the main job of flowers on many plants?
options: Reproduction—helping the plant make seeds
Digesting rocks into soil vitamins
Pumping sap like an animal heart
Scaring away all sunlight
sci_p0_g3_plants_easy_04.explanation: Flowers contain reproductive parts. After pollination and fertilization, seeds (often inside fruits) can form.
theoryLines: Flowers are key to many plant life cycles.
Pollinators often assist flowering plants.

sci_p1_g4_body_easy_01.stem: Where does digestion of food begin?
options: In the mouth, where chewing and saliva start breaking food down
Only in the hair follicles
Only in the fingernails
Only in the outer ear
sci_p1_g4_body_easy_01.explanation: Teeth grind food and saliva begins chemical breakdown. Digestion continues in the stomach and intestines.
theoryLines: Mechanical and chemical digestion work together.
The digestive tract is a long pathway for food.

sci_p1_g4_body_easy_02.stem: What is the main job of the lungs?
options: Exchange gases—taking in oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide
Store undigested bones
Produce pollen for plants
Pump blood instead of the heart
sci_p1_g4_body_easy_02.explanation: Air enters the lungs, where oxygen moves into blood and carbon dioxide moves out to be exhaled.
theoryLines: Breathing supports cellular energy needs.
Lung health matters for activity and life.

sci_p1_g4_body_easy_03.stem: Why are teeth important for digestion?
options: They break food into smaller pieces that are easier to swallow and digest.
They filter wastes from the blood like kidneys.
They carry nerve signals to the toes only.
They produce red blood cells.
sci_p1_g4_body_easy_03.explanation: Chewing increases food's surface area so enzymes can work better. Different teeth shapes suit cutting and grinding.
theoryLines: Dental care supports good nutrition.
Digestion is harder with very large unchewed bites.

sci_p1_g4_body_easy_04.stem: What is the main job of the heart?
options: Pump blood through the circulatory system
Make bile for plant roots
Store memories in bone marrow only
Digest proteins in the mouth
sci_p1_g4_body_easy_04.explanation: Each heartbeat pushes blood into vessels. Circulation delivers oxygen and nutrients and removes wastes.
theoryLines: Heart muscle works continuously.
Exercise can strengthen cardiovascular fitness.

sci_p1_g4_body_hard_01.stem: If your pulse is faster, what is usually true?
options: Your heart is beating more times per minute.
Your bones have disappeared.
Your skin has stopped sensing touch.
Your stomach has become a lung.
sci_p1_g4_body_hard_01.explanation: Pulse rate matches heart rate. Exercise, excitement, or fever can raise how often the heart beats.
theoryLines: You can measure pulse at wrist or neck.
Resting rates are usually lower than exercise rates.

sci_p1_g4_body_hard_02.stem: How does oxygen from the air reach body cells?
options: Lungs put oxygen into blood, and blood carries it to cells.
Oxygen travels only through hair strands.
Oxygen is digested in the large intestine first.
Oxygen reaches cells only through the skin's sweat glands.
sci_p1_g4_body_hard_02.explanation: Gas exchange in the lungs loads red blood cells with oxygen. Circulation then delivers that oxygen throughout the body.
theoryLines: Respiratory and circulatory systems work together.
Cells use oxygen to release energy from nutrients.

sci_p1_g4_body_hard_03.stem: Why does blood flow to muscles increase during exercise?
options: Active muscles need more oxygen and nutrients delivered quickly.
Muscles stop using energy during exercise.
Blood flow increases to turn muscles into fat instantly.
Exercise shuts down the heart's pumping.
sci_p1_g4_body_hard_03.explanation: Working muscles have higher demand. The body responds by sending more blood where it is needed most.
theoryLines: Circulation adjusts to activity level.
Breathing rate often rises along with heart rate.

sci_p1_g4_body_hard_04.stem: What happens when you touch something hot?
options: Nerves quickly send danger signals so you can pull away.
Your bones dissolve to cool the object.
Your hair digests the heat.
Your lungs store the heat as sugar.
sci_p1_g4_body_hard_04.explanation: Sensory nerves detect heat and pain. The nervous system triggers a fast response to protect you from burns.
theoryLines: Reflexes can act very quickly.
Nerves link sensors, spinal cord, and brain.

sci_p1_g4_body_hard_05.stem: How do kidneys mainly help keep the body in balance?
options: Removing wastes and extra water from the blood
Producing oxygen for photosynthesis
Chewing food before it reaches the mouth
Replacing the brain during sleep
sci_p1_g4_body_hard_05.explanation: Filtering blood protects the internal environment. Urine carries removed wastes out of the body.
theoryLines: Excretory organs manage wastes.
Blood composition stays within healthy ranges partly thanks to kidneys.

sci_p1_g4_body_hard_06.stem: What can skipping a warm-up before intense activity increase the chance of?
options: Muscle strains and other injuries
Instant photosynthesis in skin
Growing a second skeleton overnight
Never needing water again
sci_p1_g4_body_hard_06.explanation: Cold, tight muscles and sudden hard effort raise injury risk. Warming up prepares tissues for stress.
theoryLines: Preparation supports safe performance.
Cool-downs after exercise also help recovery.

sci_p1_g4_experiments_easy_01.stem: What should a good hypothesis be?
options: A clear, testable prediction based on what you know
A secret answer you refuse to check
A random doodle unrelated to the question
A final grade for the experiment before testing
sci_p1_g4_experiments_easy_01.explanation: Good hypotheses guide what to measure. Experiments then produce evidence about the prediction.
theoryLines: Testable ideas drive investigations.
Revise thinking when evidence disagrees.

sci_p1_g4_experiments_easy_02.stem: What belongs in a data table during an experiment?
options: Organized measurements and observations from each trial
Only jokes with no numbers
Only the title of your favorite movie
Only guesses with no recording of results
sci_p1_g4_experiments_easy_02.explanation: Tables capture what happened in a structured way. Labels, units, and trial numbers keep data usable.
theoryLines: Good records support analysis.
Others should be able to read your table.

sci_p1_g4_experiments_easy_03.stem: Which tool measures length most directly?
options: A ruler or meter stick
A thermometer
A stopwatch only
A balance scale only
sci_p1_g4_experiments_easy_03.explanation: Rulers measure distance or length. Other tools measure different quantities like time, mass, or temperature.
theoryLines: Match the tool to the variable.
Read the scale carefully at eye level.

sci_p1_g4_experiments_easy_04.stem: In an experiment on fertilizer and plant height, what is the fertilizer amount usually called?
options: Independent variable (what you change)
Unit of temperature
Safety goggle type
Title of the graph only
sci_p1_g4_experiments_easy_04.explanation: You change fertilizer levels on purpose. Plant height would be what you measure as a possible effect.
theoryLines: Independent variable: what you change.
Dependent variable: what you measure.

sci_p1_g4_experiments_easy_05.stem: Which is a basic science-class safety rule?
options: Follow teacher directions and wear required protective gear.
Run with glassware for speed trials.
Taste unknown powders to identify them.
Remove labels from chemical bottles for fun.
sci_p1_g4_experiments_easy_05.explanation: Rules and protective gear prevent injuries. Listening carefully keeps everyone safer during investigations.
theoryLines: Safety is part of scientific practice.
Tell a teacher about spills or accidents right away.

sci_p1_g4_experiments_easy_06.stem: Why is a control setup useful in an experiment?
options: Shows what happens without the experimental change
Lets you skip measuring the test group
Proves every hypothesis true automatically
Removes units from all data
sci_p1_g4_experiments_easy_06.explanation: Without a control, it is harder to know whether your change mattered. The control is the comparison baseline.
theoryLines: Fair tests need thoughtful comparisons.
Keep non-tested conditions the same.

sci_p1_g4_experiments_hard_01.stem: Why do scientists often repeat the same trial many times?
options: To build confidence that results are not just a one-time accident
To ignore safety rules
To change two variables secretly
To avoid writing units
sci_p1_g4_experiments_hard_01.explanation: Repeats reveal consistency. Outliers become clearer, and average trends are more trustworthy.
theoryLines: Reliability grows with careful repetition.
Report all honest trials, not only favorites.

sci_p1_g4_experiments_hard_02.stem: A student used a bent ruler for every length measurement. What is the concern?
options: A faulty tool can create systematic measurement error.
Bent rulers always improve accuracy.
Tool condition never affects data.
Errors only happen in chemistry, not life science.
sci_p1_g4_experiments_hard_02.explanation: If the tool is wrong the same way each time, all values can be shifted. Check equipment before collecting data.
theoryLines: Sources of error should be considered.
Calibrated, undamaged tools matter.

sci_p1_g4_experiments_hard_03.stem: Why convert all length data to the same unit before graphing?
options: Mixed units make comparisons and graphs misleading or confusing.
Graphs forbid labels of any kind.
Units are optional once numbers exist.
Different units automatically mean the same amount.
sci_p1_g4_experiments_hard_03.explanation: Three inches and three centimeters are not equal. Consistent units let patterns show correctly.
theoryLines: Unit consistency is part of data quality.
Note conversions in your lab notebook.

options: "Based on our trials, seedlings with more light grew taller on average."
"I wanted taller plants, so that must be what happened."
"The plants grew because my lucky pencil was blue."
"We did not measure, but we are sure anyway."
sci_p1_g4_experiments_hard_04.explanation: Scientific conclusions cite evidence. They describe what data show rather than only wishes or unrelated luck.
theoryLines: Tie claims to measured results.
Mention sample size or limits when useful.

sci_p1_g4_experiments_hard_05.stem: What is watching birds at a feeder without changing anything mainly called?
options: Observation
An experiment that changes a variable
A control group chemical test
A measurement of mass with a balance
sci_p1_g4_experiments_hard_05.explanation: Observation gathers information carefully. An experiment would add a planned change, such as feeder type, to test an effect.
theoryLines: Both skills are valuable in science.
Questions determine whether you only observe or also experiment.

sci_p1_g4_animals_easy_01.stem: Why are fish well adapted to life in water?
options: Have gills and bodies suited for swimming in water
Have lungs only for climbing trees
Make nectar in underwater flowers
Grow fur instead of scales in oceans
sci_p1_g4_animals_easy_01.explanation: Gills and fins suit life in water. Body shape often reduces drag while swimming.
theoryLines: Habitat shapes animal adaptations.
Not all water animals are fish, but fish share key traits.

sci_p1_g4_animals_easy_02.stem: What is a caterpillar becoming a butterfly an example of?
options: Metamorphosis during a life cycle
Photosynthesis in animal cells
Hibernation inside a seed coat
Camouflage turning into migration
sci_p1_g4_animals_easy_02.explanation: Metamorphosis is a major body-form change across life stages. Butterflies are a classic example.
theoryLines: Life-cycle stages can look very different.
Each stage may have different needs.

sci_p1_g4_animals_easy_03.stem: How do bees help plants reproduce?
options: Move pollen from one flower to another
Cut off all of a plant's roots
Replace sunlight with flashlight beams
Turn petals into insects
sci_p1_g4_animals_easy_03.explanation: Pollen transfer enables fertilization in flowering plants. Many crops and wild plants benefit from bee pollination.
theoryLines: Pollinators support ecosystems and food supply.
Flower traits often attract pollinators.

options: A whale
A tuna fish
A robin
A frog
sci_p1_g4_animals_easy_04.explanation: Whales are mammals that live in water. They breathe air with lungs and feed milk to their young.
theoryLines: Mammals can live in many habitats.
Habitat alone does not decide the animal group.

options: By eating plants such as grass
By photosynthesizing with green fur
By hunting sharks in deep oceans
By drinking only motor oil
sci_p1_g4_animals_easy_05.explanation: As herbivores, cows convert plant material into energy and nutrients. Grazing is their main feeding strategy.
theoryLines: Energy enters many farms' food chains through plants.
Animal diets reflect adaptations.

sci_p1_g4_animals_easy_06.stem: What is a bird with a thick, strong beak most likely adapted to do?
options: Crack hard seeds or nuts
Filter ocean plankton with gills
Spin spider silk for webs
Absorb water only through roots
sci_p1_g4_animals_easy_06.explanation: Beak form matches feeding jobs. Thick beaks handle hard foods; other shapes suit nectar, meat, or probing mud.
theoryLines: Structure and function go together.
Comparing species shows adaptation patterns.

sci_p1_g4_animals_hard_01.stem: When a hawk hunts a mouse, what role is the hawk playing?
options: Predator
Producer
Decomposer fungus
Pollinating seed
sci_p1_g4_animals_hard_01.explanation: Predators catch and eat prey. Hawks are carnivores that hunt smaller animals.
theoryLines: Predator–prey pairs appear throughout food webs.
Hunting adaptations include sharp vision and talons in many birds of prey.

sci_p1_g4_animals_hard_02.stem: Why can camels survive well in desert conditions?
options: They conserve water and tolerate heat well
They need constant rainforest rainfall
They breathe only with fish gills
They hibernate under sea ice
sci_p1_g4_animals_hard_02.explanation: Desert specialists manage heat and limited water. Camels are classic examples of such adaptations.
theoryLines: Extreme habitats demand extreme adaptations.
Behavior and body traits both matter.

sci_p1_g4_animals_hard_03.stem: What is an insect that looks like a leaf most likely using?
options: Camouflage to avoid being eaten
Echolocation to find nectar
Gills to breathe on land
Migration to leave Earth's orbit
sci_p1_g4_animals_hard_03.explanation: Looking like a leaf hides the insect from predators. Camouflage is a defensive adaptation.
theoryLines: Appearance can improve survival odds.
Predators may also use camouflage when hunting.

sci_p1_g4_animals_hard_04.stem: Why do tadpoles usually live in water but may live more on land later?
options: Go through metamorphosis with changing body features
Stay identical from birth to adulthood
Are mammals that drink milk as tadpoles
Photosynthesize until they grow wings
sci_p1_g4_animals_hard_04.explanation: Frog development transforms swimming tadpoles into four-legged adults. Breathing and movement features change with the stage.
theoryLines: Amphibian life cycles often need water early on.
Habitat needs can shift during growth.

sci_p1_g4_animals_hard_05.stem: How does protecting forests, wetlands, and grasslands help animals?
options: It preserves habitats where they find food, water, and shelter
It removes all predators overnight worldwide
It stops animals from needing adaptations
It turns every species into house pets
sci_p1_g4_animals_hard_05.explanation: Habitat protection keeps ecosystems functional. Without habitat, even well-adapted animals cannot thrive.
theoryLines: Conservation focuses on places as well as species.
Healthy habitats support biodiversity.

sci_p1_g5_body_easy_01.stem: The kidneys are part of which body job?
options: Filtering wastes from blood
Pumping air into feathers
Making chlorophyll for skin
Storing pollen in bone marrow
sci_p1_g5_body_easy_01.explanation: Kidneys clean blood and help control water and salt balance. Wastes leave as urine.
theoryLines: Excretion removes harmful leftovers.
Organ systems cooperate to keep conditions stable.

sci_p1_g5_body_easy_02.stem: Why can you feel a pulse?
options: Blood surges through arteries with each heartbeat
Bones vibrate from photosynthesis
Hair follicles beat like drums
Skin cells pump oxygen into the air
sci_p1_g5_body_easy_02.explanation: Arterial pulses match heartbeats. Feeling pulse is a simple way to monitor heart rate.
theoryLines: Pulse points include wrist and neck.
Heart rate responds to activity and rest.

options: Message pathways that carry signals through the body
Stomach chambers that store rocks
Leaf veins that photosynthesize in humans
Second skeletons outside the skin
sci_p1_g5_body_easy_03.explanation: The nervous system communicates with electrical and chemical signals. Fast messaging coordinates sensing and movement.
theoryLines: Brain, spinal cord, and nerves form a network.
Damage to nerves can affect feeling or movement.

sci_p1_g5_body_easy_04.stem: Why are nutrients from food important for your body?
options: Provide energy and materials for growth and repair
Replace the need for oxygen completely
Turn blood into plant sap
Stop cells from ever needing water
sci_p1_g5_body_easy_04.explanation: Proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, and minerals each play roles. Balanced eating supports body function.
theoryLines: Digestion releases nutrients for absorption.
Different foods supply different nutrient mixes.

sci_p1_g5_body_easy_05.stem: What happens to your lungs when you inhale?
options: Fill with air so oxygen can enter the blood
Fill with food for digestion
Pump blood to the feet only
Produce urine for the kidneys
sci_p1_g5_body_easy_05.explanation: Inhaling brings fresh air into tiny air sacs. Oxygen crosses into blood while carbon dioxide exits.
theoryLines: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs.
Respiratory health affects energy and endurance.

sci_p1_g5_body_easy_06.stem: Besides the sense of touch, how else does skin help your body?
options: Protecting the body and helping control temperature
Photosynthesizing meals for the brain
Filtering blood like a kidney
Storing long-term factual memories
sci_p1_g5_body_easy_06.explanation: Skin is a barrier against injury and many germs. Sweating and blood-flow changes in skin help with temperature control.
theoryLines: Skin is the body's largest organ.
Cuts should be cleaned to support healing and reduce infection risk.

sci_p1_g5_body_medium_01.stem: Why is oxygen-poor blood sent to the lungs?
options: It can pick up oxygen before returning to the body
It can be turned into stomach acid
It can become white bone tissue
It can leave the body permanently through sweat only
sci_p1_g5_body_medium_01.explanation: The heart routes blood to the lungs for gas exchange, then sends oxygen-rich blood out to body tissues.
theoryLines: Circulation has pulmonary and systemic pathways.
Gas exchange keeps cells supplied with oxygen.

sci_p1_g5_body_medium_02.stem: What does muscle fatigue after intense activity often mean?
options: Muscles have used a lot of energy and need rest and recovery
Muscles have permanently turned into fat overnight
Bones no longer attach to tendons
Nerves have permanently shut off forever
sci_p1_g5_body_medium_02.explanation: Hard work depletes energy supplies and stresses muscle fibers. Rest, water, and nutrients support recovery.
theoryLines: Training gradually builds endurance.
Pain that is sharp or severe should be reported to an adult.

sci_p1_g5_body_medium_03.stem: What is one important job of the liver?
options: It helps process nutrients and clean many harmful substances from the blood.
It pumps air into the lungs with each breath.
It stores urine made by the skin.
It replaces the need for a digestive system.
sci_p1_g5_body_medium_03.explanation: The liver is a busy chemical factory. It processes nutrients and helps manage toxins and wastes in the blood.
theoryLines: Organ systems share overlapping jobs.
A healthy lifestyle supports liver function.

sci_p1_g5_body_medium_04.stem: Why does staying hydrated help during long sports practices?
options: Water lost in sweat must be replaced for the body to work well.
Water freezes muscles so they cannot move.
Water removes oxygen from blood on purpose.
Water stops nerves from sending any signals.
sci_p1_g5_body_medium_04.explanation: Sweating cools you but reduces body water. Replacing fluids helps circulation, temperature control, and performance.
theoryLines: Thirst and dark urine can signal low fluid levels.
Plan water breaks in hot weather.

sci_p1_g5_body_medium_05.stem: Why does food move into the intestines after the stomach?
options: Continue digestion and absorb nutrients into the blood
Begin photosynthesis with chlorophyll
Form new skull bones immediately
Pump oxygen into the lungs
sci_p1_g5_body_medium_05.explanation: The small intestine is a major site of nutrient absorption. The large intestine helps reclaim water and form waste.
theoryLines: Digestion is a multi-step pathway.
Absorbed nutrients travel by blood to cells.

sci_p1_g5_body_medium_06.stem: Why do scientists or doctors measure a person's pulse?
options: To learn about heart rate and how hard the circulatory system is working
To measure exact hair length in millimeters only
To learn stomach enzyme brand names
To count the number of bones grown that hour
sci_p1_g5_body_medium_06.explanation: Pulse is a window into heart activity. It can show rest, exercise response, or possible health concerns.
theoryLines: Heart rate is beats per minute.
Context matters when interpreting pulse.

sci_p1_g5_body_hard_01.stem: What does regular cardio exercise (like brisk walking or swimming) most directly strengthen?
options: The heart and endurance of the circulatory and respiratory systems
Only fingernail hardness
Only the ability to digest rocks
Only night vision in complete darkness
sci_p1_g5_body_hard_01.explanation: Cardio challenges heart and lungs in a healthy way over time. Fitness improvements show up in endurance and recovery.
theoryLines: Physical activity supports long-term health.
Choose activities that are safe and enjoyable.

sci_p1_g5_body_hard_02.stem: Why is warming up properly before sprinting useful?
options: Increases blood flow and prepares muscles for sudden hard effort
Removes lactic acid by stopping breathing
Converts muscle into bone for speed
Eliminates the need for shoes and safety
sci_p1_g5_body_hard_02.explanation: Warm tissues move more freely and receive more blood. That preparation can improve performance and reduce injury risk.
theoryLines: Warm-ups are part of smart training.
Intensity should rise gradually.

sci_p1_g5_body_hard_03.stem: What are arteries, veins, and capillaries all types of?
options: Blood vessels that transport blood throughout the body
Bones in the wrist only
Types of digestive enzymes
Parts of a plant root tip
sci_p1_g5_body_hard_03.explanation: Different vessels have different roles: arteries usually carry blood away from the heart, veins return it, and capillaries exchange materials with tissues.
theoryLines: The vessel network reaches nearly every body region.
Healthy vessels support oxygen delivery.

sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_01.stem: Which question is best investigated with a testable hypothesis?
options: Does fertilizer amount affect bean plant height after two weeks?
Which song is the most beautiful forever?
What is the luckiest color of pencil?
Should people prefer cats or dogs as a moral rule?
sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_01.explanation: Scientific questions are ones you can test with measurements. Beauty and pure opinion questions are not fair experiment targets.
theoryLines: Testable questions lead to measurable variables.
Not every interesting question is a science experiment.

sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_02.stem: If you change only the type of soil and measure plant growth, what is soil type called?
options: Independent variable
Dependent variable only
Unit conversion chart
Safety contract signature
sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_02.explanation: The independent variable is what the experimenter changes. Growth results would be the dependent variable.
theoryLines: Name variables clearly before you start.
Keep other conditions constant.

sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_03.stem: What should a lab log include?
options: Procedures, observations, measurements, and dates
Only emojis with no data
Only the final guess, with methods erased
Only a list of friends' names
sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_03.explanation: Detailed logs let you and others understand what was done and found. They support honest analysis and replication.
theoryLines: Science depends on clear communication.
Write observations as they happen.

sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_04.stem: Why might one unusual trial not be enough to trust a conclusion?
options: A single result could be a mistake or random chance.
Unusual trials always prove the hypothesis.
Science never uses more than one measurement.
Repeating trials is against lab rules.
sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_04.explanation: Outliers happen. More trials help you see whether a pattern is real or just noise.
theoryLines: Sample size and repeats matter.
Investigate possible errors when results look odd.

sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_05.stem: Which tool is best for measuring an object's mass in class?
options: A balance or scale
A meter stick only
A thermometer only
A compass only
sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_05.explanation: Balances and scales measure mass (or weight, depending on the device). Length and temperature need different tools.
theoryLines: Select instruments that match the quantity.
Record mass with units such as grams.

sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_06.stem: If a chemical spills during a lab, what should you do first?
options: Alert the teacher and follow the class spill procedure
Wipe it with your bare hands and taste to identify it
Ignore it if it looks like water
Hide the spill so nobody notices
sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_06.explanation: Teachers know the safe cleanup steps for different materials. Quick, honest reporting prevents bigger problems.
theoryLines: Never guess with unknown substances.
Protective gear and procedures reduce risk.

sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_07.stem: In a test about a medicine-plant growth myth, what are the untreated plants often called?
options: Control group used for comparison
Independent variable amount
Graph title font
Broken thermometer collection
sci_p1_g5_experiments_easy_07.explanation: Untreated plants show baseline growth. Comparing them with treated plants reveals whether the treatment mattered.
theoryLines: Controls anchor interpretation of results.
Treat groups the same except for the tested factor.

sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_01.stem: What is an owl catching a mouse an example of?
options: A predator–prey relationship
A plant pollinating a fungus
A rock cycle stage
A seed germinating in darkness only
sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_01.explanation: Owls hunt prey for food. Predator–prey links move energy through food webs.
theoryLines: Night hunters often have sharp senses.
Prey species have defenses too, such as hiding or speed.

sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_02.stem: What body features do insects typically have?
options: Six legs and three main body parts
Feathers and hollow mammal bones only
Gills and fur at the same time as adults on land
No legs and a backbone like fish
sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_02.explanation: Adult insects usually show a head, thorax, and abdomen with six legs. They are a huge, diverse animal group.
theoryLines: Classification uses shared body features.
Not every small crawling animal is an insect.

sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_03.stem: Why do farmers often value bees?
options: Bees pollinate crops that produce fruits and seeds
Bees produce rainfall on demand
Bees replace soil nutrients with plastic
Bees hunt whales for ocean farms
sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_03.explanation: Many fruits and vegetables depend on pollinators. Bee activity can raise crop yields and support wild plants.
theoryLines: Ecosystem services help people as well as wildlife.
Protecting pollinator habitat matters.

sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_04.stem: Rabbits are herbivores. What does that mean?
options: Eat plants
Eat only other mammals
Make food from sunlight in their fur
Do not need energy from food
sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_04.explanation: Herbivores feed on plant material. Rabbit teeth and digestion are suited to that diet.
theoryLines: Diet categories help describe food-web roles.
Herbivores are often prey for carnivores.

options: A snake
A robin
A dolphin
A butterfly
sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_05.explanation: Snakes are reptiles. Reptiles typically have dry scaly skin and different life-cycle traits from birds, mammals, and insects.
theoryLines: Animal groups share defining characteristics.
Habitat alone does not tell you the group.

sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_06.stem: Why are gills useful for many aquatic animals?
options: Allow many aquatic animals to take oxygen from water
Let land mammals photosynthesize
Store pollen for winter nests
Turn carbon dioxide into fur
sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_06.explanation: Water holds dissolved oxygen. Gills extract it so fish and some other aquatic animals can breathe underwater.
theoryLines: Gas exchange structures fit the environment.
Lungs are common for breathing air.

sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_07.stem: In a food web, what are producers usually?
options: Plants (and some other organisms) that make food with light energy
Only top predators with no prey
Only fungi that hunt mammals
Only animals that migrate at night
sci_p1_g5_animals_easy_07.explanation: Producers form the energy base. Consumers depend on that energy directly or indirectly.
theoryLines: Food webs start with energy capture.
Without producers, consumer populations collapse.

sci_p1_g5_animals_medium_01.stem: If a plant disease kills most producers in an area, what is likely?
options: Animals that eat those plants—and then their predators—may decline too.
Predators will start photosynthesizing instead.
Food webs become unrelated to energy.
Herbivores will need no food afterward.
sci_p1_g5_animals_medium_01.explanation: Energy and population effects ripple upward. Losing producers stresses the entire web.
theoryLines: Species interactions create dependence.
Ecosystem health starts with primary production.

sci_p1_g5_animals_medium_02.stem: What is thick blubber in a marine mammal mainly an adaptation for?
options: Insulation against cold water
Flying long distances in air
Photosynthesizing under ice
Walking on desert sand dunes
sci_p1_g5_animals_medium_02.explanation: Fat layers trap heat in chilly seas. Insulation is critical where water pulls heat away quickly.
theoryLines: Cold environments favor heat-saving traits.
Behavior and body chemistry can also help.

sci_p1_g5_animals_medium_03.stem: Why does a snowshoe hare with a white winter coat use camouflage?
options: Blend into snowy surroundings and avoid predators
Attract bees for pollination
Breathe underwater with hidden gills
Migrate to the moon each January
sci_p1_g5_animals_medium_03.explanation: Seasonal coat color matching snow makes the hare harder to spot. Camouflage improves survival odds.
theoryLines: Some adaptations change with seasons.
Predator vision shapes prey defenses.

sci_p1_g5_animals_medium_04.stem: Which statement about mammals is accurate?
options: Mammals are vertebrates that usually have hair and produce milk.
Mammals never live in water.
Mammals are the only animals with eyes.
Mammals all lay jelly-coated frog eggs.
sci_p1_g5_animals_medium_04.explanation: Shared traits define mammals across habitats—from bats to whales to humans—despite different lifestyles.
theoryLines: Vertebrates have backbones.
Milk feeding is a mammal hallmark.

sci_p1_g5_animals_medium_05.stem: Why is it important to leave nesting wildlife alone?
options: Disturbance can cause parents to abandon eggs or young.
Nests explode when photographed from far away.
Young animals never need protection.
Nests are not part of animal survival strategies.
sci_p1_g5_animals_medium_05.explanation: Breeding success depends on quiet, safe nesting sites. People can watch respectfully from a distance.
theoryLines: Human behavior affects wildlife outcomes.
Laws often protect nests of certain species.

sci_p1_g5_animals_medium_06.stem: Why do birds that migrate long distances usually migrate?
options: Find better climate and food resources in different seasons
Practice swimming with gills
Avoid ever needing energy
Turn into mammals for winter
sci_p1_g5_animals_medium_06.explanation: Migration tracks shifting food and weather. It is an energetic journey timed to seasonal change.
theoryLines: Not all birds migrate.
Navigation can use multiple environmental cues.

sci_p1_g5_animals_hard_01.stem: How can building over wetlands without protections mainly harm animals?
options: Destroying habitat they need for food, breeding, and shelter
Giving every species unlimited new space automatically
Stopping weather from changing ever again
Converting predators into producers overnight
sci_p1_g5_animals_hard_01.explanation: Wetlands support many species. Filling or paving them removes critical resources and can collapse local populations.
theoryLines: Land-use choices have ecological consequences.
Habitat conservation is a core protection strategy.

sci_p1_g5_animals_hard_02.stem: In a food chain, what do producers provide for the rest of the living things?
options: Food energy made from sunlight
Only shade and cooler air
Nothing useful for animals
Only rocks and minerals
sci_p1_g5_animals_hard_02.explanation: Producers such as plants capture sunlight and make food. That food energy then moves to animals that eat plants and to animals that eat other animals.
theoryLines: Producers make food using sunlight.
Energy moves from producers to consumers along a food chain.

sci_p1_g5_animals_hard_03.stem: Why are many bats active at night instead of during the day?
options: There is less competition and danger from daytime hunters
Their ears only work in bright sunlight
They must drink salt water every hour
They can live only underwater
sci_p1_g5_animals_hard_03.explanation: Many bats hunt at night when fewer daytime predators are active and when their night-hunting senses work well.
theoryLines: Nocturnal animals are active mainly at night.
Bats often use hearing and echolocation to find food in the dark.

sci_p1_g6_body_easy_01.stem: What is the main job of the digestive system?
options: Break food down so the body can use nutrients
Carry oxygen into every bone
Pump air out of the lungs only
Keep the body cold in every season
sci_p1_g6_body_easy_01.explanation: The digestive system breaks food into smaller pieces and nutrients the body can absorb and use for energy and growth.
theoryLines: Digestion breaks food into usable nutrients.
Organs such as the stomach and intestines help digest food.

options: It pumps blood through the body
It makes all the light we see
It covers the body like skin
It stores unused food forever
sci_p1_g6_body_easy_02.explanation: The heart is a strong muscle that pumps blood so oxygen and nutrients can reach body cells.
theoryLines: The heart is part of the circulatory system.
Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to tissues.

sci_p1_g6_body_easy_03.stem: Why does your body need water every day?
options: Water helps body systems work and stay balanced
Water replaces the need for sleep
Water turns bones into metal
Water stops the heart from beating
sci_p1_g6_body_easy_03.explanation: Water helps transport materials, control temperature, and keep cells and organs working well.
theoryLines: The body is made of a large amount of water.
Drinking water supports healthy body function.

sci_p1_g6_body_easy_04.stem: What is the main job of the lungs?
options: Bring oxygen into the blood and remove carbon dioxide
Digest all the food you eat
Control eyesight in bright light
Make new bones grow longer
sci_p1_g6_body_easy_04.explanation: When you breathe, the lungs take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide as a waste gas.
theoryLines: The lungs are the main organs of breathing.
Oxygen from air moves into the blood in the lungs.

sci_p1_g6_body_easy_05.stem: Where does most of the energy your body uses come from?
options: Food you eat
Only the color of your clothes
Sounds you hear
Shadows on the wall
sci_p1_g6_body_easy_05.explanation: Food provides chemical energy. Digestion and body processes turn that energy into fuel for movement, growth, and warmth.
theoryLines: Food is the body's main energy source.
Nutrients from food help cells do work.

sci_p1_g6_body_medium_01.stem: How does oxygen get from the lungs to the rest of the body?
options: Blood carries oxygen from the lungs to body cells
Blood carries light from the eyes to the toes
Blood turns oxygen into solid rock
Oxygen travels only through the hair
sci_p1_g6_body_medium_01.explanation: Oxygen enters the blood in the lungs. Circulating blood then delivers that oxygen to cells throughout the body.
theoryLines: The circulatory system moves blood around the body.
Red blood cells help carry oxygen.

sci_p1_g6_body_medium_02.stem: Why do working muscles need a steady supply of oxygen?
options: Oxygen helps muscles release energy from nutrients
Oxygen paints the muscles a new color
Oxygen replaces bones during exercise
Oxygen stops muscles from ever resting
sci_p1_g6_body_medium_02.explanation: Active muscles need more energy. Oxygen helps cells release energy from food so muscles can keep working.
theoryLines: Muscle cells use oxygen to make energy.
Breathing and blood flow increase during hard activity.

sci_p1_g6_body_medium_03.stem: What is an important job of the kidneys?
options: Filter waste from the blood and help make urine
Pump oxygen straight into the ears
Store sunlight under the skin
Heat the body by burning bones
sci_p1_g6_body_medium_03.explanation: Kidneys clean the blood by removing wastes and extra water, which leave the body as urine.
theoryLines: Kidneys are part of the excretory system.
Healthy kidneys help keep blood chemistry balanced.

sci_p1_g6_body_medium_04.stem: What does the nervous system mainly do?
options: Send messages between the brain, senses, and body parts
Digest food in the stomach only
Make light for the eyes
Carry blood instead of the heart
sci_p1_g6_body_medium_04.explanation: Nerves and the brain carry signals that help you sense the world, think, and control movement.
theoryLines: The nervous system includes the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.
Nerve signals travel quickly through the body.

sci_p1_g6_body_medium_05.stem: Why is warming up before hard exercise helpful?
options: It gently prepares muscles for stronger activity
It removes the need for oxygen
It turns muscles into bone
It stops the heart from pumping
sci_p1_g6_body_medium_05.explanation: A warm-up increases blood flow and loosens muscles so they are ready for harder movement and less likely to strain.
theoryLines: Warm muscles work more safely during exercise.
Light activity before a workout prepares the body.

sci_p1_g6_body_medium_06.stem: What is one important job of the skin?
options: Protect the body and help sense touch
Make light for night vision
Pump blood to the lungs
Digest food in the mouth
sci_p1_g6_body_medium_06.explanation: Skin is a protective covering. It also helps with touch sensing and helps control body temperature.
theoryLines: Skin is the body's outer protective layer.
Nerve endings in the skin detect touch, heat, and pain.

sci_p1_g6_body_hard_01.stem: What does your pulse mainly tell you about?
options: How fast your heart is beating
How long your hair is growing
How much light your eyes store
How thick your skin feels
sci_p1_g6_body_hard_01.explanation: A pulse is the throb you feel when blood is pushed by each heartbeat. Counting it shows heart rate.
theoryLines: Pulse rate rises during exercise and strong feelings.
Heartbeats push waves of blood through arteries.

sci_p1_g6_body_hard_02.stem: What is the main job of blood vessels?
options: Carry blood to and from body parts
Create images in the eyes
Make sounds for hearing
Store unused air in bones
sci_p1_g6_body_hard_02.explanation: Arteries, veins, and capillaries form pathways that move blood around the body.
theoryLines: Blood vessels are tubes that transport blood.
The heart and vessels work together as a system.

sci_p1_g6_body_hard_03.stem: Why do body cells need oxygen?
options: To help release energy from food nutrients
To turn hearing into sight
To replace water with sand
To stop all chemical reactions
sci_p1_g6_body_hard_03.explanation: Cells use oxygen in processes that release energy from nutrients so the body can work and stay alive.
theoryLines: Cellular respiration uses oxygen to help make usable energy.
Without enough oxygen, cells cannot work well.

sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_01.stem: What is a hypothesis in a science experiment?
options: A testable idea about what might happen
The final score of a sports game
A list of tools with no purpose
A drawing that cannot be checked
sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_01.explanation: A hypothesis is an educated guess you can test with an experiment and evidence.
theoryLines: Scientists write hypotheses before testing ideas.
Results can support or not support a hypothesis.

sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_02.stem: Why do scientists change only one variable at a time in a fair test?
options: So they can tell what caused the result
So every measurement becomes identical forever
So they never need to record data
So the experiment finishes without tools
sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_02.explanation: If too many things change at once, you cannot know which change caused the outcome.
theoryLines: A fair test keeps most conditions the same.
The independent variable is the one you purposely change.

sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_03.stem: Why should you write down what happens during an experiment?
options: A clear log helps you remember and share results
Notes make the equipment heavier
Writing replaces the need for safety
Logs turn water into ice instantly
sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_03.explanation: Recording observations and measurements lets you check your work and compare results later.
theoryLines: Scientists keep careful records of procedures and data.
Good notes make experiments easier to repeat.

sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_04.stem: Why do scientists often repeat an experiment?
options: To check whether the results are reliable
To invent a new planet each time
To avoid measuring anything
To erase all earlier evidence
sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_04.explanation: Repeating a test helps show whether results happen again and are not just a lucky accident.
theoryLines: Reliable results can be repeated under similar conditions.
Repeating trials reduces the chance of a one-time mistake.

sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_05.stem: Why do scientists use standard units when they measure?
options: So others can understand and compare the measurements
So every object becomes the same size
So no tools are ever needed
So experiments never need safety rules
sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_05.explanation: Units such as centimeters, grams, and degrees Celsius let people share clear, comparable data.
theoryLines: Standard units make measurements meaningful to others.
Using the right unit matches the kind of measurement.

sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_06.stem: What is a control in many science experiments?
options: A comparison setup that does not get the tested change
A rule that bans all measuring tools
A guess that can never be checked
A chart with no labels at all
sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_06.explanation: A control group or control setup shows what happens without the tested change, so you can compare results fairly.
theoryLines: Controls help scientists see the effect of one change.
Comparing treatment and control makes conclusions stronger.

sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_07.stem: What is the most important reason to follow safety rules in a lab?
options: To protect people and prevent accidents
To make experiments finish faster only
To avoid writing any observations
To keep results secret from everyone
sci_p1_g6_experiments_easy_07.explanation: Safety rules reduce harm from spills, heat, sharp tools, and other lab risks.
theoryLines: Wear safety gear when a procedure calls for it.
Ask an adult before using unfamiliar lab materials.

sci_p1_g6_animals_easy_01.stem: Which trait do mammals usually share?
options: They have hair or fur and feed milk to their young
They breathe only with gills in water
They are covered only in dry scales and never grow hair
They make food from sunlight like green plants
sci_p1_g6_animals_easy_01.explanation: Mammals are warm-blooded animals with hair or fur. Mothers produce milk for their babies.
theoryLines: Dogs, cats, whales, and humans are mammals.
Milk feeding is a key mammal trait.

sci_p1_g6_animals_easy_02.stem: What kind of eater is a cow?
options: A herbivore that mainly eats plants
A carnivore that eats only meat
An animal that never needs food
A producer that makes sunlight
sci_p1_g6_animals_easy_02.explanation: Cows eat grass and other plants, so they are herbivores.
theoryLines: Herbivores eat plants.
Cows have teeth suited for chewing plant material.

sci_p1_g6_animals_easy_03.stem: What helps fish live successfully in water?
options: They use gills to take oxygen from water
They grow lungs that only work in deserts
They drink only boiling water
They make nests from dry leaves only
sci_p1_g6_animals_easy_03.explanation: Fish take dissolved oxygen from water through gills and have bodies shaped for swimming.
theoryLines: Gills let fish breathe underwater.
Fins help fish move and keep balance.

sci_p1_g6_animals_easy_04.stem: How do bees help many flowering plants?
options: They carry pollen from flower to flower
They turn wood into metal
They replace sunlight for plants
They pump blood into plant stems
sci_p1_g6_animals_easy_04.explanation: As bees visit flowers for nectar, pollen sticks to them and moves to other flowers, helping plants make seeds.
theoryLines: Pollination helps plants reproduce.
Bees are important pollinators.

options: Wings and lightweight bodies
Gills for breathing underwater
Thick shells like turtles
Roots that grow into soil
sci_p1_g6_animals_easy_05.explanation: Birds have wings, feathers, and body features that make flight possible for many species.
theoryLines: Feathers help with flight and keeping warm.
Not every bird flies well, but wings are a bird trait.

sci_p1_g6_animals_easy_06.stem: How do reptiles usually get the heat they need?
options: They warm up from the environment around them
They make their own heat the way mammals always do
They melt ice with electric sparks
They never need any warmth at all
sci_p1_g6_animals_easy_06.explanation: Most reptiles are ectothermic, so they rely on sunlight and warm surroundings to manage body temperature.
theoryLines: Lizards often bask in the sun to warm up.
Reptile activity can slow down in cold weather.

options: An animal that hunts and eats other animals
A plant that makes all its own meat
An animal that eats only rocks
A cloud that forms over the ocean
sci_p1_g6_animals_easy_07.explanation: Predators catch prey for food. Lions, hawks, and sharks are examples of predators.
theoryLines: Predators are consumers in food chains.
Prey animals are hunted by predators.

sci_p1_g6_animals_medium_01.stem: What does a food web show better than a single food chain?
options: Many overlapping feeding relationships in an ecosystem
Only one animal eating one plant forever
The exact birthday of every animal
How clouds form during storms
sci_p1_g6_animals_medium_01.explanation: A food web connects many food chains and shows how energy can move through several paths.
theoryLines: Most animals eat more than one kind of food.
Food webs show how living things depend on one another.

sci_p1_g6_animals_medium_02.stem: What can help some mammals stay warm in cold weather?
options: Thick fur or a layer of body fat
Growing gills on their backs
Turning completely into plants
Stopping all blood flow
sci_p1_g6_animals_medium_02.explanation: Fur and fat help trap heat so mammals can survive cold habitats.
theoryLines: Adaptations help animals live in their environments.
Insulation reduces heat loss in cold places.

sci_p1_g6_animals_medium_03.stem: How can camouflage help an animal survive?
options: It helps the animal blend in with its surroundings
It makes the animal glow brighter than the sun
It replaces the need for food
It turns predators into plants
sci_p1_g6_animals_medium_03.explanation: Camouflage colors or patterns make an animal harder to see, which can help it hide from predators or sneak up on prey.
theoryLines: Camouflage is a useful adaptation.
Many insects, fish, and mammals use camouflage.

options: The stages an organism goes through as it grows and reproduces
A list of clouds in alphabetical order
A map of only mountain rocks
A single meal an animal eats once
sci_p1_g6_animals_medium_04.explanation: A life cycle describes stages such as egg, young, and adult for animals, or seed to plant for many plants.
theoryLines: Different species have different life-cycle stages.
Reproduction continues the life cycle for the next generation.

sci_p1_g6_animals_medium_05.stem: Why do many birds build nests?
options: To protect eggs and raise their young
To store sunlight for winter
To pump blood through trees
To stop all weather changes
sci_p1_g6_animals_medium_05.explanation: Nests give eggs and chicks a safer place to develop until they are ready for more independence.
theoryLines: Nest design can differ by bird species.
Parents often feed and guard young in the nest.

options: The place where an organism lives and finds what it needs
A tool used only to measure temperature
A type of blood cell
A shadow made by the moon
sci_p1_g6_animals_medium_06.explanation: A habitat provides food, water, shelter, and space for living things.
theoryLines: Forests, deserts, ponds, and oceans are habitats.
If a habitat changes a lot, animals may struggle to survive.

sci_p1_g6_animals_medium_07.stem: How can animals help plants spread their seeds?
options: By carrying seeds on fur or in droppings to new places
By turning seeds into pure metal
By blocking all sunlight forever
By pumping blood into every leaf
sci_p1_g6_animals_medium_07.explanation: Animals move seeds when they eat fruit or when seeds stick to them, helping plants grow in new locations.
theoryLines: Seed dispersal spreads plants across an area.
Wind, water, and animals can all move seeds.

sci_p1_g6_animals_hard_01.stem: What usually happens when predators become scarce in an ecosystem?
options: Prey populations may grow larger for a while
All plants instantly disappear
Rain stops falling forever
Every animal turns into a producer
sci_p1_g6_animals_hard_01.explanation: Predators help control prey numbers. With fewer predators, prey can increase until food or space runs short.
theoryLines: Predator and prey populations affect each other.
Balance in ecosystems depends on many living links.

sci_p1_g6_animals_hard_02.stem: What can happen when animals lose their natural habitat?
options: They may struggle to find food, shelter, and safe places to live
They automatically gain unlimited food
They no longer need water
Plants stop needing sunlight
sci_p1_g6_animals_hard_02.explanation: Habitat loss removes the resources animals need, so populations can decline or animals must move.
theoryLines: Protecting habitats helps protect wildlife.
Human activities can shrink or damage habitats.

sci_p1_g6_animals_hard_03.stem: How do many bats find food in the dark?
options: They use echolocation by listening to returning sound echoes
They read road maps with sunlight only
They taste colors in the air
They dig wells for salt water
sci_p1_g6_animals_hard_03.explanation: Bats send out sounds and listen for echoes that bounce off insects and other objects, helping them hunt at night.
theoryLines: Echolocation works even when there is little light.
Hearing is especially important for many night-active bats.

sci_p1_g6_animals_hard_04.stem: Why do amphibians often need moist places to live?
options: Their skin usually needs moisture, and many lay eggs in water
They only eat dry sand
They breathe only hot desert air
They grow feathers that must stay dusty
sci_p1_g6_animals_hard_04.explanation: Many amphibians have permeable skin and begin life in water, so wet habitats are important for survival.
theoryLines: Frogs and salamanders are amphibians.
Amphibian eggs often develop in ponds or other wet places.

sci_vol_g1_body_medium_01.stem: What is the heart's job in the circulatory system?
options: It pumps blood through the body
It paints the bones yellow
It makes all the food you eat
It stores unused oxygen in hair
sci_vol_g1_body_medium_01.explanation: The heart pushes blood so oxygen and nutrients can travel to body parts.
theoryLines: Blood moves in a loop through the body.
A beating heart keeps circulation going.

sci_vol_g1_body_medium_02.stem: Why is drinking water important for your body?
options: It helps keep your body working and feeling well
It replaces the need to breathe
It turns muscles into stone
It stops you from ever resting
sci_vol_g1_body_medium_02.explanation: Water helps your body stay hydrated so cells and organs can do their jobs.
theoryLines: People need water every day.
Thirst is a signal that your body needs fluid.

sci_vol_g1_body_hard_01.stem: What do muscles help your body do?
options: Move body parts
Make sunlight for plants
Grow teeth made of wood
Stop all breathing forever
sci_vol_g1_body_hard_01.explanation: Muscles pull on bones and other parts so you can walk, lift, smile, and move in many ways.
theoryLines: Muscles work by tightening and relaxing.
Exercise helps keep muscles strong.

sci_vol_g1_body_hard_02.stem: What is an important job of bones in the body?
options: Support the body and protect soft organs
Digest food in the stomach
Carry smells to the nose
Make rain clouds form
sci_vol_g1_body_hard_02.explanation: Bones form the skeleton, which holds you up and helps protect parts such as the brain and heart.
theoryLines: The skeleton gives the body shape.
Bones and muscles work together for movement.

options: They move pollen so plants can make seeds
They turn petals into rocks
They remove all sunlight
They pump oxygen into the soil only
sci_vol_g1_animals_medium_01.explanation: Bees visit flowers and carry pollen, which helps plants reproduce.
theoryLines: Pollination is important for many fruits and seeds.
Bees are helpful insects in gardens and farms.

sci_vol_g1_animals_medium_02.stem: Why can camels live well in a hot desert?
options: Their bodies are adapted to save water and handle heat
They must swim every hour
They eat only ice cubes
They freeze solid each day
sci_vol_g1_animals_medium_02.explanation: Camels have adaptations such as storing fat and handling dry conditions that help them survive in deserts.
theoryLines: Desert animals often save water carefully.
Adaptations match an animal to its habitat.

sci_vol_g1_animals_hard_01.stem: Why is it helpful when many different animals live in a place?
options: A variety of living things helps keep nature systems healthier
Rain becomes unnecessary
Food disappears forever
Light stops reaching Earth
sci_vol_g1_animals_hard_01.explanation: Biodiversity means many kinds of living things. Together they support food webs and healthier habitats.
theoryLines: Different animals play different roles in nature.
Protecting habitats protects many species.

sci_vol_g1_animals_hard_02.stem: What makes a lion a predator?
options: It hunts and eats other animals
It makes food from sunlight
It only eats rocks and sand
It never needs food or water
sci_vol_g1_animals_hard_02.explanation: Lions catch prey for meat, so they are predators in their food chain.
theoryLines: Predators help control prey populations.
Lions are carnivores.

sci_vol_g1_plants_medium_01.stem: What can happen if a plant gets far too much water?
options: Roots can get too wet and the plant may become unhealthy
The plant always grows into a mountain
The plant never needs sunlight again
Leaves turn into solid metal
sci_vol_g1_plants_medium_01.explanation: Overwatering can keep roots from getting enough air and can harm the plant.
theoryLines: Plants need the right amount of water—not too little and not too much.
Healthy soil should not stay soggy all the time for most plants.

sci_vol_g1_plants_medium_02.stem: Why are some seeds shaped to catch the wind?
options: So they can travel to new places to grow
So they become heavier than stones
So animals cannot ever find food
So blood can flow through leaves
sci_vol_g1_plants_medium_02.explanation: Light, winged, or fluffy seeds can blow to new ground, helping plants spread.
theoryLines: Seed dispersal moves seeds away from the parent plant.
Wind is one way seeds travel.

sci_vol_g1_plants_hard_01.stem: What can grow from a seed inside a fruit?
options: A new plant
A cloud of only salt
A bone made of glass
A river of pure metal
sci_vol_g1_plants_hard_01.explanation: Seeds contain the start of a new plant. With water, warmth, and the right conditions, a seed can sprout.
theoryLines: Fruits often protect and help spread seeds.
Germination is when a seed begins to grow.

sci_vol_g1_plants_hard_02.stem: Why do plants grow toward the light?
options: Plants need light to make food through photosynthesis, so they grow toward it.
Plants need water, and water only comes from light.
Plants feel warmer near the light and prefer to stay warm.
Plants need light to pump nutrients through their stems.
sci_vol_g1_plants_hard_02.explanation: Plants grow toward light because they need it to carry out photosynthesis and make food. This behavior is called phototropism.

sci_vol_g2_body_medium_01.stem: What is the role of joints in your body?
options: Joints connect bones and allow your body to bend and move
Joints carry oxygen through the blood to all parts of your body
Joints filter waste out of your blood as it flows through them
Joints protect your teeth by absorbing shocks when you chew
sci_vol_g2_body_medium_01.explanation: Joints are the places where two bones meet. They allow your body to bend, twist, and move in different directions.

sci_vol_g2_body_medium_02.stem: What do the lungs do in the human body?
options: The lungs breathe in air and pass oxygen to the blood while removing carbon dioxide.
The lungs pump blood around the entire body.
The lungs filter old blood and produce new blood cells.
The lungs protect the heart from damage by surrounding it.
sci_vol_g2_body_medium_02.explanation: The lungs are responsible for gas exchange: they take in oxygen from the air and release carbon dioxide as a waste product. The oxygen passes into the blood.

sci_vol_g2_body_hard_01.stem: Why is it important to brush your teeth every day?
options: To remove food particles and harmful bacteria that can cause cavities and tooth decay.
To make your teeth grow longer and stronger more quickly.
To help your lungs breathe better throughout the day.
To help the heart pump blood more easily to the rest of the body.
sci_vol_g2_body_hard_01.explanation: Brushing your teeth removes food particles and bacteria. If left on the teeth, bacteria produce acids that cause cavities and tooth decay.

sci_vol_g2_body_hard_02.stem: Why is sleep important for your body?
options: It helps your body rest and recover
It digests food without any organs
It replaces circulating blood with air
It turns bones into rubber
sci_vol_g2_body_hard_02.explanation: During sleep, the body rests and recovers so you can grow, learn, and feel ready for a new day.
theoryLines: Kids need enough sleep each night.
Rest supports a healthy body and mind.

sci_vol_g2_experiments_easy_01.stem: Why do graphs need clear labels on the axes?
options: So readers know what the numbers and categories mean
So the graph can hide all of the data
So hypotheses become unnecessary
So experiments never need measuring
sci_vol_g2_experiments_easy_01.explanation: Axis labels tell people what was measured and how to read the graph correctly.
theoryLines: A graph is a picture of data.
