Clear labels make science communication easier.

sci_vol_g2_experiments_easy_02.stem: What is a beaker used for in many experiments?
options: Holding and pouring liquids carefully
Measuring the height of mountains only
Listening to animal sounds
Making shadows disappear
sci_vol_g2_experiments_easy_02.explanation: A beaker is a container for liquids during science investigations.
theoryLines: Lab tools help scientists handle materials safely.
Choose the right tool for the job.

sci_vol_g2_experiments_medium_01.stem: Which tool is best for measuring the length of a pencil?
options: A ruler
A thermometer
A magnet
A magnifying glass only
sci_vol_g2_experiments_medium_01.explanation: A ruler measures length in units such as centimeters or inches.
theoryLines: Different tools measure different properties.
Length is measured with a ruler or measuring tape.

sci_vol_g2_experiments_medium_02.stem: What is the dependent variable in an experiment?
options: What you measure to see the result of a change
The one thing you purposely change
A tool you never use
A safety rule about coats
sci_vol_g2_experiments_medium_02.explanation: The dependent variable is the outcome you measure after changing something else.
theoryLines: Independent variable: what you change.
Dependent variable: what you measure.

sci_vol_g2_experiments_hard_01.stem: What makes a good scientific observation?
options: Noticing and describing what you actually see or measure
Guessing a story with no evidence
Ignoring all data on purpose
Changing the results to look nicer
sci_vol_g2_experiments_hard_01.explanation: Observations are careful notes about what really happens, using senses and tools.
theoryLines: Observations come before conclusions.
Accurate observations help science stay honest.

options: Temperature
Length of a table
How heavy a rock is
How loud a sound is
sci_vol_g2_experiments_hard_02.explanation: A thermometer tells how hot or cold something is.
theoryLines: Temperature is measured in degrees.
Scientists choose tools that match what they want to measure.

sci_vol_g2_animals_medium_01.stem: Why do many birds build nests?
options: To keep eggs and chicks safer while they grow
To store sunlight inside feathers
To stop wind from ever blowing
To turn trees into oceans
sci_vol_g2_animals_medium_01.explanation: A nest is a sheltered place where birds can protect eggs and raise young.
theoryLines: Different birds build different kinds of nests.
Parent birds often care for chicks in the nest.

sci_vol_g2_animals_medium_02.stem: What can happen if prey animals become very numerous?
options: They may use up food and space more quickly
Forests instantly turn into deserts only from light
Water disappears from Earth forever
Predators stop needing energy
sci_vol_g2_animals_medium_02.explanation: Too many prey animals can strain food supplies and habitats until numbers fall again.
theoryLines: Populations depend on available resources.
Predators and food limits help balance ecosystems.

sci_vol_g2_animals_hard_01.stem: Why should people protect animal habitats?
options: Animals need places with food, water, and shelter to survive
Animals never use habitats at all
Protecting land removes all plants
Habitats are useful only for making noise
sci_vol_g2_animals_hard_01.explanation: When habitats are protected, animals can find what they need to live and raise young.
theoryLines: Habitat protection helps wildlife and people.
Loss of habitat is a major threat to animals.

sci_vol_g2_animals_hard_02.stem: What is a special feature of reptiles, like lizards and snakes?
options: Reptiles have dry, scaly skin that helps protect their bodies and conserve water.
Reptiles live only in the water and breathe through gills.
Reptiles have thick fur that keeps them warm in cold weather.
Reptiles keep their body temperature warm from the inside, just like humans.
sci_vol_g2_animals_hard_02.explanation: Reptiles are covered in dry, scaly skin that protects their bodies and reduces water loss. Unlike mammals, reptiles are cold-blooded and depend on their environment for warmth.

sci_vol_g2_plants_medium_01.stem: What is the main role of a fruit?
options: To hold and protect the plant's seeds and help spread them to new places.
To absorb water and minerals from the soil.
To capture sunlight and make food for the plant.
To carry out photosynthesis instead of the leaves.
sci_vol_g2_plants_medium_01.explanation: A fruit grows around the seeds of a flowering plant. Its job is to protect the seeds and help spread them. Animals eat the fruit and carry the seeds to new places in their droppings. Some fruits are designed to float on water or be blown by the wind.
theoryLines: Fruits develop from the flower of a plant after it has been pollinated.
Spreading seeds away from the parent plant gives new plants more space and resources to grow.

sci_vol_g2_plants_medium_02.stem: Why are plants called producers in a food chain?
options: They make food using sunlight
They hunt other plants for meat
They never need energy
They only live where animals cannot live
sci_vol_g2_plants_medium_02.explanation: Green plants use sunlight to make food, so they produce the energy that starts many food chains.
theoryLines: Photosynthesis lets plants make food.
Animals depend on plants, directly or indirectly, for food energy.

sci_vol_g2_plants_hard_01.stem: Where do many conifer trees keep their seeds?
options: In cones
Only inside metal boxes
Only under ocean waves
Only in animal fur forever
sci_vol_g2_plants_hard_01.explanation: Conifers such as pines produce cones that hold and protect seeds.
theoryLines: Conifers are trees that often stay green year-round.
Cones help release seeds when conditions are right.

sci_vol_g2_plants_hard_02.stem: Why should people not pick every wild flower they see?
options: Leaving flowers helps plants make seeds and support wildlife
Rain becomes harmful to plants
Flowers turn blood into water
Roots stop working if people walk nearby
sci_vol_g2_plants_hard_02.explanation: Flowers help plants reproduce. Taking too many can hurt plant populations and animals that use them.
theoryLines: Conservation means caring for living things and habitats.
Enjoy nature without taking more than you need.

sci_vol_g3_body_medium_01.stem: What does the circulatory system do?
options: It uses the heart to pump blood through the body, delivering oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
It breaks down food inside the stomach.
It supports the body through bones and cartilage.
It protects the body through the outer layer of skin.
sci_vol_g3_body_medium_01.explanation: The circulatory system is made up of the heart, blood vessels, and blood. The heart pumps blood through a network of blood vessels that reach every part of the body. Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to cells and collects waste products, like carbon dioxide, to be removed.
theoryLines: The heart is a muscular pump that beats continuously to keep blood moving.
Blood vessels include arteries, veins, and tiny capillaries that reach into every tissue.

sci_vol_g3_body_hard_01.stem: Which body system carries messages from the brain to the muscles?
options: The nervous system
The digestive system
The breathing system alone
The skeleton by itself
sci_vol_g3_body_hard_01.explanation: Nerve signals travel from the brain and spinal cord to muscles so you can move on purpose.
theoryLines: The nervous system controls communication in the body.
Muscles respond to nerve messages.

sci_vol_g3_body_hard_02.stem: What is the main job of the liver?
options: It cleans the blood by removing waste and harmful substances.
It helps the lungs take in more oxygen.
It produces light energy for the body to use.
It makes bones stronger by adding calcium.
sci_vol_g3_body_hard_02.explanation: The liver is one of the most important organs in the body. It filters the blood, breaks down harmful chemicals, and removes waste products. It also helps process the nutrients absorbed from food so cells can use them for energy and growth.
theoryLines: The liver is the largest internal organ in the human body.
The liver also produces bile, which helps the digestive system break down fats.

sci_vol_g3_experiments_easy_01.stem: What should you do before writing a final conclusion?
options: Look carefully at your observations and data
Ignore every measurement you made
Invent results without a test
Throw away the science notebook
sci_vol_g3_experiments_easy_01.explanation: A conclusion should be based on evidence gathered during the investigation.
theoryLines: Evidence supports scientific claims.
Conclusions come after collecting and checking data.

sci_vol_g3_experiments_easy_02.stem: What should you do if one measurement looks very different from the others?
options: Check it again and think about possible mistakes
Always delete all of your data
Change the hypothesis to match one odd number only
Stop using units forever
sci_vol_g3_experiments_easy_02.explanation: An outlier may be an error. Rechecking helps you decide whether to keep, fix, or explain the unusual result.
theoryLines: Careful checking improves data quality.
Repeating a measurement can reveal mistakes.

sci_vol_g3_experiments_hard_01.stem: What is a controlled variable in an experiment?
options: Something you keep the same on purpose
The result you hope to invent
A tool you refuse to use
A random guess with no plan
sci_vol_g3_experiments_hard_01.explanation: Controlled variables stay constant so the test is fair and only one main factor is being studied.
theoryLines: Fair tests control conditions carefully.
Keeping variables steady makes results clearer.

sci_vol_g3_experiments_hard_02.stem: Why do scientists use a control group?
options: To compare what happens without the tested change
To avoid collecting any evidence
To make every trial identical by magic
To replace measuring with guessing
sci_vol_g3_experiments_hard_02.explanation: A control group shows the normal result, so you can see the effect of the change you tested.
theoryLines: Comparison makes experimental results meaningful.
Controls help scientists trust their conclusions.

options: Plants such as grass
Only other cows
Only living metal
Only ocean salt
sci_vol_g3_animals_easy_01.explanation: Cows are herbivores, so their diet is mostly plants.
theoryLines: Herbivores eat plant material.
A cow's teeth help it chew tough plants.

sci_vol_g3_animals_easy_02.stem: Where do plants get the energy they use to make food?
options: From sunlight
From hunting animals
From drinking blood
From melting rocks only
sci_vol_g3_animals_easy_02.explanation: Plants capture sunlight and use it to make food during photosynthesis.
theoryLines: Sunlight is the energy source for most food chains.
Consumers depend on plant-made food energy.

sci_vol_g3_animals_hard_01.stem: How do fish get oxygen while living in water?
options: They take oxygen from water using gills
They breathe only dry desert air
They store sunlight in their fins
They never need oxygen at all
sci_vol_g3_animals_hard_01.explanation: Gills pull dissolved oxygen out of water so fish can live underwater.
theoryLines: Water contains dissolved oxygen.
Gills are breathing organs for fish.

sci_vol_g3_animals_hard_02.stem: Why are fins important for fish?
options: They help fish swim, steer, and keep balance
They turn water into dry land
They make fish breathe through feathers
They stop fish from ever moving
sci_vol_g3_animals_hard_02.explanation: Fins are body parts that help fish move through water and stay steady.
theoryLines: Different fins have different jobs in swimming.
Fish bodies are adapted for life in water.

sci_vol_g3_plants_easy_01.stem: Why do some trees shed their leaves in the fall?
options: To save water and energy during the cold, dark winter months
Because they receive too much sunlight during the summer
Because their roots stop producing new cells in the fall
All trees shed their leaves at exactly the same time every year
sci_vol_g3_plants_easy_01.explanation: Trees shed their leaves in fall to reduce water loss and save energy when sunlight is limited and temperatures drop in winter.

sci_vol_g3_plants_easy_02.stem: How can fertilizer help a plant?
options: It can add nutrients the plant needs to grow
It replaces sunlight completely
It stops roots from needing water
It turns leaves into animals
sci_vol_g3_plants_easy_02.explanation: Fertilizer supplies minerals and nutrients that support healthy plant growth when used carefully.
theoryLines: Plants take nutrients from the soil.
Too much fertilizer can harm plants and the environment.

sci_vol_g3_plants_hard_01.stem: What happens to a plant when it does not get enough water?
options: The plant wilts, stops growing, and may eventually die.
The plant grows taller to find rain coming from nearby mountains.
The plant produces more leaves to collect moisture from the air.
The plant grows its roots sideways toward other nearby plants.
sci_vol_g3_plants_hard_01.explanation: Water is essential for plants. Without enough water, a plant cannot carry out photosynthesis, its cells lose pressure, and it wilts. It may die if water is not provided.

sci_vol_g3_plants_hard_02.stem: How do green plants make sugars for food?
options: Through photosynthesis using light, water, and carbon dioxide
By hunting at night for meat
By freezing water into metal
By copying animal digestion only
sci_vol_g3_plants_hard_02.explanation: In photosynthesis, plants use sunlight to make sugars from water and carbon dioxide.
theoryLines: Photosynthesis happens mainly in green leaves.
The sugars plants make store energy.

sci_vol_g4_body_hard_01.stem: What is the main role of teeth in digestion?
options: To chew and break food into smaller pieces, making it easier to swallow and digest.
To breathe oxygen in and out of the mouth.
To pump blood through the digestive system.
To cool down hot food before you swallow it.
sci_vol_g4_body_hard_01.explanation: Teeth break food into smaller pieces through chewing. This mechanical breakdown is the first step in digestion and makes it easier for the stomach and intestines to process food.

sci_vol_g4_body_hard_02.stem: What happens when you take a deeper breath?
options: More air enters the lungs
Digestion suddenly stops forever
Blood disappears from the body
Bones stop supporting you
sci_vol_g4_body_hard_02.explanation: A deep breath fills the lungs with more air, bringing in more oxygen.
theoryLines: Lungs expand when you inhale.
Deeper breathing can help after hard exercise.

sci_vol_g4_experiments_easy_01.stem: Why do scientists often repeat a test several times?
options: To see if the results stay about the same
To avoid writing any notes
To change the question every second
To invent a new hypothesis without data
sci_vol_g4_experiments_easy_01.explanation: Repeating trials helps show whether findings are reliable.
theoryLines: Reliable results can be repeated.
One unusual trial might be a mistake.

sci_vol_g4_experiments_easy_02.stem: Why should you plan an experiment before you begin?
options: A plan helps you test your idea safely and clearly
Plans make measuring tools unnecessary
Plans erase the need for a hypothesis
Plans stop all observations
sci_vol_g4_experiments_easy_02.explanation: Planning helps you choose materials, steps, variables, and safety rules before you start.
theoryLines: A clear procedure makes experiments easier to follow.
Good plans improve fairness and safety.

sci_vol_g4_experiments_hard_01.stem: What is one useful job of a chart in an experiment?
options: It organizes data so patterns are easier to see
It replaces the need for any measurements
It becomes the hypothesis by itself
It makes conclusions without evidence
sci_vol_g4_experiments_hard_01.explanation: Charts and tables help scientists arrange numbers and observations clearly.
theoryLines: Organized data is easier to compare.
Graphs and charts communicate results to others.

sci_vol_g4_experiments_hard_02.stem: Why should you change only one variable at a time in an experiment?
options: So you can tell exactly which change caused the result, making the experiment fair.
So the experiment finishes as quickly as possible.
So that all variables increase at the same rate.
So the hypothesis is proven correct without needing any results.
sci_vol_g4_experiments_hard_02.explanation: If you change more than one thing at a time, you cannot know which change caused the result you observed. Changing only one variable while keeping everything else the same makes it a fair test. This is one of the most important rules of good experimental design.
theoryLines: A fair test means only the independent variable changes while all other conditions stay the same.
Experiments that change one variable at a time produce results that are easier to interpret and trust.

sci_vol_g4_animals_hard_01.stem: What is one clear difference between most birds and fish?
options: Birds have feathers, while fish have scales and gills
Birds breathe only with gills underwater
Fish grow feathers for flight
Neither group needs oxygen
sci_vol_g4_animals_hard_01.explanation: Birds are feathered animals that usually breathe air with lungs. Fish typically have scales and use gills in water.
theoryLines: Animal groups share sets of traits.
Comparing traits helps classify living things.

sci_vol_g4_animals_hard_02.stem: What is pollen's important role for flowering plants?
options: It helps plants reproduce by reaching other flowers
It turns roots into metal wires
It stops photosynthesis forever
It replaces water in every plant
sci_vol_g4_animals_hard_02.explanation: Pollen carries material needed for seed production when it moves to the right part of a flower.
theoryLines: Pollination is needed for many plants to make seeds.
Wind and animals can move pollen.

sci_vol_g5_body_easy_01.stem: Why does exercise help the heart stay healthy?
options: It gives the circulatory system a helpful workout
It stops blood from moving at all
It removes the need for oxygen
It turns the heart into bone
sci_vol_g5_body_easy_01.explanation: Regular activity makes the heart stronger so it can pump blood more effectively.
theoryLines: Exercise raises heart rate for a while.
A strong heart supports overall fitness.

sci_vol_g5_body_easy_02.stem: What do the kidneys do in the body?
options: They filter wastes from the blood
They pump air into the ears
They store sunlight under the skin
They digest food in the mouth
sci_vol_g5_body_easy_02.explanation: Kidneys clean the blood by removing wastes that leave the body as urine.
theoryLines: Kidneys help keep blood balanced.
The excretory system removes wastes.

sci_vol_g5_body_easy_03.stem: What can happen if the body does not get enough water?
options: A person can become dehydrated and feel unwell
Bones instantly turn to rubber
Breathing becomes unnecessary
Food energy stops mattering forever
sci_vol_g5_body_easy_03.explanation: Without enough water, the body cannot work well. Dehydration can cause thirst, tiredness, and other problems.
theoryLines: Water is essential every day.
Hot weather and exercise increase the need to drink.

sci_vol_g5_body_easy_04.stem: What does the circulatory system do?
options: It pumps blood carrying oxygen and nutrients to all parts of the body.
It contracts muscles to help the body move and exercise.
It moves air in and out of the lungs during breathing.
It connects bones together and allows the skeleton to move.
sci_vol_g5_body_easy_04.explanation: The circulatory system — made up of the heart, blood, and blood vessels — pumps blood to every cell in the body, delivering oxygen and nutrients while removing waste products.

sci_vol_g5_body_medium_01.stem: Why is eating a balanced diet important?
options: Different foods give the body a mix of nutrients it needs
Only one food group is ever useful
Food is unrelated to energy
Balanced meals stop all growth
sci_vol_g5_body_medium_01.explanation: A balanced diet includes a variety of foods that supply energy, vitamins, minerals, and other nutrients.
theoryLines: Fruits, vegetables, grains, proteins, and dairy can all play roles.
Good nutrition supports growth and health.

sci_vol_g5_body_medium_02.stem: What is the brain's main role in the body?
options: It is the control center for thinking, sensing, and movement
It digests all food by itself
It pumps blood like a second heart
It makes sunlight for the eyes
sci_vol_g5_body_medium_02.explanation: The brain receives information, makes decisions, and sends signals that guide the body.
theoryLines: The brain is part of the nervous system.
Learning and memory happen in the brain.

sci_vol_g5_body_hard_01.stem: Why should you warm up before intense exercise?
options: Warming up prepares muscles for harder work
It removes oxygen from the blood
It freezes joints solid
It stops the heart from beating
sci_vol_g5_body_hard_01.explanation: Light warm-up activity increases blood flow and gets muscles ready, which can lower the chance of strain.
theoryLines: Muscles work better when they are warmed up.
Safe exercise includes warm-up and cool-down time.

sci_vol_g5_body_hard_02.stem: What causes the strong urge to breathe when you hold your breath for a short time?
options: A buildup of carbon dioxide (CO₂) in your blood signals your brain to breathe
Your body completely runs out of oxygen and shuts down all processes
Your digestive system sends signals that interrupt the breathing reflex
Your skeleton becomes too heavy and presses on your lungs
sci_vol_g5_body_hard_02.explanation: When you hold your breath, CO₂ builds up in your blood. Sensors detect this and send a signal to your brain, which triggers the urge to breathe.

sci_vol_g5_experiments_easy_01.stem: Why should students not do risky experiments without adult supervision?
options: Safety rules and adult help prevent injuries
Adults remove the need for any data
Supervision makes measuring impossible
Safety rules hide all results
sci_vol_g5_experiments_easy_01.explanation: Some materials and tools can be dangerous. An adult helps keep the investigation safe.
theoryLines: Lab safety protects people and property.
Ask before using heat, chemicals, or sharp tools.

sci_vol_g5_experiments_easy_02.stem: What does it mean when another team can repeat your experiment and get a similar result?
options: Your result is more likely to be reliable
Your hypothesis must be false forever
Measuring tools are no longer needed
The experiment had no variables
sci_vol_g5_experiments_easy_02.explanation: Replication means others can get similar results, which builds confidence in the findings.
theoryLines: Science becomes stronger when results can be repeated.
Clear methods help other people replicate a test.

sci_vol_g5_experiments_medium_01.stem: Why should you wear safety goggles during a science experiment?
options: To protect your eyes from harmful chemicals or flying debris.
To get more oxygen while working with chemicals.
To keep your hands clean and avoid spreading germs.
Because all science experiments must be done outdoors.
sci_vol_g5_experiments_medium_01.explanation: Safety goggles protect your eyes from splashes, harmful chemicals, and any flying particles that might occur during an experiment.

sci_vol_g5_experiments_medium_02.stem: What should you do if your results do not support your hypothesis?
options: Accept the evidence and revise your thinking
Change the data until it matches the guess
Throw away the science notebook
Pretend the test never happened
sci_vol_g5_experiments_medium_02.explanation: A hypothesis is an idea to test. If evidence disagrees, scientists update their ideas.
theoryLines: Evidence matters more than being right the first time.
Learning from unexpected results is part of science.

options: A testable possible answer to a science question
A final conclusion with no evidence
A list of unrelated jokes
A broken measuring tool
sci_vol_g5_experiments_medium_03.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable possible answer to a science question. You check it with an experiment and evidence, so it is not a final conclusion or a random guess.
theoryLines: Hypotheses guide investigations before you collect results.
Evidence can support a hypothesis or show that it is not supported.

sci_vol_g5_animals_easy_01.stem: What makes amphibians unique in how and where they live?
options: They can live both in water and on land during their lifetime
They breathe only through gills for their entire life
They use only their lungs from the moment they hatch
They live exclusively in the driest desert environments
sci_vol_g5_animals_easy_01.explanation: Amphibians like frogs and salamanders hatch in water and breathe through gills, then develop lungs and can also live on land as adults.

sci_vol_g5_animals_easy_02.stem: How do bats often find insects in the dark?
options: They use echolocation with sound echoes
They read by bright sunlight only
They taste colors on leaves
They dig tunnels filled with fire
sci_vol_g5_animals_easy_02.explanation: Many bats send out sounds and listen for echoes bouncing off prey and objects.
theoryLines: Echolocation helps night hunters.
Bats are mammals that are often active after dark.

sci_vol_g5_animals_easy_03.stem: Why do snails often stay in damp places?
options: Moisture helps keep their soft bodies from drying out
They need dry sand to breathe
They melt if they touch water
They hunt only in bright deserts
sci_vol_g5_animals_easy_03.explanation: Snails have soft, moist bodies and can dry out if their surroundings are too dry.
theoryLines: Many soft-bodied animals need humid habitats.
A snail's slime also helps it move.

sci_vol_g5_animals_easy_04.stem: What kind of skeleton do many insects have?
options: An exoskeleton on the outside of the body
A skeleton made only of feathers
No support for the body at all
A wooden skeleton that grows leaves
sci_vol_g5_animals_easy_04.explanation: Insects have a hard outer covering called an exoskeleton that supports and protects them.
theoryLines: Exoskeletons are outside the body.
Humans have an endoskeleton inside the body.

sci_vol_g5_animals_medium_01.stem: Why is protecting habitats important for animals?
options: Animals need habitat resources like food, water, and shelter
Animals can live well with no habitat at all
Habitats are useful only for making noise
Protecting land removes all living things
sci_vol_g5_animals_medium_01.explanation: When habitats stay healthy, animals can find what they need to survive and reproduce.
theoryLines: Habitat loss threatens many species.
Conservation helps protect ecosystems.

sci_vol_g5_animals_medium_02.stem: Which sequence shows a butterfly's life cycle?
options: Egg, caterpillar, pupa, adult butterfly
Seed, root, flower, fruit only
Egg, adult bird, nest, feather
Tadpole, fish, shark, whale
sci_vol_g5_animals_medium_02.explanation: Butterflies go through complete metamorphosis: egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa, and adult.
theoryLines: Metamorphosis means a big change in body form.
Each stage has a different job in the life cycle.

sci_vol_g5_animals_hard_01.stem: What is one main job of a fish's fins?
options: Helping the fish move and stay balanced in water
Making feathers for flight
Producing pollen for flowers
Filtering blood like kidneys
sci_vol_g5_animals_hard_01.explanation: Fins help fish swim, turn, and keep steady in the water.
theoryLines: Fish are adapted for swimming.
Body shape and fins work together in water.

sci_vol_g5_animals_hard_02.stem: Which statement correctly compares birds and fish?
options: Most birds breathe air with lungs; fish usually use gills
Fish have feathers and fly long distances
Birds take oxygen only from underwater gills
Neither group can move from place to place
sci_vol_g5_animals_hard_02.explanation: Birds and fish are both animals, but they have different body features for different habitats.
theoryLines: Lungs and gills are different ways to get oxygen.
Traits help scientists sort animals into groups.

sci_vol_g6_body_medium_01.stem: Why is it important to brush your teeth at least twice a day?
options: Brushing removes bacteria and food particles that cause tooth decay and gum disease
Brushing helps the digestive system break down food faster in the stomach
Brushing increases the amount of air that flows into your lungs
Brushing increases blood flow to your brain and improves memory
sci_vol_g6_body_medium_01.explanation: Brushing your teeth removes harmful bacteria and food particles, preventing cavities and gum disease and keeping your mouth healthy.

sci_vol_g6_body_medium_02.stem: What is one important benefit of getting enough sleep?
options: The body can rest and recover for the next day
Digestion becomes unnecessary
Circulation permanently stops
Bones dissolve overnight
sci_vol_g6_body_medium_02.explanation: Sleep helps the body and brain recover so you can learn, grow, and stay healthy.
theoryLines: Kids generally need more sleep than adults.
Rest is part of a healthy lifestyle.

sci_vol_g6_body_hard_01.stem: Why should meals include a variety of healthy foods?
options: Different foods supply different nutrients the body needs
Eating only candy gives every nutrient
Food variety removes the need for water
Nutrients are unrelated to growth
sci_vol_g6_body_hard_01.explanation: A balanced diet provides proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, and minerals in useful amounts.
theoryLines: No single food has every nutrient you need.
Healthy eating supports energy and growth.

sci_vol_g6_body_hard_02.stem: What role do teeth play at the beginning of the digestive process, and why does this step matter for the rest of digestion?
options: They break food into smaller pieces, creating more surface area so digestive juices can work more efficiently throughout the digestive system.
They produce saliva on their own, and that saliva is the only chemical step needed before nutrients pass directly into the bloodstream.
They pump digestive acid upward from the stomach into the mouth to chemically soften food before it is swallowed.
They generate heat that warms and softens food so the small intestine can absorb it without any further breakdown.
sci_vol_g6_body_hard_02.explanation: Teeth chew and grind food into small pieces. This mechanical breakdown increases the total surface area of the food, which allows digestive juices — including enzymes in saliva and stomach acid — to reach more of the food and break it down more efficiently. Without this first step, chemical digestion would be much slower and less complete.
theoryLines: Digestion begins in the mouth: teeth provide mechanical breakdown while saliva begins chemical digestion of starches.
Breaking food into smaller pieces increases surface area, making it easier for digestive enzymes in the stomach and small intestine to do their work.

sci_vol_g6_experiments_medium_01.stem: If one data point is far from the others, what is a smart next step?
options: Recheck the measurement and look for errors
Delete the whole experiment instantly
Ignore units from then on
Invent a new planet to explain it
sci_vol_g6_experiments_medium_01.explanation: Unusual values may be mistakes. Checking again helps you decide what the data really show.
theoryLines: Careful review improves scientific trust.
Repeating a trial can confirm or correct a result.

options: Units tell what the number means so others can compare it
Units hide the true size of objects
Units make tools stop working
Units replace the need for safety
sci_vol_g6_experiments_medium_02.explanation: A number without a unit is unclear. Saying 5 centimeters is different from saying 5 kilograms.
theoryLines: Standard units help people share data.
Always write the unit with the number.

sci_vol_g6_experiments_medium_03.stem: What should a careful observation include?
options: Details about what you actually see, hear, or measure
Only opinions with no evidence
Changed numbers to look perfect
A conclusion written before any test
sci_vol_g6_experiments_medium_03.explanation: Good observations stick to evidence from senses and instruments.
theoryLines: Observations come first; conclusions come later.
Clear notes help other people understand your work.

sci_vol_g6_animals_easy_01.stem: What is a key trait that most reptiles share?
options: They have dry, scaly skin that helps prevent water loss
They live only in water and breathe through gills their whole life
They are warm-blooded and maintain a steady internal body temperature
They have thick fur that keeps their body warm in cold weather
sci_vol_g6_animals_easy_01.explanation: Reptiles are cold-blooded animals covered with dry, scaly skin. The scales help protect them and reduce water loss from their bodies.

sci_vol_g6_animals_easy_02.stem: Why are plants the starting point of many food chains?
options: They make food energy from sunlight
They hunt animals for every meal
They never take in water
They produce blood for consumers
sci_vol_g6_animals_easy_02.explanation: Plants are producers. Animals that eat plants, and animals that eat those animals, depend on that food energy.
theoryLines: Producers capture energy from the sun.
Consumers get energy by eating other living things.

sci_vol_g6_animals_easy_03.stem: How do fins help a fish survive?
options: They help the fish swim and keep its balance
They let the fish breathe on dry land only
They turn water into fresh air instantly
They grow feathers for flying
sci_vol_g6_animals_easy_03.explanation: Fins are swimming adaptations that help fish move through water.
theoryLines: Fish bodies are shaped for aquatic life.
Movement helps fish find food and escape danger.

sci_vol_g6_animals_easy_04.stem: Which trait belongs to birds but not to fish?
options: Feathers
Gills for underwater breathing
Scales covering the whole body
Living only underwater forever
sci_vol_g6_animals_easy_04.explanation: Feathers are a key bird trait. Fish typically have scales and use gills in water.
theoryLines: Comparing traits helps identify animal groups.
Birds and fish are adapted to different habitats.

sci_vol_g6_animals_hard_01.stem: Why is pollen important to flowering plants?
options: It is needed for plants to reproduce and make seeds
It cools the sun each night
It replaces soil for every root
It stops insects from visiting flowers
sci_vol_g6_animals_hard_01.explanation: When pollen reaches the right flower parts, seeds can form and a new plant generation can begin.
theoryLines: Pollination connects flowers for reproduction.
Bees and other animals often help move pollen.

sci_vol_g6_animals_hard_02.stem: Why is biodiversity valuable in an ecosystem?
options: Many kinds of living things help keep natural systems more stable
Having only one species is always better
Biodiversity removes all food webs
It stops plants from needing sunlight
sci_vol_g6_animals_hard_02.explanation: A rich mix of species supports food webs, recycling, and healthier habitats.
theoryLines: Biodiversity means variety of life.
Protecting habitats protects many species at once.

sci_g3_body_001.stem: Which organ do we mainly use to hear?
options: Ears
Eyes
Nose
Tongue
sci_g3_body_001.explanation: Ears collect sound and send hearing signals to the brain.
theoryLines: Hearing is one of the five senses.
Sound enters the ears and is interpreted by the brain.

sci_g3_body_002.stem: What is one important job of the skin?
options: It protects the body and helps you feel touch
It digests food in the stomach
It pumps blood like the heart
It makes all of your bones
sci_g3_body_002.explanation: Skin covers and protects the body. Nerve endings in skin help you sense touch, heat, and pain.
theoryLines: Skin is the body's outer covering.
Touch sensors in skin send messages to the brain.

sci_g3_body_003.stem: Which body part helps you taste food?
options: Tongue
Ears
Elbows
Knees
sci_g3_body_003.explanation: Taste buds on the tongue help you detect flavors such as sweet, salty, sour, and bitter.
theoryLines: Taste is one of the senses.
Smell and taste often work together.

options: Nose
Eyes
Feet
Stomach
sci_g3_body_004.explanation: The nose detects odors and sends smell information to the brain.
theoryLines: Smell helps you notice foods and dangers such as smoke.
Air carrying odor particles enters the nose.

sci_g3_body_005.stem: What happens to light after it enters your eyes?
options: Signals travel to the brain so you can see
The light digests food in the stomach
The light turns into sound in the ears
The light becomes blood in the heart
sci_g3_body_005.explanation: Eyes detect light and send nerve signals to the brain, which builds the images you see.
theoryLines: Vision depends on both the eyes and the brain.
The optic nerve carries visual signals.

sci_g3_body_006.stem: Why should you brush your teeth?
options: To help keep teeth clean and healthy
To make lungs breathe underwater
To stop bones from supporting you
To remove the need for food
sci_g3_body_006.explanation: Brushing removes food bits and plaque that can harm teeth and gums.
theoryLines: Dental hygiene protects teeth.
Healthy teeth help you chew food well.

sci_g3_body_007.stem: What is the main job of muscles?
options: They help the body move
They store unused air forever
They make sunlight for plants
They replace the skeleton completely
sci_g3_body_007.explanation: Muscles tighten and relax to move bones and other body parts.
theoryLines: Skeletal muscles work with bones.
You use muscles whenever you walk, jump, or smile.

sci_g3_body_008.stem: What do skeleton bones help do?
options: Support the body and protect soft organs
Digest meals by themselves
Carry smells into the lungs
Turn water into metal
sci_g3_body_008.explanation: Bones form a strong frame that holds you up and helps guard organs such as the brain.
theoryLines: The skeleton gives the body shape.
Bones and muscles work together for movement.

sci_g3_body_009.stem: Which organs are the main parts of the breathing system?
options: The lungs
The stomach only
The fingernails
The hair on your head
sci_g3_body_009.explanation: Air travels to the lungs, where oxygen enters the blood.
theoryLines: Breathing brings oxygen into the body.
The respiratory system includes airways and lungs.

options: It pumps blood through the body
It tastes food on the tongue
It grows new hair each hour
It stores leftover sunlight
sci_g3_body_010.explanation: The heart is a muscle that pushes blood so materials can travel to body cells.
theoryLines: Blood carries oxygen and nutrients.
A heartbeat keeps circulation moving.

sci_g3_body_011.stem: How does drinking water help the body?
options: It helps keep the body hydrated and working well
It replaces the need to sleep
It turns muscles into stone
It stops all sweating forever
sci_g3_body_011.explanation: Water supports many body processes and helps you stay healthy.
theoryLines: People need water every day.
Dehydration can make you feel tired or dizzy.

sci_g3_body_012.stem: Which habits help keep the body healthy?
options: Eating well, moving often, resting, and staying clean
Never drinking water
Skipping sleep every night
Avoiding all fruits and vegetables forever
sci_g3_body_012.explanation: Healthy routines support energy, growth, and strong body systems.
theoryLines: Lifestyle choices affect health.
Exercise, sleep, and nutrition work together.

sci_g3_body_013.stem: Why do you breathe faster after hard exercise?
options: The body needs more oxygen for working muscles
The stomach suddenly stops digesting
Bones need less blood
The eyes stop sending signals
sci_g3_body_013.explanation: Active muscles use more oxygen, so breathing and heart rate increase to deliver it.
theoryLines: Exercise raises the body's oxygen demand.
Faster breathing helps bring in more air.

sci_g3_body_014.stem: Which organ is an important part of the digestive system?
options: The stomach
The eyelashes
The fingernails
The outer ear only
sci_g3_body_014.explanation: The stomach helps break food down so nutrients can be absorbed later.
theoryLines: Digestion begins in the mouth and continues in the stomach and intestines.
Digestive organs work as a team.

sci_g3_body_015.stem: What does circulating blood mainly transport?
options: Oxygen and nutrients to body parts
Only unused rocks
Only sounds from outside
Only shadows from sunlight
sci_g3_body_015.explanation: Blood carries useful materials such as oxygen and nutrients, and it also helps remove wastes.
theoryLines: The circulatory system moves blood.
Cells need a steady delivery of oxygen and food energy.

sci_g3_body_016.stem: Why should you wash your hands before eating?
options: To help remove germs that could make you sick
To make food taste colder
To stop bones from growing
To replace brushing your teeth
sci_g3_body_016.explanation: Clean hands reduce the chance of spreading harmful microbes to your mouth and food.
theoryLines: Handwashing is a simple health habit.
Soap and water help remove dirt and germs.

sci_g3_body_017.stem: What does the brain do with messages from the senses?
options: It interprets them so you understand what you sense
It turns them into food for the stomach
It stores them only in the fingernails
It sends them to the hair to digest
sci_g3_body_017.explanation: Sense organs detect the world, and the brain makes meaning from those signals.
theoryLines: Seeing, hearing, smell, taste, and touch all involve the brain.
The nervous system links senses to thinking and action.

sci_g3_body_018.stem: What does a balanced diet provide?
options: A mix of nutrients the body needs to stay healthy
Only sugar and nothing else
A way to avoid all water
Energy that never comes from food
sci_g3_body_018.explanation: Eating different healthy foods supplies proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, and minerals.
theoryLines: Variety helps cover nutrient needs.
Good food choices support growth and energy.

sci_g3_body_019.stem: What do the lungs take into the blood?
options: Oxygen
Only undigested rocks
Only leftover light
Only sound waves
sci_g3_body_019.explanation: In the lungs, oxygen from air moves into the blood, and carbon dioxide leaves the blood to be exhaled.
theoryLines: Gas exchange happens in the lungs.
Oxygen is needed by body cells.

sci_g3_body_020.stem: Which structure helps protect the spinal cord and support the head and body?
options: The spine (backbone)
The tongue alone
The earlobes
The toenails
sci_g3_body_020.explanation: The backbone supports the body and helps protect the spinal cord.
theoryLines: Vertebrae are the bones of the spine.
Good posture helps protect the back.

sci_g3_body_021.stem: What often happens to your pulse after running hard?
options: It becomes faster
It disappears completely
It turns into a smell signal
It measures only eye color
sci_g3_body_021.explanation: During activity the heart beats faster, so the pulse rate rises.
theoryLines: Pulse is a sign of heart rate.
Resting brings the pulse back down.

sci_g3_body_022.stem: Why should you wear a helmet for biking or skating?
options: To help protect your head from injury
To make hearing louder
To digest food faster
To stop blood from circulating
sci_g3_body_022.explanation: A helmet cushions the head if you fall and helps prevent serious injuries.
theoryLines: The brain is protected by the skull and by safe habits.
Safety gear reduces risk during sports.

sci_g3_body_023.stem: What is one job of the liver?
options: It helps process materials in the blood
It pumps air into the ears
It stores unused sunlight
It replaces the skeleton
sci_g3_body_023.explanation: The liver has many jobs, including helping process nutrients and clean certain substances from the blood.
theoryLines: The liver is a large organ in the abdomen.
Body organs work together to keep you healthy.

sci_g3_body_024.stem: What does chewing food in the mouth help do?
options: Break food into smaller pieces for digestion
Turn food into pure oxygen
Send food straight into the lungs
Stop saliva from forming
sci_g3_body_024.explanation: Teeth cut and crush food so it is easier to swallow and digest.
theoryLines: Digestion begins in the mouth.
Saliva mixes with food while you chew.

sci_g3_body_025.stem: Which sentence about bones and muscles is true?
options: Muscles pull on bones to make movement
Bones digest food without muscles
Muscles replace blood vessels
Bones pump air into the stomach
sci_g3_body_025.explanation: When muscles contract, they pull on bones and body parts move.
theoryLines: Bones provide levers for movement.
Joints allow bones to move in different ways.

sci_g3_body_026.stem: Why does your body need rest after a long day?
options: Rest helps the body recover energy
Rest permanently stops breathing
Rest removes the need for water
Rest turns muscles into stone
sci_g3_body_026.explanation: Rest and sleep give your body time to recover so you feel ready again.
theoryLines: Being active uses energy.
Recovery is part of staying healthy.

sci_g3_body_027.stem: What is a healthy habit for your eyes?
options: Take breaks from screens and avoid staring at bright glare
Look directly at the sun for a long time
Rub dirt into your eyes each morning
Never blink during the day
sci_g3_body_027.explanation: Protecting eyes from strain and bright glare helps keep vision comfortable and safer.
theoryLines: Eyes are delicate sense organs.
Good lighting and breaks support eye comfort.

sci_g3_body_028.stem: What do the kidneys help remove from the blood?
options: Wastes that leave the body as urine
All of the body's oxygen forever
Every red blood cell permanently
Only unused sunlight
sci_g3_body_028.explanation: Kidneys filter blood and help form urine that carries wastes away.
theoryLines: Excretion removes wastes from the body.
Healthy kidneys support clean, balanced blood.

sci_g3_body_029.stem: Why is breakfast helpful for many kids?
options: It gives energy to start the day
It stops all learning at school
It removes the need to drink water
It freezes muscles until night
sci_g3_body_029.explanation: Eating in the morning provides fuel after a night without food.
theoryLines: Food supplies energy for activity and thinking.
A healthy breakfast can include fruits, grains, and protein foods.

sci_g3_body_030.stem: What is a reflex, such as pulling your hand away from something hot?
options: A quick automatic body response
A slow choice that always needs a long speech
A way bones digest food
A type of plant photosynthesis
sci_g3_body_030.explanation: Reflexes happen fast to protect the body, often before you think about them.
theoryLines: The nervous system controls reflex actions.
Reflexes help keep you safer.

sci_g3_body_031.stem: Which foods are especially helpful for strong bones because they provide calcium?
options: Milk, yogurt, and other calcium-rich foods
Only candy and soda
Only dry paper
Only pure salt water
sci_g3_body_031.explanation: Calcium helps build and maintain strong bones and teeth.
theoryLines: Dairy foods are common calcium sources.
Some leafy greens and fortified foods also provide calcium.

sci_g3_body_032.stem: What is true about sleep for growing kids?
options: Sleep helps the body grow and recover
Sleep is useless for health
Sleep replaces all food needs
Sleep stops the brain from learning forever
sci_g3_body_032.explanation: During sleep, the body repairs itself and supports growth and memory.
theoryLines: Kids usually need plenty of nighttime sleep.
A regular bedtime supports better rest.

sci_g3_body_033.stem: What does saliva help do in the mouth?
options: Moisten food and begin digestion
Pump blood to the toes
Create bone cells instantly
Turn air into solid metal
sci_g3_body_033.explanation: Saliva wets food and contains substances that start breaking some foods down.
theoryLines: Digestion begins before food reaches the stomach.
Chewing mixes food with saliva.

sci_g3_body_034.stem: What is a safe habit in the kitchen?
options: Ask an adult before using heat or sharp tools
Touch hot pans with bare hands
Run with knives for fun
Taste unknown cleaners
sci_g3_body_034.explanation: Kitchens have heat and sharp objects. Adult help and careful habits prevent injuries.
theoryLines: Safety rules protect people at home.
Hot surfaces and sharp tools need extra care.

sci_g3_body_035.stem: Why can very loud noise be harmful?
options: It can damage hearing over time
It makes bones grow faster forever
It improves digestion instantly
It turns eyes into ears
sci_g3_body_035.explanation: Loud sounds can hurt the delicate parts of the ear that help you hear.
theoryLines: Protect your ears in noisy places.
Hearing is precious and not always easy to repair.

sci_g3_body_036.stem: What does the nervous system send between the brain and the body?
options: Messages that control sensing and movement
Only leftover food scraps
Only unused sunlight
Only rainwater
sci_g3_body_036.explanation: Nerves carry signals so you can feel, think, and move.
theoryLines: The brain and nerves work together.
Fast signals help the body respond quickly.

sci_g3_body_037.stem: Why is regular exercise good for you?
options: It strengthens muscles and helps the heart
It removes the need to breathe
It stops blood from circulating
It replaces sleep completely
sci_g3_body_037.explanation: Being active builds fitness, supports the heart, and helps you feel stronger.
theoryLines: Exercise is part of a healthy lifestyle.
Different activities help the body in different ways.

sci_g3_body_038.stem: How can you protect your eyes outdoors on a very bright day?
options: Wear sunglasses and avoid staring at the sun
Look at the sun without blinking
Cover your eyes with muddy hands
Keep your eyes open underwater with soap
sci_g3_body_038.explanation: Bright sunlight can strain or harm eyes. Sunglasses and safe habits help protect vision.
theoryLines: Never look directly at the sun.
Eye protection is part of outdoor safety.

sci_g3_body_039.stem: Why do people shiver when they are cold?
options: Shivering muscle activity helps make heat
Shivering turns blood into ice on purpose
Shivering digests food faster than chewing
Shivering stops the need for warm clothes
sci_g3_body_039.explanation: Shivering is a body response that uses muscle movement to produce warmth.
theoryLines: The body tries to keep a steady temperature.
Warm clothing also helps in cold weather.

sci_g3_body_040.stem: Which organs are a major part of the body's waste-filtering system?
options: The kidneys
The eyebrows
The toenails
The earlobes
sci_g3_body_040.explanation: Kidneys filter wastes from blood and help make urine.
theoryLines: The excretory system removes wastes.
Healthy kidneys support internal balance.

sci_g3_body_041.stem: What is true about water loss on a hot day?
options: The body can lose more water through sweat
Hot weather removes the need to drink
Sweat adds unlimited water to the body
Heat freezes all body fluids
sci_g3_body_041.explanation: Sweating helps cool you, but it also means you need to replace lost fluids by drinking water.
theoryLines: Hot weather increases fluid needs.
Drinking water helps prevent dehydration.

sci_g3_body_042.stem: What is an important job of the small intestine?
options: Absorb digested nutrients into the blood
Pump air into the lungs
Store unused sunlight
Make all of the body's bones
sci_g3_body_042.explanation: After food is broken down, the small intestine absorbs nutrients so they can travel through the blood.
theoryLines: Digestion prepares nutrients for absorption.
Blood carries absorbed nutrients to cells.

sci_g3_body_043.stem: What is a healthy way to care for yourself when you have a cold?
options: Rest, drink fluids, and keep hands clean
Share drinks with everyone at school
Skip sleep for several nights
Rub dirt into your nose
sci_g3_body_043.explanation: Rest and fluids help your body recover. Clean hands help stop germs from spreading.
theoryLines: Hygiene helps protect you and others.
The body needs energy to fight illness.

sci_g3_body_044.stem: Why do hard-working muscles need more oxygen?
options: Active muscles use more oxygen to make energy
Oxygen paints muscles a new color
Muscles stop needing blood during exercise
Oxygen turns muscles into bone
sci_g3_body_044.explanation: When muscles work harder, they need more energy, so the body delivers more oxygen-rich blood.
theoryLines: Breathing and heart rate rise during exercise.
Oxygen helps release energy from nutrients.

sci_g3_body_045.stem: How does a child's brain help with learning?
options: It stores information and helps practice new skills
It digests homework paper for fuel
It pumps blood instead of the heart
It replaces the need for sleep and food
sci_g3_body_045.explanation: The brain learns by forming and strengthening connections as you practice and remember.
theoryLines: Learning happens in the nervous system.
Sleep and practice both support learning.

sci_g3_body_046.stem: Why are fruits and vegetables helpful in a daily diet?
options: They provide vitamins, minerals, and fiber
They remove all need for water
They replace oxygen in the lungs
They turn bones into rubber
sci_g3_body_046.explanation: Fruits and vegetables supply nutrients that support health and growth.
theoryLines: Colorful produce often means a variety of nutrients.
Fiber helps digestion.

sci_g3_body_047.stem: What does a clean bandage help do for a small cut?
options: Protect the wound while it heals
Stop blood from ever clotting
Replace the need to wash hands
Turn skin into bone overnight
sci_g3_body_047.explanation: A bandage keeps dirt out and helps protect the skin as it repairs itself.
theoryLines: Clean wounds carefully before covering them.
Ask an adult for help with deeper cuts.

sci_g3_body_048.stem: What does sweating help the body do in hot weather?
options: Cool down as sweat evaporates
Heat up as much as possible
Stop all blood flow
Digest food without saliva
sci_g3_body_048.explanation: When sweat evaporates from the skin, it helps lower body temperature.
theoryLines: Sweating is a cooling response.
Drinking water replaces fluids lost in sweat.

sci_g3_body_049.stem: How do you feel a gentle touch on your arm?
options: Skin sensors send messages to the brain
Bones taste the touch first
Hair digests the signal
Lungs pump the feeling into the stomach
sci_g3_body_049.explanation: Touch receptors in the skin detect contact and send nerve signals to the brain.
theoryLines: Touch is one of the senses.
The nervous system carries touch information.

sci_g3_body_050.stem: How do body systems work together?
options: They cooperate so the whole body can stay alive and active
Each system works alone and never interacts
Only one system is ever needed
Systems take turns disappearing each day
sci_g3_body_050.explanation: For example, lungs bring in oxygen, blood carries it, and muscles use it for energy.
theoryLines: Body systems are connected.
Teamwork among organs keeps you healthy.

sci_g3_body_051.stem: What can you observe about your pulse after jumping jacks?
options: It usually beats faster than at rest
It permanently disappears
It measures only hair length
It turns into a smell signal
sci_g3_body_051.explanation: Activity makes the heart work harder, so pulse rate increases for a while.
theoryLines: Pulse rate is a useful health observation.
After rest, pulse often returns toward normal.

sci_g3_body_052.stem: Why is good posture helpful for your back?
options: It supports the spine and can reduce strain
It stops bones from existing
It removes the need for muscles
It freezes joints permanently
sci_g3_body_052.explanation: Sitting and standing tall helps the backbone carry your body weight more comfortably.
theoryLines: The spine supports the head and trunk.
Strong core muscles also help posture.

options: A polished glass window
A piece of rough sandpaper
A gravel driveway
A pinecone covered with scales
sci_phb_g1_materials_med_01.explanation: Smooth materials feel even when you touch them. Glass is often smooth compared with sandpaper or gravel.
theoryLines: Texture describes how a surface feels.
Materials can be smooth or rough.

sci_phb_g1_materials_med_02.stem: What best describes the texture of a sponge when you touch it?
options: It is soft and can be squeezed easily
It is hard and cannot be bent or compressed
It is rough and sharp like coarse sandpaper
It feels like cold, smooth metal
sci_phb_g1_materials_med_02.explanation: A sponge is a soft material that can be easily squeezed and compressed because it contains many tiny holes filled with air.

sci_phb_g1_materials_med_03.stem: Which material often feels cold to the touch at room temperature?
options: Metal
A thick dry towel
A wool sweater
A foam pillow
sci_phb_g1_materials_med_03.explanation: Metal conducts heat away from your hand quickly, so it often feels cooler than cloth or foam.
theoryLines: Different materials feel different when touched.
Metals are good heat conductors.

sci_phb_g1_materials_med_04.stem: What kind of material is plastic?
options: A man-made material created from chemicals, not found naturally.
A natural material made directly from wood.
A material that comes from inside animals.
A material that is exactly the same as glass.
sci_phb_g1_materials_med_04.explanation: Plastic is a man-made material. It is manufactured from chemicals, many of which come from oil. Unlike wood or stone, plastic does not exist in nature — people invented and produce it. Plastic is lightweight, waterproof, and can be shaped into many different forms.
theoryLines: Most plastics are made from petroleum, a type of fossil fuel.
Because plastic does not break down easily in nature, it can pollute the environment for hundreds of years.

sci_phb_g1_materials_hard_01.stem: How can you compare which material is harder?
options: See which one scratches the other more easily
Weigh only their colors
Listen for the loudest shadow
Measure how sweet they taste
sci_phb_g1_materials_hard_01.explanation: Harder materials can scratch softer ones. A careful scratch test helps compare hardness.
theoryLines: Hardness is a property of materials.
Scientists compare properties with simple tests.

sci_phb_g1_materials_hard_02.stem: What happens to a soft sponge when you press down hard on it?
options: It changes shape while pressed but returns to its original shape when released
It breaks apart into tiny pieces that cannot be put back together
It hardens and becomes as stiff as a piece of metal
It always stays exactly the same shape no matter how hard you press
sci_phb_g1_materials_hard_02.explanation: A sponge is a soft, elastic material. When you press it, it compresses and changes shape, but it springs back to its original form when you let go.

sci_phb_g1_materials_hard_03.stem: How can you tell if a surface is rough?
options: It feels uneven and may create more friction
It always tastes salty
It becomes invisible in daylight
It melts at the sound of music
sci_phb_g1_materials_hard_03.explanation: Rough surfaces have bumps or texture you can feel, and they often grip more than smooth surfaces.
theoryLines: Friction is greater on many rough surfaces.
Touch is a useful way to observe texture.

sci_phb_g1_materials_hard_04.stem: Why do people use different materials for different objects?
options: Different materials have different useful properties
Every material behaves exactly the same
Materials have no properties at all
Objects never need matching materials
sci_phb_g1_materials_hard_04.explanation: We choose materials for strength, flexibility, waterproofing, weight, and other properties that fit the job.
theoryLines: Properties guide material choices.
A raincoat and a sponge are made for different needs.

sci_phb_g1_earth_space_med_01.stem: What does the sun give us during the daytime?
options: Light and warmth that let us see and keep Earth at a comfortable temperature
Cold winds and heavy rain that fall from the sky
Fresh drinking water that drips down from the clouds
Gravity that pulls all objects down to the ground
sci_phb_g1_earth_space_med_01.explanation: The sun provides light and heat during the day. Its light lets us see, and its warmth keeps the Earth at temperatures that support life.

options: An object blocking light
An object creating extra sunlight
Sound bouncing off a wall
Wind spinning in a circle
sci_phb_g1_earth_space_med_02.explanation: When light cannot pass through an object, a darker shape called a shadow forms behind it.
theoryLines: Light travels in straight lines.
Opaque objects block light and cast shadows.

sci_phb_g1_earth_space_med_03.stem: When does outdoor weather usually feel coldest?
options: In winter in many places
Only at noon in midsummer
Only during a heat wave
Only when the sun is closest at midnight
sci_phb_g1_earth_space_med_03.explanation: In many regions, winter brings colder temperatures than other seasons.
theoryLines: Seasons change temperature patterns.
People dress warmly for cold weather.

sci_phb_g1_earth_space_med_04.stem: What can you often see in the night sky?
options: The Moon and stars
Only ocean waves
Only underground roots
Only classroom chalkboards
sci_phb_g1_earth_space_med_04.explanation: At night the sky looks dark, and the Moon and stars are easier to notice.
theoryLines: The Moon reflects sunlight.
Stars are distant suns that look like points of light.

sci_phb_g1_earth_space_hard_01.stem: Why do we have day and night on Earth?
options: Earth spins on its axis, so different sides face the Sun at different times
The Moon moves in front of the Sun to create nighttime
The Sun travels all the way around Earth once every 24 hours
Thick clouds block all sunlight and cause complete darkness at night
sci_phb_g1_earth_space_hard_01.explanation: Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun experiences day, and the side facing away experiences night.

sci_phb_g1_earth_space_hard_02.stem: What can thick clouds do to sunlight during the day?
options: Block some light and make the ground look dimmer
Turn the sun into the Moon
Stop Earth from rotating
Make shadows impossible forever
sci_phb_g1_earth_space_hard_02.explanation: Cloud cover can reduce the sunlight that reaches the ground, so a day may look gray and less bright.
theoryLines: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals.
Weather can change how much sunlight we receive.

sci_phb_g1_earth_space_hard_03.stem: Why does summer feel hotter than other seasons?
options: The Sun stays up longer and shines more directly, bringing extra light and warmth.
The Sun moves much closer to Earth and becomes visibly larger in summer.
The Moon reflects extra sunlight in summer to make the weather warmer.
It always rains in summer, and rain traps heat in the air.
sci_phb_g1_earth_space_hard_03.explanation: In summer, the part of Earth you live on is tilted toward the Sun. This means the Sun is higher in the sky, its rays hit the ground more directly, and it stays up for more hours each day. More direct sunlight over a longer time means more heat.
theoryLines: Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun, is what causes the seasons.
When the Northern Hemisphere has summer, the Southern Hemisphere has winter, and vice versa.

sci_phb_g1_earth_space_hard_04.stem: Why do we wear a raincoat when it rains?
options: To keep our body dry and protected from getting wet in the rain.
To see the Moon more clearly through the rainy clouds.
To help Earth absorb rainwater faster into the ground.
To make rain fall more slowly and gently.
sci_phb_g1_earth_space_hard_04.explanation: We wear a raincoat so rain does not soak our body and clothes. The waterproof material keeps us dry and protected while it is raining.
theoryLines: Waterproof materials make water run off instead of soaking in.
We choose clothes that match the weather to stay comfortable and protected.

sci_phb_g1_environment_med_01.stem: Why is it important to put trash in a trash bin?
options: It keeps our surroundings clean and prevents animals from getting hurt by litter
Trash bins are only decoration and do not actually help the environment
Leaving trash outside is fine because rain washes it all away quickly
The sun will break down all garbage outdoors before it causes any harm
sci_phb_g1_environment_med_01.explanation: Throwing trash in a bin keeps the environment clean, prevents animals from eating harmful waste, and stops litter from polluting soil and water.

sci_phb_g1_environment_med_02.stem: What do plants need to grow and stay healthy?
options: Water and sunlight
Only packaged nutrients bought from a store
Salt water and deep shade to grow well
Sand and freezing cold weather to survive
sci_phb_g1_environment_med_02.explanation: Plants need water and sunlight to carry out photosynthesis, the process they use to make their own food and grow.

sci_phb_g1_environment_med_03.stem: Why should muddy boots stay off classroom carpets?
options: Mud can dirty the floor and make cleanup harder
Mud makes math problems easier
Mud replaces the need for books
Mud turns desks into trees
sci_phb_g1_environment_med_03.explanation: Keeping mud outside helps the classroom stay clean and safe to walk in.
theoryLines: Caring for shared spaces is part of responsibility.
Dirt tracked indoors creates more work for everyone.

sci_phb_g1_environment_med_04.stem: What do animals need from the place where they live?
options: Food, water, shelter, and enough space to survive
Only sunlight and fresh air to stay alive
A large open ocean and constant rainfall
Large numbers of the same kind of animal living very close together
sci_phb_g1_environment_med_04.explanation: Animals need food, water, shelter, and space in their habitat to meet their basic survival needs and raise their young.

sci_phb_g1_environment_hard_01.stem: Why is it important to save water and not waste it?
options: Fresh water is a limited resource and all living things need it to survive
There is so much water on Earth that it can never run out
Saving water and saving sunlight are exactly the same thing
Water only comes from rivers and cannot be found underground or recycled
sci_phb_g1_environment_hard_01.explanation: Although Earth has a lot of water, only a small amount is fresh and clean enough for living things to use, so it is important to use it carefully.

sci_phb_g1_environment_hard_02.stem: What can litter do if it ends up in the sea?
options: Harm water, animals, and coastal places
Automatically clean the ocean
Feed every fish a healthy meal
Turn salt water into fresh juice
sci_phb_g1_environment_hard_02.explanation: Trash in the ocean can injure animals and pollute habitats.
theoryLines: People should dispose of trash properly.
Protecting oceans protects wildlife.

sci_phb_g1_environment_hard_03.stem: Why are trees in a park helpful?
options: They give shade, homes for animals, and fresher air
They remove all need for water on Earth
They stop seasons from changing
They turn playgrounds into deserts
sci_phb_g1_environment_hard_03.explanation: Trees provide shade, shelter, and oxygen while making parks nicer places to visit.
theoryLines: Plants support healthy environments.
Parks need care so living things can thrive.

sci_phb_g1_environment_hard_04.stem: What should visitors do when they enjoy a nature area?
options: Leave plants and animals alone and take trash with them
Carve names into every tree
Leave food wrappers on trails
Chase wildlife for fun
sci_phb_g1_environment_hard_04.explanation: Respectful visitors protect habitats so other people and wildlife can enjoy them too.
theoryLines: Leave no trash behind.
Nature places stay healthier when people are careful.

sci_phb_g2_materials_hard_01.stem: How does metal differ from wood when it comes to conducting heat?
options: Metal conducts heat much better than wood does
Wood always conducts heat better than any other material
Metal and wood conduct heat in exactly the same way
Wood melts and turns into a liquid when heated, but metal stays solid
sci_phb_g2_materials_hard_01.explanation: Metal is an excellent conductor of heat, while wood is a poor conductor. That is why a metal spoon heats up quickly in hot soup but a wooden spoon stays cool.

sci_phb_g2_materials_hard_02.stem: How can you tell that a material is transparent?
options: Light can pass through it clearly
It always feels sticky
It blocks every bit of light
It melts only when you whisper
sci_phb_g2_materials_hard_02.explanation: Transparent materials such as clear glass or clear plastic let you see through them.
theoryLines: Transparent, translucent, and opaque describe how light passes through materials.
Windows are often made of transparent material.

sci_phb_g2_materials_hard_03.stem: Why is plastic often used for light containers and toys?
options: It can be lightweight, strong, and easy to shape
It always dissolves in cold water instantly
It is the heaviest material on Earth
It can only be used for cooking pans
sci_phb_g2_materials_hard_03.explanation: Plastic's properties make it useful for many everyday objects that should not be too heavy.
theoryLines: Material properties guide how we use materials.
Plastics should be recycled or disposed of responsibly.

sci_phb_g2_materials_hard_04.stem: What can happen to wax when it is heated?
options: It can melt from a solid into a liquid
It turns into a living plant
It becomes colder than ice automatically
It changes into pure metal
sci_phb_g2_materials_hard_04.explanation: Heating can change wax from solid to liquid. This is a physical change of state.
theoryLines: Solids can melt when they gain enough heat.
Cooling can make melted wax become solid again.

sci_phb_g2_earth_space_med_01.stem: What is a sign that it might rain soon?
options: Dark clouds gathering in the sky, filled with water droplets.
A bright, clear Moon visible during the day.
A perfectly blue sky with no clouds in sight.
Stars appearing in the sky during the afternoon.
sci_phb_g2_earth_space_med_01.explanation: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. When clouds become dark and thick, they hold a lot of water. That is a sign that the water may fall as rain. Watching cloud shapes and colors is one way to predict the weather.
theoryLines: Dark, heavy clouds are often a sign that rain is on its way.
Meteorologists — weather scientists — use clouds, temperature, and air pressure to forecast the weather.

options: Moving air
Silent moonlight only
Underground roots growing
Shadows walking by themselves
sci_phb_g2_earth_space_med_02.explanation: Wind is air in motion, often caused by uneven heating of Earth's surface.
theoryLines: Warm air and cool air can help create wind.
Wind is part of everyday weather.

sci_phb_g2_earth_space_hard_01.stem: Why do we experience different seasons throughout the year?
options: Earth’s tilted axis causes different regions to receive more or less sunlight as it orbits the Sun
The Moon moves closer to Earth in summer and farther away in winter
Ocean currents change the temperature of the entire planet each season
The Sun orbits Earth at different speeds during different times of year
sci_phb_g2_earth_space_hard_01.explanation: Earth’s axis is tilted, so as it orbits the Sun, the Northern and Southern Hemispheres take turns being tilted toward the Sun, causing the seasons.

sci_phb_g2_earth_space_hard_02.stem: What happens to a puddle of water on a warm, sunny day?
options: The heat from the sun causes the water to evaporate and turn into water vapor in the air
The water sinks straight down into the ground and is gone forever
The puddle grows larger because sunlight creates extra water
Sunlight hardens the surface of the puddle so it stays as a permanent solid
sci_phb_g2_earth_space_hard_02.explanation: Heat from the sun gives water molecules enough energy to escape from the liquid surface and rise into the air as invisible water vapor. This is called evaporation.

sci_phb_g2_earth_space_hard_03.stem: Why does the Dead Sea feel so salty?
options: It contains a very large amount of dissolved salt
It is made of pure melted sugar
It has no minerals at all
It freezes every afternoon
sci_phb_g2_earth_space_hard_03.explanation: The Dead Sea is extremely salty because lots of salt stays dissolved in its water.
theoryLines: Some lakes and seas have different amounts of salt.
Salty water can make floating feel easier.

sci_phb_g2_earth_space_hard_04.stem: What role do clouds play in weather?
options: Clouds hold water droplets and can bring rain, snow, or shade.
Clouds reflect starlight to make the night sky brighter.
Clouds block the Sun completely and are the main cause of night.
Clouds produce sunlight and spread it across Earth's surface.
sci_phb_g2_earth_space_hard_04.explanation: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals floating in the air. When enough droplets collect together, they become heavy and fall as rain or snow. Clouds also block sunlight, which can make a day feel cooler and darker — an important part of Earth's weather system.
theoryLines: The water cycle — evaporation, condensation, and precipitation — is what forms clouds and brings rain.
Different cloud types, such as cumulus and stratus, are linked to different types of weather.

sci_phb_g2_environment_med_01.stem: Why should empty bottles be recycled when possible?
options: Recycling helps reuse materials and reduce waste
Recycling makes litter grow faster
Recycling removes all oxygen from air
Recycling turns parks into deserts
sci_phb_g2_environment_med_01.explanation: Recycling keeps useful materials in use and can reduce trash that harms the environment.
theoryLines: Reduce, reuse, and recycle help the planet.
Sorting recyclables correctly matters.

sci_phb_g2_environment_hard_01.stem: Why is burning trash outdoors a poor idea?
options: It can release harmful smoke into the air
It always cleans the atmosphere
It creates only pure drinking water
It helps every animal breathe better
sci_phb_g2_environment_hard_01.explanation: Burning waste can pollute air and create unsafe fumes.
theoryLines: Clean air supports healthy people and wildlife.
Dispose of trash through safe, approved methods.

sci_phb_g2_environment_hard_02.stem: What can pollution do to a stream?
options: Make the water unsafe for living things
Automatically create more freshwater fish
Turn the stream into solid gold
Remove the need for clean habitats
sci_phb_g2_environment_hard_02.explanation: Chemicals, trash, and other pollutants can harm plants, animals, and people who depend on clean water.
theoryLines: Clean water is an important natural resource.
Preventing pollution protects ecosystems.

options: Trees provide oxygen, shade, and homes for wildlife
Trees remove all soil from Earth
Trees stop rain from ever falling
Trees replace the need for sunlight
sci_phb_g2_environment_hard_03.explanation: Trees help the environment by making oxygen, giving shade, and supporting animals.
theoryLines: Plants release oxygen that animals need.
Tree planting is a helpful conservation action.

sci_phb_g2_environment_hard_04.stem: What do ants do to help other ants find food they have discovered?
options: They leave a chemical scent trail so other ants can follow the path to the food
They make loud sounds to call all the other ants to the food
They carry the food back silently without communicating with the colony
They build a wall around the food to block other animals from reaching it
sci_phb_g2_environment_hard_04.explanation: Ants leave a pheromone (chemical scent) trail from the food back to the nest. Other ants follow this invisible trail to find and collect the food.

sci_phb_g3_materials_eas_01.stem: Which material is a good conductor of electricity?
options: Metal such as copper
Dry wood
Rubber
Plastic wrap
sci_phb_g3_materials_eas_01.explanation: Metals allow electric current to flow easily, so they are used in wires.
theoryLines: Conductors let electricity pass through.
Insulators such as rubber resist electric flow.

sci_phb_g3_materials_eas_02.stem: What state of matter is water normally found in at room temperature?
options: Liquid
Solid
Gas
Plasma
sci_phb_g3_materials_eas_02.explanation: At room temperature, water is a liquid. It becomes ice (solid) when cooled below 32°F (0°C) and turns to steam (gas) when heated above 212°F (100°C).

sci_phb_g3_materials_hard_01.stem: What usually makes an ice cube melt faster?
options: Warmer surroundings
Putting it in a colder freezer
Keeping it away from all heat forever
Wrapping it in thicker ice
sci_phb_g3_materials_hard_01.explanation: Heat energy makes ice melt. A warmer place transfers heat more quickly to the ice.
theoryLines: Melting is a change from solid to liquid.
Temperature affects how fast ice melts.

sci_phb_g3_materials_hard_02.stem: What is the difference between a physical change and a chemical change?
options: A physical change may alter form, while a chemical change makes a new substance
Physical changes always create brand-new elements
Chemical changes never happen in kitchens
Melting iron is always a chemical change into wood
sci_phb_g3_materials_hard_02.explanation: Melting and tearing are physical changes. Burning wood is a chemical change because new substances form.
theoryLines: Physical changes do not make a new kind of matter.
Chemical changes rearrange matter into new materials.

options: Earth rotating so that our part of the planet faces toward the Sun.
The Moon moving in front of the Sun and reflecting light downward.
The Sun traveling around Earth once every 24 hours.
Rain clouds moving away to let sunlight through.
sci_phb_g3_earth_space_eas_01.explanation: Earth spins on its own axis once every 24 hours. When the part of Earth where you live turns to face the Sun, sunlight reaches you and it becomes daytime. As Earth continues spinning, that same part faces away from the Sun and it becomes night.
theoryLines: Earth's rotation — its spin on its axis — is what creates the cycle of day and night.
The Sun does not move around Earth; Earth's spin just makes it look that way from the ground.

sci_phb_g3_earth_space_eas_02.stem: Where does the Moon's light come from?
options: It reflects light from the Sun
It makes its own fire like a campfire
It glows using ocean salt only
It borrows light from Earth's core
sci_phb_g3_earth_space_eas_02.explanation: The Moon does not produce its own visible light. We see sunlight bouncing off its surface.
theoryLines: The Moon can look bright even though it reflects sunlight.
Moon phases depend on how we see the lit side.

sci_phb_g3_earth_space_hard_01.stem: Why are places near the Mediterranean Sea often milder than inland deserts?
options: Nearby seas help moderate temperature
Deserts are always next to glaciers
Oceans remove all sunlight
Sand creates tropical rain every hour
sci_phb_g3_earth_space_hard_01.explanation: Large bodies of water heat and cool more slowly than land, so coastal climates are often milder.
theoryLines: Geography affects climate.
Water can reduce extreme temperature swings.

sci_phb_g3_earth_space_hard_02.stem: What is condensation in the water cycle?
options: Water vapor cooling and forming tiny liquid droplets
Ice turning instantly into solid metal
Rocks dissolving into pure oxygen
Sunlight freezing into snowflakes
sci_phb_g3_earth_space_hard_02.explanation: When cooled water vapor becomes liquid droplets, clouds or dew can form.
theoryLines: Condensation is the opposite of evaporation.
Clouds often form by condensation in the air.

sci_phb_g3_environment_eas_01.stem: What usually starts a simple food chain?
options: Plants that make food from sunlight
Lions that eat only rocks
Clouds that hunt insects
Cars that grow leaves
sci_phb_g3_environment_eas_01.explanation: Producers such as plants capture sunlight and provide food energy for consumers.
theoryLines: Food chains show who eats whom.
Energy flows from producers to consumers.

options: It saves materials and can reduce waste
It makes trees disappear faster on purpose
It pollutes rivers automatically
